The rest of taxi, ground operations, and return to 13L for takeoff were uneventful with the following exception: all communications from Tower, although a different voice assumed to be a supervisor, continued to contain LOTS of urgency in voice, words, and tone from both Ground and Tower Controllers to all aircraft. When conducting single runway operations, especially during deteriorating weather conditions, Ground and Tower Controllers should make a conscious effort to avoid speaking too fast and share information when similar sounding flight numbers are on frequency. When recognized Controller saturation and urgency, we can increase our guard and awareness against expectation bias. Additionally, we could possibly slow the cadence when appropriate while reading back clearances. Scenario in DAL wasn't optimum. Runway change had just occurred due to winds out of limits. 13R closed. Winds shifting and Rain/low visibility to the south of field. During taxi, four to five Aircraft are shutdown on Taxiway B due to weather at east gates. Six Aircraft shutdown on M for the same reason. Taxi instructions for Aircraft X, 'Taxi to 13L via B hold short of M5;' given initially. EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time) time now given (not known prior to this) by Ground of (time) void by (time). Ground then gave us hold short 13L at M5. Cross 13L, A5, A, 13L, contact Tower. Corporate jet in hold area just north of Taxiway A, approaching 13L holding short. Ground Controller and Tower Controller sounded rushed / voice inflection during transmissions from taxi out to this point with all aircraft. Tower Controller stated, 'Aircraft X, lineup and wait Runway 13L.' F/O read back instructions to Controller verbatim, to lineup and wait 13L, with no response from ATC which seemed normal. 'Before Takeoff Checklists complete, final clear, 13L verified;' and I looked right, to double check final clear, rounding corner on A I looked left and saw a Company aircraft rounding corner on M6 toward 13L with LUAW (Lineup and Wait) Lights configured. I stated this to F/O, while simultaneously stopping aircraft at 45 degrees facing 290 degree estimate, just past the hold short line. Tower Controller then cleared other Company aircraft for takeoff 13L. He then stated to us 'Aircraft X, it appears you're past hold short line, taxi without delay across 13L to B, contact Ground and we will get you right back out. Never heard COMM jam or readback from other Aircraft X. When we were cleared LUAW and we read it back (all sounded normal in headset and transmission) and therefore I don't know how I could have prevented mistake. First time we knew of other Company aircraft call sign was when Tower cleared the aircraft for takeoff. The rest of DAL Ground Ops through departure phase was uneventful. Runway change / single runway operations / weather changing / departure gate closed, definitely played into non-standard operations both for ATC and Aircrew. Similar call signs should have been noted or announced by ATC to help prevent any confusion on ATC to aircraft instructions. Cadence and voice inflection are critical components in managing risk during less than optimal conditions for ATC. Although the task loading and pace for our phase of flight and internal communications did not feel rushed, the additive conditions, especially late notice EDCT could have contributed. When I recognized Controller saturation potential and their urgency, we could have slowed down our transmissions and pace or have been more directive to them to slow down. Not only our craft, but all the aircraft that were on the taxi, could have helped slow things a bit.
ASRS:1804662.s: During single runway operations in deteriorating weather, a pilot stopped after receiving a lineup and wait clearance due to visual conflict with another aircraft displaying similar lights. The other aircraft was subsequently cleared for takeoff, and the pilot was instructed to cross the runway, highlighting risks from controller urgency and similar call signs.

ASRS:1804712.n: Flight was scheduled to depart ZZZ. We arrived in the flight deck and performed all the normal procedures we have for a normal push back. Captain did the preflight walk around and I loaded the FMC. We agreed the OFP (Operational Flight Plan) looked good and the rest of the flight plan looked sufficient for a potentially bumpy ride to ZZZ1. Captain advised to Flight Attendants to stay seated out of ZZZ until we knew the ride would allow for their safe duties. I was the flying pilot and after Captain did his first flight of the day and PM (Pilot Monitoring) duty brief, I briefed the SID. We planned for a normal pushback with 2 engine start for a quick taxi for departure. We performed the BEFORE TAKEOFF CHECKLIST on taxi out down the ramp for takeoff on runway XX.While we were taxiing down to runway XX, I noticed there was a split between the L and R duct pressure. I made note of it to Captain and we briefly discussed these splits we have seen before in this aircraft and recall it being a known normal occurrence. I cycled the L PACK (Left) switch to OFF and back to AUTO as well as the ISOLATION VALVE switch to OPEN and AUTO and saw the duct pressure needles sync together. We decided it would be a safe action to depart and noted we would keep an eye on the duct pressure and pressurization.We departed runway XX and CLIMBED VIA THE SID. I hand flew the departure to the mid 20s and then turned the autopilot on. I noted Captain mentioned 2 different times that the aircraft was pressurizing normally though the duct pressure still was split. The ride was mostly good and the flight attendants were up but the seat belt was still on. As we approached our level off altitude of FL340 the CABIN ALTITUDE horn and the MASTER WARNING lights illuminated. We verified the CABIN ALTITUDE was high on the pressurization panel and performed the Immediate Action items for CABIN ALTITUDE WARNING OR RAPID DEPRESSURIZATION/EMERGENCY DESCENT. The CABIN ALTITUDE was not controllable, and we continued with the descent. There was a definite issue with immediate communication over the inter-phone with the masks on and all the noise. Getting the mask on and the audio panel correct to be able to speak and hear over the speaker poses a threat in this airplane if not practiced. We were able to communicate with each other and ATC but it was challenging with all the noise and distractions.Captain identified as a priority flight with ZZZ Center and we began the initial descent over the mountains. I initially turned off the AUTOPILOT to pitch over and begin the procedure. Once we were established in a descent, I turned the AUTOPILOT back on and descended to FL190 with the high terrain in mind. We saw an aircraft below us on the TCAS and had to shallow the descent initially before we were cleared lower. Captain proceeded with completing the checklist and communicating with the Flight attendants, passengers, and dispatch. Descending through approximately 16,000 feet I noticed the CABIN ALTITUDE was in a normal range of around 7,000 feet and we took off the oxygen masks. We leveled off at 11000 in the vicinity of ZZZ2. Initially we were planning on diverting to ZZZ2 because we were so close, but Captain's experience and familiarity with ZZZ3. This led to the decision to divert and there was difficulty communicating with dispatch possibly due to our low altitude so we opted to landing in ZZZ3. The flight attendants and passengers were all briefed for the diversion to ZZZ3. I left the AUTOPILOT on and we flew the RNAV (GPS) Runway XY 29 approach and landing. All checklists were completed before ZZZZZ intersection and the landing was normal. CFR ( Aircraft Rescue & Firefighting) was there upon arrival.We were parked at the hard stand in ZZZ3 and the ramp personnel brought over the ramp to allow the passengers to vacate the aircraft. Operations were there to help while we figured out the plan of action for the passengers. Captain discussed the situation with the ChiefPilot, Dispatch, and Maintenance and I aided the flight attendants with passengers. I walked to the OUTFLOW VALVE and noted a mesh substance blocking the OUTFLOW VALVE from fully closing. Captain manually opened and closed the valve and I videoed the movement.
ASRS:1804712.s: The flight crew experienced an uncontrolled cabin altitude increase during climb to FL340 due to a mesh blockage in the outflow valve. They executed an emergency descent to 11,000 feet and diverted to ZZZ3 for a safe landing after maintenance confirmed the valve obstruction.

ASRS:1804737.n: On Departure out of ZZZ the crew experienced significant audio distortions on COMM 1. Switched to COMM 2. In the vicinity of ZZZ1 contact was lost with ATC for a period of approximately 10 minutes. ACARS was also lost at this time. Upon reestablishing contact ATC was able to hear the crew loud and clear but on board the ability to receive ATC transmissions was significantly degraded and there was significant static and noise on both frequencies. As the flight progressed the quality of the reception continued to degrade and COMM 1 became completely unusable. The QRH was run and the MEL, FOM and AOM (Aircraft Operation Manual) were utilized. The decision was made to Identify as an emergency and continue to the planned destination. Due to the inability to contact the company, ATC was requested to tell the company of the communication issue. As the flight progressed the quality of the reception continued to degrade on COMM 2 until it was barely usable. Upon entering the approach segment of the flight NAV 1 and 2 provided unreliable lateral and vertical information. The flight concluded safely at the destination. Flight crew that handed off the aircraft noted issues with the ACARS no other pertinent information was provided by the crew as they departed. ACARS was usable for the preflight and initial departure portion of the flight.The cause of the radio communications failure is not known by this crew member at this point in time.Air traffic control was very professional and they were immensely helpful and indispensable throughout the event. While departing ZZZ, on climb out and then more noticeable as we neared ZZZ1, static / screeching distortions were noted on COMM 1. At least three times, we asked ATC how they heard us, and the reply was 5x5. We could hear ATC at a 2 or 3. We advised ATC of this. Conditions deteriorated throughout the flight, causing us to utilize COMM 2 as primary.After a short period, COMM 2 began a degradation similar to COMM 1. All flight instrumentation, engine gauges, etc. showed normal parameters. QRH / FOM checked, Captain and I monitored and with COMM 2 not improving, and notification updated information to ATC, Identified as an emergency. Plan and back up plans were made by crew, flight attendants briefed, company notified. Flight continued with no further issues. It should be noted that during a period of time, no COMMS were heard, and we queried ATC to make sure we had not lost all communication. Additionally on approach (visual conditions) both lateral and vertical guidance was observed unreliable. Furthermore upon accepting the aircraft from the previous crew, the Captain noted issues with the 'ACARS' noting we may have to reset the ACARS.The cause of the action is outside of the scope of this crew member. ATC was outstanding. Helpful professional and went above and beyond.
ASRS:1804737.s: The flight crew experienced progressive audio distortion and eventual loss of COMM 1 and 2, plus unreliable NAV guidance on approach, while departing ZZZ. They declared an emergency, utilized the QRH, and landed safely, though the specific cause of the communication and navigation failures remains unknown.

ASRS:1804752.n: MYF RNAV28R approach, circle to land 23. On final approach between fixes NESTY and PENNY aircraft descended to 2,000 feet prior to 2,500, the descent minimum at PENNY. MYF tower controller issued altitude alert and I corrected back to 2,500 feet. Continued approach and airport was visual, above minimums.Circled to 23, tower was trying to clear previous arrived aircraft off runway and I had to execute a missed approach. Tower stated to execute missed approach procedures. I looked at chart and it was to fly straight to 3,000. Raised gear and flaps and climbed to 3,000 feet. At 1,000 feet I engaged autopilot and contacted approach on a new frequency. Autopilot was having the aircraft descend and I disengaged autopilot and it was seemed to be still engaged and I struggled with controls to climb again. Departure control commanded that I climb to 3,000 and I stated that I seemed to be having trim issues as I was fighting to climb. I continued to the headings that were issued by Approach and returned for another approach without further incident. Suggest not using the autopilot until all desired settings are set, and review of missed approach procedures for circling approaches since they are not the same as depicted on the missed approach plate.
ASRS:1804752.s: The pilot descended below 2,500 feet on the MYF RNAV28R approach and executed a missed approach after circling to runway 23. During the climb, the autopilot erroneously commanded a descent, causing trim issues that required manual control to recover before returning for a successful landing.

ASRS:1804757.n: Pushed back from the ZZZ gate X, during push back, we received the okay from ground crew personnel that we can start engine 1. During engine start of the number one engine, it was noted that we had a hung start as the N2 gauge only got up to about 31 percent. Once the Captain and I noticed the indications, we went into shutdown procedures of the number 1 engine. We did note the engine 1 ITT temperature rapidly increase, before it decreased. After shutting down the engine to prepare to restart, ground crew personnel attempted to notify us that there was a fire. However, due to faulty headsets of ground personnel, this information was hard to make sense of. At this point to confirm a potential fire, we contacted the flight attendants to check the rear of the aircraft and look out the windows to confirm the fire potential. The flight attendants did not see any flames or smoke. The decision was made to open the main cabin door, to allow the pilot in command to visually verify there was a fire threat. After the pilot in command visually inspected the area, he was able to confirm that there was a fire and we promptly called for an aircraft evacuation of the passengers and crew. Fire units were notified promptly by ground crew and notification to ZZZ Ground Control of evacuation of passengers on the ramp. The Captain and myself (First Officer) continued to do the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist and the Passenger Evacuation Procedure Checklist. Pushing back we were cleared to start the number one engine. While starting the engine we noticed the engine went to 30 percent N2 and N1 was hanging at 6 to 7 percent. When we were doing the shutdown procedure we noticed the ITT gauge started going up rapidly then went down to zero after we shut down the engine and had no other messages appear on the aircraft. After we shut down the engine the rampers were trying to tell us something, but their radio had a lot of static and I could not understand them. I thought they said fire, but I was not sure because of all the static on the radio. We had no indication on the EICAS of an engine fire. I had my First Officer call the Flight Attendant and check to see if there was a fire. They called back and said they could not see anything. Still unable to understand what ramp was saying, I decided to open the cabin door to visually check, and there was a fire on the number 1 engine. I ran back inside and told the Flight Attendants to evacuate the aircraft. The First Officer and I ran the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist. After we finished the checklist I shut off the aircraft and made sure everyone was off the aircraft.
ASRS:1804757.s: During pushback at ZZZ, the flight crew experienced a hung start on engine 1 followed by a fire, which was confirmed after ground crew warnings were obscured by radio static. The crew visually verified the fire, evacuated all passengers and crew, and completed the engine fire emergency checklist.

ASRS:1804760.n: We were flying back to ZZZ on a clear dark night, arriving on day four. It was my leg (Captain), PF (Pilot Flying). About 20 miles out we were given a vector to ZZZZZ which is about 6 miles south of ZZZZZ1, the final approach fix for runway XXL. The controller asked us to keep our speed up to 210 or better until final as she had other inbound aircraft that she was sequencing in. We switched to green needles and sequenced the approach according to our normal procedures. When we were about 10 miles from ZZZZZ, approximately abeam ZZZZZ1, we called the field in sight. The controller gave us a heading of 080, cleared us for the approach and switched us to tower. She noted that the other aircraft would be following us and to keep 170 or better to final. At this point we were about 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 at about 90 degrees intercept. The heading the controller gave us would take us inside the final approach fix before we intercepted the final bearing. Seeing this, the FO (First Officer) noted that we had not begun our decent to final approach fix altitude yet. I called for the descent, flaps 20 as we slowed to final approach speed. As PF, I noted that the flight guidance would not give us a good intercept because the intercept was too great. At this moment, the autopilot began the turn to final too soon. I turned off the auto pilot and began hand flying. As we began the turn to final I called for flaps 30, and then flaps 45 as we neared the final bearing. As we were completing the turn, the FO (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were still high and that we should increase our rate of decent, we were about 2000 MSL, I steepened our decent and he selected 1000 fpm as we rolled out. I called for and we completed the landing checklist. Tower came up and checked us in. We had not called at the FAP (Final Approach Path) as we were busy flying. At this point, we were about 4 miles from the end of the runway at about 1800 MSL. The tower gave us landing clearance and noted that we were low as the PF I called for us to stop our decent, and I leveled the aircraft at about 1500 MSL. I noted that I had not completed the turn correctly and we were not quite on final bearing. I corrected and called for zero VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) and adjusted to get on final. The FO complied and we continued inbound. At about 3 miles from the runway on final bearing our GPWS alarm went off, PULL UP. As PF, I called for a climb and began a climb at about 5 degrees nose up. As we began our climb, the GPWS alarm went off again, saying PULL UP, I increased the climb, and we climbed about 200ft, as we were very close to glideslope. I was about to call for a missed approach, when I noted that the climb had put us on glideslope, and the PAPI's confirmed us on glideslope. Seeing this, I reestablished our decent and the FO called stabilized at about 3 miles. We landed normally, completed our checklists and shut down the aircraft in accordance with our normal procedures. We have procedures and training guidance that should have prevented this. In this case, there were several errors I made on this approach. As PF, I should not have accepted the vector inside the final approach fix with such a large intercept heading. As Captain, I knew that the flight guidance would be unable to make the turn correctly and we would need more room to make the turn to final. I should have asked to continue our course and give the controller other options. This likely would have prevented the whole series of errors. I should have started my decent to FAF altitude sooner. We were at 3,000 feet, 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 as we turned, and I delayed our decent to 2,400 ft. for several seconds as I turned off the flight guidance and began the turn. If we had been at 2,400 MSL we would not have required a large decent in the turn to final. When the tower checked us in at 4 miles and noted that we were low, I should have called for and established a climb back to glideslope instead of just leveling out. We were very close to glideslope and we should have re-intercepted it first. When the GPWS alarm went off, I should have immediately called for a Missed Approach. We were low (hence the alarm) and there is no space or time for altitude errors on final. Any delay calling for a Missed Approach puts safety at risk. Finally, there was probably some 'get-home-itis' in our minds as we were flying. Arriving late at night, at home field on day four, we were tired and wanted the trip to be over. Going missed would have delayed our landing. Also, we were also trying to satisfy the controller who was sequencing us in front of another aircraft. We needed to focus on our flight, not her decisions or problems.
ASRS:1804760.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a GPWS "PULL UP" alarm during a night approach to ZZZ due to an improper intercept and delayed descent. The crew recovered by climbing to the glideslope and landing normally, attributing the errors to fatigue, pressure to satisfy ATC sequencing, and poor decision-making.

ASRS:1804780.n: We were waiting at spot XX along with another aircraft at spot XX1. Spot XX1 was cleared to taxi, and shortly after that we were instructed to taxi to [runway] XXR via Kilo. We were told the aircraft on our right waits for us. The aircraft to the right did yield and we started to pull out of spot XX to make a left turn onto Kilo. I looked right and then left and saw the aircraft that exited spot XX1 turn right onto Kilo. As we were turning left I called out stop, stop, stop." The Captain stopped the aircraft quickly. There was room for the plane from spot XX1 to continue taxiing. The Ground Controller then stated to give way and that he meant to tell us the plane at XX1 was going the opposite direction on Kilo to join Lima to XXR. Neither of us were aware of that when it occurred. The Captain called the Flight Attendants to check on them and one said that she fell into a wall in the galley, but wanted to continue with the flight to ZZZ1. The same Flight Attendant stated to the Captain in ZZZ1 that she was fit to fly back to ZZZ.[Reporter added incident was due to] Poor taxi instructions given by ZZZ Ground Control. We never should have been cleared to taxi until the traffic from spot XX had cleared us going the opposite direction, or our clearance to taxi should have included to give way to opposite direction traffic from spot XX1." We were positioned at ZZZ ramp spot XX. An aircraft at spot XX1 was cleared to taxi to [runway] XXR, but I wasn't paying attention to his routing. I thought I heard via 'Kilo.' Immediately after that, we were cleared to [runway] XXR via Kilo, and told an airplane on Kilo to our right waits on us. The airplane at spot XX1 began taxiing and I began my taxi so as to be in front of the airplane on our right that was taxiing, but waiting on us. I can't be positive, and it may have been just my expectation, but I thought I saw the airplane from spot XX1 (on our left now) start a left turn on Kilo. With him safely in front of us (I thought), I briefly looked down at the FMC then to my right to make sure we were clear of the airplane on Kilo. The First Officer then said, stop, stop, stop." The aircraft from spot XX1 had turned to the right not left, and was now right in front of us. He had been cleared to the runway via Kilo, K5, Lima. We had not been moving very fast since we had just left spot XX, but I applied the brakes quickly to ensure safe separation. This, I learned later, had caused our number one Flight Attendant, who I did not know was standing, to lose her balance and fall against the galley area. Ground Control then apologized for not letting us know, or to give way. We continued to the runway and I spoke with the crew to make sure they were okay, our number one especially. They all said they were okay and that they were good to continue to ZZZ1. In flight, the number one Flight Attendant told me she wanted to file an injury on duty report. I was very concerned for her at that point, but she said she was just a little sore, she could perform all her duties, and we would be okay to continue. I concurred with her that it would be safe to continue to ZZZ1. We were scheduled to turn around and fly back to ZZZ.I was still very concerned, so I asked the number one to coordinate with her supervisor and get guidance since she wanted to also fly back to ZZZ. I called safety to get guidance as well. Our Flight Attendant stated she was fine to fly back and could perform any and all her duties. After observing, and speaking with her, the First Officer and I both concurred with her assessment that it was safe and reasonable to continue. We landed uneventfully in ZZZ and a team member met the airplane for our number one."
ASRS:1804780.s: Pilots and a flight attendant were involved during taxi at ZZZ when conflicting ground instructions caused a near collision with another aircraft on taxiway Kilo. The reporter attributed the incident to poor taxi instructions, resulting in a sudden stop that caused the flight attendant to fall and sustain minor injuries.

ASRS:1804874.n: Odor in aft galley. Flight attendants reported metallic smell in galley after pushback back from gate. Check galley and lavatory extensively for location of smell. Pilots returned to the gate immediately. Passengers deplaned aircraft, fire crew was called to assess. No additional information. After doing the demo, I walked into the rear galley. I immediately smelled an intense metal burning smell. I removed my mask and asked the C FA if he smelled it too. He pulled his down and said he did. Pilots announced FA's to be seated. I called the A and said call the pilot and tell them to not take off because of the smell. C FA and I began touching all the surfaces to find any hot spots. He checked the lavs. Called pilots and told them the smell was the strongest from ovens. He said we were going back to the gate and deplaning. Pilot made PA at arrival to gate we were deplaning to take their belongings due to unusual smell. Non rev pilot came to the back and said he smelled it too. Fire dept met plane. After deplaning fire dept came on board and said they also smelled it. Capt also smelled it. Mx was called. Mx did not seem to believe us at first and did not smell anything. Later after hours of them being on the plane another mx worker said he smelled it and that it got stronger at different times.Mx to take people more seriously and try not to talk down to people
ASRS:1804874.s: Cabin crew detected an intense metallic burning smell in the aft galley ovens after pushback, prompting the pilots to return to the gate and deplane passengers. Fire crews confirmed the odor, but maintenance initially dismissed the report before later admitting the smell intensified over time.

ASRS:1804917.n: Upon arriving at ZZZ, I asked the local FBO to fuel my aircraft. At their request, I allowed them to fuel the aircraft without me after hours. During my preflight inspection two days later, I noted the fuel quantity indicators in the wings indicated full fuel in the inner tanks. I noted that no water was present via a fuel sample despite heavy rain the day before, and that the gas caps were present on both wings. I was then distracted during my preflight inspection and did not remove the pilot side gas cap to visually inspect fuel level. The co-pilot side gas cap had previously been removed to observe fuel level in the tank. Engine start, taxi, and run up were unremarkable. Shortly after takeoff on runway XX, I noticed that the pilot side fuel cap had departed from the airplane and fuel was coming out of the wing at a tremendous rate. Fearing a severe weight imbalance, I Identified as an emergency and returned to land on runway 18 without further incident or damage. Extensive search of the airport grounds failed to locate the missing gas cap. No damage was noted in the gas cap receiver. I suspect that the gas cap was either damaged or installed incorrectly and the preflight inspection failed to uncover the fault.Chain of events:- Local airport staff removed both gas caps and fueled the plane unobserved.- Pilot side gas cap was either damaged or incorrectly reinstalled after fueling- Preflight inspection was not specifically performed on the pilot side gas cap- During takeoff, the gas cap came loose and departed from the aircraft- In-flight emergency was declared- Landing was successful without further incident or damageHuman Performance Considerations:- Other factors, such as lack of water in the fuel and fuel quantity indicators, gave the impression of properly installed fuel caps- Other activities occurring around the aircraft during the preflight inspection provided distractions that prevented a full inspection of the aircraft- Failure to remove and inspect the gas cap resulted with in-flight failure
ASRS:1804917.s: After unobserved fueling by FBO staff, the pilot side gas cap departed during takeoff, causing rapid fuel loss. The pilot declared an emergency and landed safely, attributing the incident to a likely damaged or incorrectly installed cap that was missed during a distracted preflight inspection.

ASRS:1804934.n: Took off runway XX at ZZZ, around 500 ft. AGL, we lost a lot of engine power, heard a loud metal clanking/rattling sound, and smelled smoke and saw white smoke. I immediately took over and turned towards runway XX. I asked Tower to land, and they cleared us on any runway surface. Once on the ground we tried to take a taxiway but the engine made the noise again so we shut down and Tower sent a tug out for us. We did not [request priority landing], but Tower did break off an approach and clear us to land on any runway surface.
ASRS:1804934.s: The pilot reported losing engine power, hearing metal clanking, and smelling smoke at 500 ft AGL after takeoff from runway XX at ZZZ. The crew returned to land on any available surface, shut down the engine due to recurring noise on the taxiway, and were towed by a tug.

ASRS:1804936.n: Merrill Tower told us to enter right downwind 25 for touch and go's. Traffic was doing a pipeline check at 900 ft., opposite direction (almost set up for left downwind runway 7). Tower told us traffic was same altitude and to offset downwind to the north. We started a slight turn to the north and spotted traffic immediately ahead and to the north. Evasive turn to the east was required. Traffic turned further north to avoid us. Passed maybe 500 ft. from each other.
ASRS:1804936.s: The pilot reported that while entering right downwind for Runway 25, Merrill Tower instructed an offset to the north due to traffic at 900 ft. The pilot spotted the aircraft ahead and executed an evasive turn east, passing within 500 ft as the other aircraft turned north to avoid a collision.

ASRS:1804940.n: Immediately after takeoff the #1 inverter failed. I inadvertently switched off the avionics master instead of the inverter switch I was intending to bring the backup inverter online. As we were in a turn to assigned heading and just starting to enter the clouds, I reduced power to stop the climb and stay below the clouds and continue back towards airport while I sorted things out. I saw the airport and by that time had my avionics back and had switched to the other inverter. I contacted the Tower and informed them I had an electrical problem and was requesting to return for landing. I was in a little too tight to land on runway XX which was the runway I had just taken off from so I requested to enter a left downwind for runway XY as there was basically no winds. The ceiling I believe was probably ragged between 500-700 feet above the ground...approximately 1100-1300 MSL. I got a little low on the downwind leg and received numerous 'don't sink ' warnings but didn't want to climb back up the extra 100-200 feet for fear I might pop in the clouds as I wasn't exactly sure what the bases were in the confusion of the moment. Visibility was good and I am based at ZZZ and am aware of the surroundings. That being the case I elected to continue at my present altitude of 1000 feet (400 AGL) turn base and final and land which I did uneventfully. I probably should have climbed up a little but didn't. I was visual the whole time during when the warnings were issued and wasn't too concerned other than to not descend below 1000 feet MSL till on final. The weather was reported to be 1100 broken but I believe it was less. Visibility reported at 3 miles which I would agree with.
ASRS:1804940.s: The pilot experienced an inverter failure and inadvertently switched off the avionics master immediately after takeoff. The pilot returned to the airport, ignored low altitude warnings to avoid entering clouds, and landed uneventfully at 1000 feet MSL.

ASRS:1804991.n: We were holding short of XXL on Sierra and another aircraft, was holding (arriving earlier). Somewhat unexpectedly, we were cleared for takeoff. I pushed the Attend button, and slowly crept toward the runway to keep the operational flow going. After a long delay, and now approaching the runway, I pushed the Attend button again, with no immediate response. I continued onto the runway. A FA then called us to state they were enforcing a passenger failure to wear a mask issue (this was also an issue during boarding). I directed the FO to ask Tower for a 30 second delay on runway, which was granted. The FA then communicated to me (the exact words I do not recall), that the situation was corrected. I was fully under the impression that they were ready for departure. We then executed the takeoff, but as it turns out, a forward FA was still standing in the isle of the cabin and had to take a seat in the aft galley. Once at level-off, we discussed the situation. This was certainly a miscommunication. In addition, they had yet to provide (me) the 'Cleared for Departure' PA. As the A FA, I was conducting my final walkthrough. I was at the last row of seats. A child that was seated in the last row with her sister and mother was not wearing her mask. The mask was in the mothers bag. This issue had been addressed earlier upon boarding. The CA dinged us for departure. I called the CA from the AFT galley to let him know the same family was not in mask compliance. I asked if I could call him back and he replied with we are on the runway. Finally got the child in compliance so I asked the D FA to call the CA to let him know the mask was on. 2 rows in front of the mask compliance issue was an elderly lady whom refused to stow her large bag on the floor nor in an overhead bin. I had a bin open to try and coax her into letting me stow the bag for her when we took off so I took the nearest jumpseat for takeoff.
ASRS:1804991.s: The Captain and Flight Attendants experienced a runway delay and miscommunication regarding a passenger mask violation and an unsecured bag before takeoff. The crew resolved the issues after the Captain requested a 30-second hold, allowing the flight to depart safely once the cabin was secured.

ASRS:1805047.n: Container X arrived with fresh fish off Aircraft X. Number of the styrofoam boxes arrived broken and damaged. This shipment originated in ZZZZ and it is showing that this was loaded into Container X at the origin for [another flight] and continued onto ZZZ on Aircraft X. Possible fish blood/fluids leakage due to damage to the boxes while in transit. At the time of breakdown, some dampness was observed on the thermo-lining used in the interior of the ULD.
ASRS:1805047.s: Ground personnel reported that Container X, containing fresh fish on Aircraft X, arrived with broken styrofoam boxes and damp thermo-lining. The damage likely caused fish fluid leakage during transit from the origin to ZZZ.

ASRS:1805063.n: First Officer, Pilot Monitoring. Captain, Pilot Flying. 3,000 feet MSL inbound to AWLEE 210 KIAS or greater assigned. Cleared for a visual approach approximately 5 miles from AWLEE 170 or greater to 5 mile final assigned. Continue on heading, allow spacing for visual approach at 210 KIAS. Abeam CRDNL given 080 heading and still cleared for visual and switched to Tower. 080 heading gave a perpendicular intercept course for final. Captain armed approach mode. Aircraft began an early turn to final simultaneously the Captain input a command that caused the plane to enter into pitch mode. I called out pitch mode and he turned autopilot off. I advised the Captain that he needed to begin a descent since we were inside the final approach fix and were 600 feet high. I entered vertical speed mode and put in a thousand ft per min rate of descent and dialed in a 45 degree intercept into the heading. Captain began slowing down and called for gear down, flaps 30, and flaps 45 at appropriate speeds I called for level off when I realized we were at 1,500 feet MSL (acceleration altitude). Simultaneously we received a call from Tower advising us that we were low for our area. I informed Tower that we were leveling and continuing our visual approach. At this point I went outside the cockpit and became focused on looking for towers that would pose a danger to our flight. I didn't recognize any threats. I thought that we could maintain this altitude and intercept the glideslope without issue. We then received a call of terrain. I said we needed to climb. No climb was initiated. We then received the audio alert of woop woop terrain. Pull up. At this point I stated we needed to climb. I began pulling back pressure and a climb was initiated. The audible signals ceased and we continued to intercept the glide slope. Once established on glide slope and on course I called out 1,000 feet stabilized and we completed the approach to a landing. As soon as we were at 1,500 MSL I should have called for a go around. I knew the Captain was disoriented and was confident that I could act as a back stop to get him onto final. I didn't call for a go around after we stopped getting the audible warnings because we were at that point established within the safe and standard parameters of the approach. However, a go-around may have been the pertinent thing to do to increase everyone's situational awareness.
ASRS:1805063.s: During a visual approach to AWLEE, the First Officer and Captain experienced an early turn and altitude deviation that triggered terrain warnings. The crew initiated a climb to intercept the glide slope and landed safely, though the First Officer noted a go-around should have been executed earlier due to the Captain's disorientation.

ASRS:1805069.n: Event took place right after takeoff. I was PF and had manually leveled off at 3,000 MSL using the 'Low Alt Cap' procedure which went as briefed. At this time the PM had called Departure Control and we were issued a climb to 4,000. The PM set 4,000, I confirmed verbally and then commanded VNAV. I continued to manually fly since we were assigned a heading. I had briefed a speed of 200 knots due to being below Class B Airspace and now came to the realization that I had just commanded the aircraft to speed up while we probably weren't high enough yet to legally accelerate. As I held the pitch to hold the airspeed, the altitude alert went off at 4,300 feet. I then clicked off the autothrottle, pulled the thrust to idle and pitched to return to 4,000 feet as the Controller called to remind us to maintain 4,000 feet. We reached 4,500 feet before descending. Flight proceeded without further incident.I had not flown much recently. Reserve lines in my home town had recently materialized and I was enjoying the absence of commuting. I hadn't flown since February with the exception of a PT and upset training in March. I felt that hand flying would be good to help regain proficiency. Our clearance was to fly runway heading for vectors, so I thought this would be a great opportunity. In hindsight I should have waited for a little less busy environment to ease back into it. The FO had flown out of ZZZ1 before and was aware that things could get busy. I should have taken this as a bit of a warning. I could have also thought about how to handle this departure a little more thoroughly. FLCH would have been the better choice in this situation. It would have held 200 knots and commanded a 500 FPM climb. Far more manageable. I was PM. The Captain was PF. Our initial clearance was 3,000 feet and runway heading. The Captain briefed a low altitude capture using 200 knots as we were under the Class B shelf and relatively light. He briefed the intention to hand fly until we were given the intercept to the initial fix on the departure. The initial level off went well and according to the brief with the Captain hand flying. Were quickly given a new heading and a climb to 4,000, which I read back to ATC and set. The Captain confirmed the altitude and called for VNAV. I watched to confirm the start of the climb, then turned to switch my iPad view to the chart page. I heard the altitude alert, looked back to see the airplane pitched higher than the flight director and realized we were climbing past 4,000. At the same time the Captain disengaged the autothrottles, reduced thrust and pitched to return to 4,000 feet. At this time the Controller called us to tell us she needed us back at 4,000 feet. The altitude was about 4,500 feet. The PF corrected back to 4,000, then were soon given another climb. Upon debrief we both realized that FLC would have been the better mode to engage as the VNAV reverted to the programmed speed that was too fast for what we were trying to do. The Captain mentioned he increased the pitch to control the speed and that caused us to climb thru the assigned altitude.As we were still in a critical phase of flight, I should have been more vigilant in monitoring the rate of climb, the speed and the vertical mode. If I had, I could of called it out to help the Captain arrest the acceleration and rate of climb in time to avoid the overshoot. I suggest that more emphasis be placed on the use of FLC and also VS mode. We seem to minimize their use as we rely on VNAV so heavily. The call to engage VNAV becomes a reflex. In this scenario, FLC or VS would of been a better mode that would of prevented the increase of speed that in turn contributed to the overshoot.
ASRS:1805069.s: The Captain hand-flew the aircraft after takeoff and engaged VNAV, causing an unintended speed increase and climb to 4,500 feet instead of the assigned 4,000 feet. The First Officer noted that using FLCH mode would have prevented the overshoot, which resulted from the Captain pitching up to control speed.

ASRS:1805073.n: Takeoff and climb to cruise was uneventful. At cruise FL260, received ATC reroute to avoid weather. Reroute was ZZZ1 then back onto the ZZZZZ arrival. About 50 miles north of ZZZ1, we were cruising at 280 kts in IMC conditions at +2 degrees TAT with engine anti-ice on. The Captain was flying. We then noticed the airspeed start to go way down then go way back up. It indicated maybe 40 kts to 300 kts (unsure exactly). 'Airspeed low' kept announcing as well. The Captain turned off the autopilot and autothrottle and set 4 degrees nose high and told me to set power. I pulled the power to 70% N1 and we compared PFDs. My airspeed indications would indicate properly for a few seconds then jump up or down. The Captain's was constantly moving up and down so we transferred control to the First Officer. I called for the QRC and the Captain read and accomplished the steps (we had missed flight directors off). We had climbed a couple hundred feet during this and I asked the Captain to notify ATC and I turned the airplane eastbound in an attempt to exit IMC. It worked and a couple minutes later we exited IMC and started a descent to warmer air. While the Captain ran the QRH for unreliable airspeed and informed ATC/dispatch, I continued to fly. As the air warmed and as we exited IMC, airspeed indications returned to normal. We reviewed pitch and power setting in the QRH to make sure the airspeeds were accurate. The rest of the descent and arrival to ZZZ was uneventful. My guess is we accumulated ice on the probes enough to make the airspeed indications go unreliable. I didn't see abnormal icing on the windshield wipers nor was icing reported. Being in IMC at +2 degrees was about perfect conditions for it. After landing, the Captain and I talked about how we were thankful for 737 MAX simulator training we had both recently completed. The training prepared us so well for this and I am thankful to our check airmen in the sims. I felt well prepared for this as described above thanks to 737 MAX training. On descent to ZZZ, Captain Pilot Flying, in IMC conditions, FL260, TAT +2. No visible icing. Engine anti ice on. Airspeed unreliable on Captain's side. Repeated 60-100 kt changes with aural 'airspeed' warning. Executed QRC/QRH. First Officer flew rest of flight. Notified ATC and notified Dispatch on ACARS. Notified Maintenance on the ground, wrote discrepancy into log book and discussed the occurrence in detail with the mechanic at the gate. [I] suspect icing, but had no indications of a fault in the pitot or air data systems.
ASRS:1805073.s: The crew experienced unreliable airspeed indications on a Boeing 737 MAX at FL260 in IMC with engine anti-ice on, likely caused by probe icing. They executed the QRH, transferred control to the First Officer, and exited IMC to restore normal indications before landing.

ASRS:1805090.n: During climbout after gear and slat retraction, we received a green [hydraulic] system fluid low warning on ECAM. We complied with the ECAM procedures and were directed to the QRH. Ran the ECAM for low hydraulic quantity. First Officer ran appropriate checklists while I communicated with ATC, coordinated with landing visual to Runway XX at ZZZ. We manually extended the gear and landed uneventfully on Runway XX stopped straight ahead, and were towed to the gate.Event caused by hydraulic system malfunction. During climbout, after gear and slat retraction, the ECAM green system hydraulic fluid low warning occurred. Deployed gear manually. Notified ATC. Completed QRH and returned to ZZZ.
ASRS:1805090.s: The crew received a green hydraulic system fluid low warning during climbout after gear retraction. They manually extended the gear, followed QRH procedures, and landed uneventfully at ZZZ due to a hydraulic system malfunction.

ASRS:1805094.n: On climbout, the #2 engine oil quantity dropped to 1 quart. We ran the QRH checklist for Engine Oil Quantity Low/Decreasing. The engine oil pressure was initially in the green band but then dropped below the green band. At this point we decided to shutdown the number 2 engine following the QRH checklist. Since the QRH stated that we consider landing at the nearest suitable field, we notified ATC and returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing. The event was caused by a rapid oil leak in the #2 engine. Shortly after takeoff we noticed our number 2 oil quantity had dropped to 1 quart indicated by an amber '1'. Aircraft was clean and the After Takeoff Checklist had just been accomplished. As Pilot Flying I continued to fly the aircraft while the Captain read the checklist 'Engine Oil Quantity Low/Decreasing'. Oil pressure was lower than Eng 1 and Eng 3 indications but still within the green band at approximately 35 psi. The pressure, at a somewhat low rate, began to decrease getting down to 30 psi over the course of approximately 2-3 minutes. At 30 psi the indication turned amber. At this time we decided, per the checklist, to secure the number 2 engine. We then notified ATC. The Captain read and executed the Engine Shutdown Inflight checklist. Once all checklists were complete the Captain assumed the Pilot Flying duties and I became the Pilot Monitoring. We opted to return to ZZZ and set up for the visual approach. We execute a flaps 35 autoland landing to [runway]. After landing and off the runway the fire/crash crew visually inspected the number 2 engine and reported nothing noticeably [wrong] with the aircraft. Once in the chocks and shutdown we were informed about a large amount of oil that had leaked out of the engine onto the aircraft. The cause was rapid oil loss in the number 2 engine.
ASRS:1805094.s: The flight crew returned to ZZZ after a rapid oil leak in the #2 engine caused quantity to drop to 1 quart and pressure to fall below 30 psi during climbout. Following the QRH, they shut down the engine and executed an uneventful autoland, with post-landing inspection confirming significant oil leakage.

ASRS:1805096.n: Aircraft X had just departed ZZZ for ZZZ1 and lost green hydraulics. They notified ATC and returned to ZZZ, landing on Runway X. Had to be towed to the gate from the runway.
ASRS:1805096.s: Aircraft X lost green hydraulics shortly after departing ZZZ for ZZZ1. The crew returned to ZZZ, landed on Runway X, and required a tow to the gate.

ASRS:1805117.n: Departing FXE on the FLL7 Departure had leveled at 2,000. Controller gave a climb to 3,000, announced traffic and handed us off to the next Approach Controller. At this time the pilot flying announced less than 100 feet vertical separation from the traffic and we received a TA annunciation. Pilot flying increased the rate of climb and we exceeded the cleared altitude by 300 feet avoiding the traffic.Suggestions - Pride [Provide] proper separation and don't hand off an aircraft to another Controller when there is a possible traffic conflict.
ASRS:1805117.s: During departure from FXE on the FLL7, a pilot reported less than 100 feet vertical separation and a TA annunciation after being handed off by the controller. The pilot increased climb rate, exceeding the cleared 3,000 feet by 300 feet to avoid traffic, attributing the event to improper separation and premature handoff.

ASRS:1805189.n: Was assigned to perform the multiple tasks for aircraft return to service after extended parking. During accomplishment of the tasks had to open the engine cowls and more specifically the thrust reverser cowls. The station currently has hydraulic cowl pumps using XXXX oil. The AMM procedure gives the tool number of a cowl pump which was correct for equipment on hand and also gives the different mil-specs of oil that can be used. The oil from my understanding is consistent with X specifications however the opening actuator for the cowl state on a placard to 'use engine oil'. The engines on that particular airplane are serviced with YYYY oil which also falls under the X specification. There was some confusion about which oil was appropriate to use for this situation since the engines use YYYY oil but cowl pumps on hand had XXXX oil and the specs were the same for both oils. We ended up taking a XXXX oil cowl pump to the tooling department at ZZZ, draining it, cleaning/flushing it, replacing the filter, relabeling it with YYYY oil and servicing it with that oil for use on the aircraft. There was just some confusion about the proper oil.
ASRS:1805189.s: A mechanic performing post-parking return-to-service tasks encountered confusion regarding whether to use XXXX or YYYY oil for hydraulic cowl pumps, despite both meeting X specifications. The mechanic resolved this by flushing and relabeling a pump with YYYY oil to match the engine fluid before servicing the thrust reverser cowls.

ASRS:1805190.n: On Date there was an unfortunate damage to the Right Horizontal Stabilizer of Aircraft X. This damage drove Safety Bulletin on Date 1, which suggested a breakdown in communication as the root cause of the damage. However, most technicians (and supervisors) believe the real root cause of this damage was caused by the inability to use the correct equipment to accomplish the task at hand due to [the] Stores Department using both sides of this bay as staging and storage for their various equipment and items (tires, crates of all types and sizes, stacked at heights of over 10 feet in some instances). The work to be accomplished was on the right hand wing tip but because of all the equipment on the ground a small 35 feet JLG or widebody lift could not be used, instead a much larger JLG was necessary, positioned much further away, resulting in contact/damage to the right horizontal stabilizer. If this was a one off, the technicians probably would not have as much heartburn but this issue of stores using Bay 3, one of our prime widebody aircraft bays, as a storage has been going on for years and has resulted in other aircraft damages in the past. This has been a well-documented and hot topic of discussion in ZZZ meetings, crew briefings, safety team raising it with messages, every level of management has been made aware of this over the years. Sadly, the situation is getting worse instead of better.At our latest ZZZ meeting Date 1, a supervisor questioned the findings of the investigation stating that in his experience working the service center, he felt the stores equipment was more of a causation factor than the loss of communication. The reply from another member of management 'I am not aware of this being an issue'. Another participant suggested there was a lot of documentation but was told 'we can look into it and maybe build a case to get the stores equipment moved'. Since the damage, this stores equipment problem has been highlighted at the daily crew briefings and what is glaring to most techs since this damage is the fact that not only has nothing been done to mitigate the issue, it has actually gotten worse since the latest damage. This aircraft has been out of service now for almost 3 weeks, (if we are to believe the finance people when they tell us that a wide body generates X money on average a day), that's a costly stores area, just looking at it from that perspective!The unfortunate reality is in the event of a damage the technician is grilled in the investigation, sent for drug and alcohol testing, always made to feel at fault, always told it was self-induced pressure, and of course have their records pulled showing they signed off a specific training course, maintenance & engineering bulletin, awareness class etc. I have examples of this from many investigation reports. I'm filing this report because the front-line mechanics don't want to for fear of repercussions if they did. Sure, there are many human factors that come into play when incidents like this happen but when you look at it, this is not complacency on the part of the mechanics. There are real pressures to get these aircraft in and worked in BAY 3 and we crutch the system on a daily basis because of these pressures. My question, how is Company living up to their values of safety always being #1 when this issue has been ignored for years despite the attention and spotlight?What is staggering to most, weeks after the latest very costly damage the situation is actually worse. The only answer could be, if you investigate and find the root cause that suits, then of course it will be impossible to mitigate and address the real root cause! I won't gain any friends for pointing this out but this issue needs to be addressed. It is our responsibility, from safety, to Management, coworkers etc., to do the right thing, provide a safe work environment, which helps keep us all safe from injury and our assets from being damaged. We owe it to each other and ourcustomers. At this juncture this needs to be a priority from senior leadership because constant suggestions and concern from the floor have hit a brick wall and frankly we on the front line don't have the authority to fix the problem.
ASRS:1805190.s: Technicians damaged Aircraft X's right horizontal stabilizer in Bay 3 while using a large lift to access the wing tip because stored equipment blocked smaller lifts. The reporter attributes the cause to long-standing storage obstructions rather than communication breakdowns, noting the aircraft has been out of service for three weeks.

ASRS:1805191.n: The scenario of my report happens multiple occasions while working with maintenance manuals and in software program from my IPAD on an almost daily basis.While working in [various programs] on my IPAD to reference AMM data, [and] to document maintenance actions, my IPAD 'times out' requiring me to log back on to all of these applications. When this happens, there is no 'history' saved to refer to, no 'recent pages' stored for reference, and no data is saved that was being entered into a log page for sign off, update or deferral purposes. I am required to log back into all applications and they open as if I have not used them at all during my shift. Any clue or trail of pages I had been viewing is lost. This happens typically at least a few times a shift, some days several times. It has happened during gate calls during troubleshooting with full planes, as well as right in the middle of entering a sign off, update or deferral into software program, and right in the middle of working a maintenance procedure on the airplane and actively referencing the selected AMM pages. All scenarios MULTIPLE times.Aside from the obvious time wasted and frustration factor of constantly re logging in and re launching applications, re finding AMM pages, and reentering log page data that was lost, the bigger concern here is the potential of an FAA ramp check to verify AMM procedure compliance. When my IPAD times out, it is without warning, without recourse or remedy. If I am 'Ramp checked' for FAA compliance and I suddenly have to 're log in' to [software programs], the appearance to the FAA inspector is that I never had these manuals open in the first place which would be false, which leaves my license open to FAA scrutiny at no fault of mine.I've inquired to the 'hangar IPAD person' that randomly comes on midnight shift but was told my issues 'couldn't happen' the way I described and my issue was basically dismissed, so no remedy or resolution was offered.
ASRS:1805191.s: A mechanic reported that their iPad frequently times out during maintenance tasks, causing loss of unsaved data and AMM page history. This issue creates a risk of appearing non-compliant during FAA ramp checks, and management dismissed the concern without offering a resolution.

ASRS:1805200.n: Preflight inspection of the aircraft started at approximately XA:45 am, where fuel was requested from the local FBO. Oil was checked, where 1.5 quarts were put in the aircraft to give it approximately 6.5 quarts of oil. All sumps were drained after the fuel was added, with no water or contaminates noted. The instrument flight plan was filed through foreflight. All control surfaces were examined and shown to be in working order. Engine startup was nominal, with no issues or indications of engine trouble. Taxi clearance was given from the north ramp to Runway X, via taxiway. While taxing out, because of opposite direction traffic on Runway XY, the ground controller asked if I could accept a Runway XY intersection departure, which I agreed to. Takeoff roll was uneventful with full power, and mixture all the way in. Aircraft rotated at approximately 60 kts, after 900 foot takeoff roll. During initial climb out from ZZZ Runway XY, on an assigned 330 heading, passing through 2,500 feet MSL, I noticed a drop of approximately 1000 RPM, with associated engine roughness. I immediately leveled the aircraft, pulled carb heat, and notified ATC with Departure. Engine power did resume while level to it's normal state, but when directed to Runway X by the Departure Controller, followed by a 5 degree descent, the engine roughness and loss of RPM's recreated itself. Due to the engine running rough, I shut down the aircraft after landing where I was met by Airport Fire Rescue personnel, and ZZZ Airport Ops. Aircraft was towed to Maintenance here at the ZZZ, where a thorough inspection of the engine, fuel, oil was conducted. No anomalies were detected or identified, leading to the probability of carb water or carb ice on departure. The weather at the time of the incident was: Temp 68 F, Dewpoint 64 F, Humidity 87%, Wind SSE 3 mph. Baro 29.94 in. Mostly Cloudy. ZZZ Tower and Departure were amazing as always, I consistently fly missions across the state, and appreciate their constant professionalism and willingness to help. A lot of my flights require a lot of coordination with local ATC's, and ZZZ is always top notch!
ASRS:1805200.s: The pilot experienced engine roughness and a 1,000 RPM drop during climbout from Runway XY at ZZZ Airport, likely caused by carburetor water or ice. After landing and shutting down, maintenance found no anomalies, and the aircraft was towed for further inspection.

ASRS:1805201.n: Today we flew to MIA, on the SSCOT5 approach, after the LECIT position, ATC authorized us to descend to 3,000 ft, later we hear on the radio frequency that an airplane is not paying attention, suddenly in the instrument appears an airplane below us in ascent, we locate it visually and it gives us the instruction to maintain the altitude and immediately after to ascend, we performed the evasion maneuver and informed ATC, who ordered us to maintain 8,000 feet.
ASRS:1805201.s: While descending to 3,000 ft on the SSCOT5 approach to MIA, the crew observed an ascending aircraft below and executed an evasion maneuver after ATC instructed them to maintain and then climb. The crew informed ATC, who subsequently cleared them to maintain 8,000 feet.

ASRS:1805208.n: On flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2, which was at the limit of our aircraft range unless there are decent tailwinds, had a hard time getting a climb, barely any tailwinds and was expecting a cumbersome arrival. So, when we were over West [State] and assigned the ZZZZZ arrival I was wondering if we would land with minimum IFR reserves. Asked Center to keep us high as long as possible and they did a pretty good job except this involved lots of vectors and altitudes when getting closer to ZZZ. So, during descent I was delaying a steep descent until closer and lower to save fuel. All of this ended up working and we landed with more than minimum reserves but it caused me to be really busy in IFR conditions.While direct to ZZZZZ1 to cross at 9,000, I was given an eastbound vector through the arrival track between ZZZZZ2 and ZZZZZ1 while descending at close to 3,000 FPM. Then told to head direct to ZZZZZ1and cross it at or below 9,000. This involved a 135 degree right turn within 10 miles of ZZZZZ1 but all was good on making the crossing altitude. Then was given 5,000 at ZZZZZ and told to cross ZZZZZ1 at or below 9,000. I entered the 5,000 in for ZZZZZ but made the error of entering a vertical 'Direct to' for ZZZZZ and engaging VNAV. Looked up and the descent rate had switched from almost 3,000 FPM to just above 1,000 FPM. Very quickly disengaged VNAV and dialed in the 3,000 FPM on the VS mode.Finally figured out there was no way I was going to make the crossing at ZZZZZ1. Told the Controller I wasn't going to make the crossing altitude at ZZZZZ when within 2 miles of ZZZZZ1 - a little late. We ended up crossing ZZZZZ at a little below 10,000 and the rest of flight went very well.Causes: 1st would be doing that VNAV to ZZZZZ - if I left everything alone, we would have been fine.2nd was coming in high and having to do a steep descent while being vectored around and given the direct-to really close to the ZZZZZ1 fix which involved lots of turning.3rd was flying a little slow and descending a little slow to save fuel which caused problems for ZZZ Approach.4th was getting barely any sleep the night before - had taken a natural energy booster later in the day and it didn't wear off until XAam or so then had to get up early.5th was keeping the flight smooth for the passenger despite the steep descent and all the turns - without a passenger I would have been more positive about getting down.6th was the low fuel situation I was concerned about - during COVID with lower air traffic I became used to getting unobstructed clearances but it is busy again - really busy this day and I didn't figure that I would have any problem getting a climb to 450, but I did and that burned more fuel than I had planned.How to avoid in the future: 1) Plan fuel for busier air traffic. 2) Don't do a VTO to the last of 2 fixes when given crossing restrictions for 2 fixes. Either VS it or if using VNAV just do the VTO to the first fix and let the VNAV figure out how to get down to the second fix. 3) Don't take that energy booster after lunch time! 4) I forgot that during descent the fuel gauges read a little low - just remember this next time.
ASRS:1805208.s: The pilot of a fuel-constrained flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 missed a 9,000-foot crossing restriction at ZZZZZ1 after incorrectly engaging VNAV to a subsequent fix while managing steep descents and vectors. The pilot attributed the error to fatigue, fuel-saving tactics, and improper automation use, resulting in a late altitude deviation that was corrected by switching to vertical speed mode.

ASRS:1805213.n: I was returning from LWC to ZZZ at 2,500 MSL approximately 9 miles NW of LWC heading NW. I Encountered another small aircraft maneuvering at my 8 o'clock. Aircraft went underneath and then turned and climbed toward me at my 5 o'clock. It appeared the aircraft was performing commercial maneuvers (chandelle?) in a possible training flight. Best option was to add power versus trying to make evasive turn north or south since I wasn't sure if the other aircraft saw me. Landed at ZZZ without incident.
ASRS:1805213.s: A pilot returning from LWC to ZZZ at 2,500 MSL encountered a small aircraft performing commercial maneuvers nearby. The pilot added power to avoid a potential collision and landed at ZZZ without incident.

ASRS:1805214.n: Conducted a part 91 flight ZZZ1 to ZZZ2.I initiated a crew brief of the SID while still on the ramp...I had the chart display mainly zoomed in on the text description box to make the text bigger. I focused on the final altitude of 17,000 to the right of the text box that pertained to all runways. I had showed the PF the altitude and said 'I will set 17,000 in the altitude select if you agree'. He responded 'affirm'. I began to read the text version of the SID to myself and it read 'Climb on a heading of 216 to intercept course 185 to ZZZZZ, then on track 108 to cross ZZZZZ1...' I announced we will arm LNAV for departure as the FMS matched this.At that point I did not finish reading and zoomed in and looked at the SID graphically but focused on the runway departure and how it fed into the initial FIX ZZZZZ. I noticed all runways fed into ZZZZZ. I knew that fix would be important on readback, (as it is at ZZZ3 for example), to ensure safety on parallel runway operations.Very short taxi out from FBO. Took off runway XXR, normal operations. Positive rate, gear up, '400 feet, flaps up select VS.' Thus, we were in VS speed as is often the case for climbout.Tower sends us to departure. I call twice, no joy. Switch back to Tower and ask to confirm frequency. Call back through 6,000 and departure responds climb and maintain 7,000. We received this clearance at approximately 6,800 feet. We executed this clearance immediately however given out pitch attitude and climb rate we overshot 7,000 feet and reached an altitude of 7,400-7,500 based on my best recollection.No TCAS alerts were issued. We maintained 7,000, were given another climb clearance and then before the ATC Controller switched us over, we were told of the possible deviation.What I have learned from this incident is to read the entire textual description in the SID and to take in the whole SID graphically as opposed to taking into account just the post departure/runway routing.I also learned poor habits can be formed from other airports, particularly our home base airport. We receive a SID on our clearance every time. We then get a heading on takeoff clearance from home base ZZZ2 ATC voiding the initial part of the clearance 99 percent of the time.Another factor is the scarcity of climb via SIDs that do not mainly incorporate 'at or above.' This incident taught me not to assume or have a bias to SID instructions.Another factor in this error was rust due to the COVID shutdown. Our awareness and CRM need improvement which will come with more recent operations I believe.
ASRS:1805214.s: The pilot and first officer of a Part 91 flight overshot a 7,000-foot clearance to 7,500 feet during climbout due to high pitch attitude and incomplete SID review. The crew attributed the deviation to poor CRM, rust from COVID shutdowns, and bias from home base operations.

ASRS:1805215.n: While flying practice ILS XX into ZZZ I experienced a loss of throttle control. This occurred when leveling off at 5,500 while being radar vectored to final approach course just outside of ZZZZZ waypoint. I requested priority handing with Approach Control and clearance given to land Runway XX. The engine RPM remained full power when throttle was reduced. I climbed to gain altitude and keep RPM below redline. Once at safe altitude and able to reach airport we begun to lean mixture to reduce RPM. Once runway was assured and at about 200 feet AGL we pull mixture full off and preformed an engine out landing to Runway XX. Was able to clear the runway and depart the plane. Safety pilot Mr. X was the only other person aboard the plane.
ASRS:1805215.s: The pilot and safety pilot experienced a throttle control failure at 5,500 feet while being radar vectored for an ILS approach. They managed engine RPM by leaning mixture and performed an engine-out landing after cutting the mixture at 200 feet AGL.

ASRS:1805216.n: I had just crossed the YRK VORTAC and began a descent from 2,600 feet MSL towards 2,300. I realized that I had descended too quickly and should have held level at 2,600 until reaching the initial fix of MYKEE for the RNAV 12 approach into HTS. Huntington Approach queried me as to my low altitude (I had descended to 2,450 feet MSL). I corrected my altitude and was then asked by Huntington Approach if I could maintain my own obstruction clearance on the approach. I answered in the affirmative and continued on the approach to a landing without any further issue. This was my initial error. I realized I was fatigued on a long flight with a strong headwind and long period of time in IMC. I should have maintained 2,600 feet MSL until crossing MYKEE.
ASRS:1805216.s: The pilot descended too quickly from 2,600 to 2,450 feet MSL before reaching the MYKEE fix for the RNAV 12 approach into HTS. Citing fatigue from a long flight in IMC, the pilot corrected the altitude and continued to land after accepting responsibility for obstruction clearance.

ASRS:1805230.n: During our final approach to Runway 35 at TVY, Aircraft Y called simulated engine failure over the radio while they were on the downwind. I was around 500 feet lower at the time of their call with most of my final approach complete.During short final/touchdown we noticed the plane buzzed over the top of our aircraft at about 200+ (ADS-B showing the information) causing undue danger in the event that we had to abort landing for whatever reason. The jump plane pilots have been known to do such events in times past. My instructor radioed to them about their unsafe bafoonery with zero recognition. It was a brief statement about a student pilot (myself) in training. He was quite unhappy with their antics and opted to not escalate it via CTAF bantering.
ASRS:1805230.s: A student pilot on final approach to Runway 35 at TVY reported a jump plane simulating an engine failure on downwind and buzzing their aircraft at 200 feet. The instructor criticized the unsafe behavior but chose not to escalate the incident over the radio.

ASRS:1805235.n: I landed at Santa Monica yesterday. I landed on Runway 21, and turned right to exit the runway to taxi to the FBO. I was pretty impressed with myself that I got stopped in time to quickly dart into the FBO, landing in a record short distance.Unfortunately for me, they have changed the procedures at SMO since the last time that [I] was there. Now, they have specific painted taxiways that they want you to follow.Of course, there's nothing painted to show where NOT to go. I'd suggest striped lines, or green paint in the 'forbidden' areas. San Diego airport has green paint, for example.I'm not aware of any NOTAM concerning the new taxiway arrangement, however in the AFD is the following notes:'ACFT MUST NOW EXIT THE RWY AT DSGND CONNECTOR TWYS. THE CONS RWY EXIT SYS IS NO LONGER AVBL.'
ASRS:1805235.s: The pilot landed at Santa Monica on Runway 21 and exited onto an unpainted area instead of the required designated connector taxiways. This occurred because the pilot was unaware of the new mandatory exit procedures published in the AFD, which removed the continuous runway exit system.

ASRS:1805237.n: I came close to 2 [helicopters] on departure in ZZZ. When I was taxiing out they called in a flight of 5 inbound for [Runway] XX. I responded that I was taxiing for [Runway] XX and I would hold short for them. While I was holding short, they flew overhead, and I only saw 3 definitive lights. 2 [helicopter] with white lights followed by 2 [helicopters] with barely recognizable dim green lights, and one in the back with a red beacon. They called clear on [Taxiway] XX as I watched the white and red lights clear the runway I could not see the dim green lights after they passed in front of me because they were barely recognizable. I made a radio call that I was departing on [Runway] XX. I taxied onto the runway with all my lights on, did not see any aircraft lights on the runway, and started my departure roll. Just as I was about to rotate I felt wake turbulence and decided to abort. I saw a black silhouette pass on my right, then another one. I cleared the runway. They claimed that they didn't call clear of the runway and that they had all their lights on. There was a pilot at [FBO] that told me they only saw 3 sets of lights and all appeared to have cleared the runway. He saw me abort and was confused as to why I did because he never saw the other 2 [helicopters].
ASRS:1805237.s: A pilot aborted takeoff on Runway XX due to wake turbulence from two unseen helicopters that had dim green lights. Although the helicopters claimed to be clear with lights on, the pilot could not see them, and a witness at the FBO also only observed three aircraft.

ASRS:1805270.n: We were descending on the ZZZZZ1 STAR. Just prior to level off at a higher altitude, the controller cleared us to descend via the STAR to 12,000 feet. The PF pointed to the altitude as I set it. However, he went out of VNAV to FLCH because he thought he heard descend to 12,000 feet now. I was busy with a frequency change and getting the new ATIS, and I missed the change in pitch mode. When I looked up, I noticed we were approaching 15,000 feet even though the fix just ahead of us had a at or above 16,000 foot restriction. I called it out and the PF immediately leveled off at 15,000 feet. I immediately informed the Controller and asked if he wanted us to climb back to 16,000 feet. He said we could just 'descend to 12,000 feet.' There was no conflict with other traffic.I believe this occurred for a number of reasons. It was a very difficult 3-day pairing made longer because of COVID. We were all exhausted, it was a high-workload environment, and the PF had not flown in over a year. He had trouble hearing ATC the entire trip which we attributed to his being off a year. Obviously, there was a breakdown in Verbalize, Verify and Monitor. Lesson learned: especially when tired and in a high-workload environment, strict adherence to SOP is essential.
ASRS:1805270.s: During descent on the ZZZZZ1 STAR, the Pilot Flying switched to FLCH mode and descended below the 16,000-foot restriction to 15,000 feet due to fatigue, hearing difficulties, and a breakdown in crew monitoring. The Pilot Monitoring called out the deviation, the aircraft leveled off, and ATC cleared the crew to continue descending to 12,000 feet.

ASRS:1805273.n: While climbing out of Denver airspace at 36,000 feet on our way to 37,000 feet we encountered a strong mountain wave. I had just requested 39,000 feet with Denver center when the incident occurred. The Controller passed me on to a different frequency and at that time we encountered the mountain wave. Almost immediately the airspeed increased into the high-speed Q and our vertical speed increased to over 8000 ft./min. We were able to level off at 37,800 feet and contact the new Controller. Upon contact I notified the Controller that we were above are signed altitude due to a mountain wave. We descended back down to 37,000 feet and then we were cleared to 39,000 feet. We were level FL360. The aircraft dipped below cruise altitude causing VMO exceedance. I disengaged autopilot to return to normal parameters when the upside of the mountain wave climbed us to FL368 before I was able to descend back to FL360. First Officer noted a climb rate approaching 8,000 FPM. ATC was notified and no traffic conflicts were present.
ASRS:1805273.s: Pilots climbing through 36,000 feet in Denver airspace encountered a strong mountain wave that caused a VMO exceedance and a climb rate over 8,000 FPM. The crew disengaged the autopilot, leveled at 37,800 feet, and descended back to 37,000 feet after notifying ATC, with no traffic conflicts reported.

ASRS:1805293.n: During our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 severe weather storms had begun to move into our course of route. ATC advised us of the weather and gave us a reroute to the ZZZ2 VOR which was significantly off route from our original flight plan. Unfortunately, after re-calulating our new flight plan and fuel, we noticed that due to our reroute we would be landing at ZZZ1 with minimum fuel. After getting our new performance numbers we slowed down to long range cruise and advised dispatch and ATC of our fuel situation. Letting them know that if we continued to fly to the ZZZ2 VOR that we would be landing with min fuel. We were given 'deviations as necessary direct ZZZ1 when able'. Our radar showed two storm cells about 3-5 miles in diameter. We decided to deviate around these cells and proceed direct ZZZ1 once clear of the storm. While navigating around these storms we began to experience updrafts and downdrafts. During our course of route the autopilot was engaged and suddenly began to deviate from FL290 by +800/-300 ft. The VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) showed a climb and descent of +/-4,000 feet per min and the cockpit windows became fogged. During this time the airplane did not feel like it was pitching this extreme and did not exceed +5/-2 degrees. Altitude miscompare flags appeared on our PFD'S (Primary Flight Display) and the VSI had a RED X for less than 5 seconds. I began to run the QRH. ATC contacted us about our altitude and asked if we were having a rough ride. We responded and advised of the situation and were cleared to descend to FL240 at pilot's discretion. After the airplane was stable at FL290 we descended to FL240 and landed at ZZZ1 with 2,400 pounds of fuel and no further incidents.
ASRS:1805293.s: Pilots flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 encountered severe storms and turbulence while deviating around cells, causing autopilot altitude deviations and instrument flags. After receiving clearance to descend to FL240, they landed safely with 2,400 pounds of fuel.
