ASRS:1805314.n: We were deviating to the southeast, around weather northwest of ZZZ, with the use of on board radar. We were not painting weather on the course we selected. Shortly after asking to deviate the aircraft began to climb. I turned off the autopilot and maintained wings level. Immediately thereafter we encountered numerous updrafts and downdrafts making it difficult for me to maintain altitude and airspeed. I did the best I could to maintain wings level and 'rode out' the turbulence which resulted in altitude deviations. The aircraft also banked left and right however the bank never exceeded 30 degrees in either direction. The entire encounter lasted approximately two minutes.In the future I will take on extra fuel and alter my flight plan and/or course to avoid areas of large precipitation / weather in their entirety. We were at FL410. We knew about the weather before we left. There were some high top reports but not many. We got closer to the line and asked for FL430. We started on top but then went into IMC conditions. We had our radar on the 100 mile range and pointed down so that the 50 mile line was painting the ground and any storms that were between 50 nm and 100 nm. If there is a storm between the 50 nm and 100 nm and it is severe the ground behind it will not paint. It will be black. Also, if the storm crosses the 50 nm line and starts to disappear then you will top that storm. We deviated to the left of course to an area that looked clear and was disappearing as we got closer. So we should have topped it. We got into the top of a buildup. First Officer turned off the auto pilot and hand flew. We got some rain and an updraft followed by a down draft and then numerous up and down drafts. we went up to 43,300 and I saw 41,800 on the down side. The event lasted about 90 seconds.In the future, look to go-around the line or cross the line where there are lower tops.
ASRS:1805314.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence and altitude deviations while deviating around weather at FL410-430. The pilot attributed the incident to misinterpreting onboard radar returns, which failed to reveal a storm buildup they inadvertently entered.

ASRS:1805340.n: While on initial descent into SFO, I obtained a METAR and D-ATIS for the airport prior to my briefing. On this particular day, the wind was from the west and quite gusty between 35 to 40 knots. I wanted to ensure the crosswind component was within my limitations as a First Officer. At the time, I noticed a discrepancy between the METAR wind direction and that of the ATIS. METARs provide wind direction in reference to true north whereas ATIS and D-ATIS provide in reference to magnetic north. At SFO, the magnetic variation is 14E, meaning we would subject that amount the direction in reference to true north to get the wind direction in magnetic north. For simplicity, I will round to 20 degrees. At the time, the wind on the METAR was 280 degrees but that on the ATIS was 300 degrees. Both reports had the same reported time and date and the rest of the information including peak wind was exactly the same on both reports. There seems to be a large discrepancy between the two since if the METAR says the wind is 280, then in magnetic that is 260 and not the 300 that was advertised by the ATIS. This 40 degree difference is quite large. I was curious and began to observe the ATIS and METARs over the next couple days and found that SFO is consistently reporting, on the ATIS, a value that is 20 degrees greater than the METAR. Possibly explanations for this could be that the wind information is coming from different sources, but it seems quite peculiar that the wind direction on the ATIS is consistently 20 degrees greater than the METAR. Any pilot would use the METAR, subtract 10 or 20 degrees, and get a wind direction of 270 or 280 degrees magnetic. The ATIS is reporting it as 310 degrees. This discrepancy can be large enough to cause confusion with crosswind landing limitations for the aircraft and pilot. I have noticed this issue prior to this flight, but did not think much of it until I noticed it consistently wrong over the past few days. If you view the METAR and ATIS for OAK and SJC, the ATIS for both reports a wind direction that is 10 degrees less than that of the METAR. This is as expected. SFO, however, reports 20 degrees greater. I addressed SFO Tower about this directly, to which they responded that they do not control this data as it comes from the 'weather people downstairs.' I am just curious if this is intentional or if this is, in fact, an error. Perhaps SFO Tower quality assurance can take a look?
ASRS:1805340.s: A First Officer descending into SFO identified a consistent 20-degree discrepancy between METAR and ATIS wind directions, suspecting an error in magnetic conversion. The pilot reported this to SFO Tower, which stated the data originates from ground weather personnel, raising concerns about potential confusion regarding crosswind limitations.

ASRS:1805398.n: ZZZ slide shop received 4 slides that were removed from Aircraft X. These slides had been deployed, then they were put in large plastic bags three of them were shipped in a wooden box and the fourth in a cardboard box with no lid. All of the reservoirs were empty but the survival kits contain signaling flares which should have been shipped as hazardous. Explosion proof boxes were provided for the return shipping to shop but were not used.
ASRS:1805398.s: Aircraft X slides were shipped to the ZZZ slide shop in plastic bags and boxes without lids, despite containing hazardous signaling flares. Explosion-proof boxes provided for return shipping were not used, violating hazardous material transport requirements.

ASRS:1805409.n: The student and I had taken off of Runway 17 and at 1,500 feet MSL turned on course to the practice area on a heading of about 230. At this point, I had the student put on their foggles to start their simulated instrument time. Tower informed us that there was an aircraft about 6 miles to the South of the airport which was going in our general direction, their path was South to North. I acknowledged the call and told Tower we would keep a lookout for the traffic. The student asked about something on the instrument panels so I looked inside to answer their question. I heard the other aircraft radio that they had us insight. Since I had not yet gotten them in sight, I hoped to now be able to since they had. I looked back outside in the general direction that the airplane was supposed to be at (right side) and saw the airplane in a steep bank at approximately 400 feet from us with no vertical difference. As soon as I saw them, I banked the airplane to the right and kept our climb pitch attitude. I reported to Tower that I had the aircraft in sight.The conditions that caused the problem were: my heads-down time answering the student's question, not having Tower get a distance from the traffic, and not being able to locate them sooner.Actions to prevent/correct the situation: do not have my head down to answer a student's question, have Tower get a distance from the traffic.
ASRS:1805409.s: An instructor and student in a training aircraft experienced a near mid-air collision at 1,500 feet MSL while climbing after takeoff. The event was caused by the instructor's heads-down distraction answering a question, which delayed visual acquisition of a nearby aircraft until it was 400 feet away.

ASRS:1805411.n: I was providing instruction to my instrument student. He was in the left seat, flying the plane on autopilot, having been cleared by me (simulating ATC) to proceed via direct to the ZZZ VORTAC at 9,500 MSL, there to commence the RNAV XX approach, expecting a circle-to-land. I obtained approval from the ZZZ tower for this practice approach, with the usual caveats about maintaining VFR, no traffic separation provided, etc. That approval was granted while we were still about 10 miles west of the VORTAC, inbound to it at 9,500 MSL and perhaps 130 mph indicated. The top of ZZZ Class D is XX00 MSL, and we had no need to enter the Class D until we were final approach fix inbound.Soon after getting approval from the tower for the practice approach, the tower informed us that there was traffic at about our 10 o'clock, southeast bound. I saw it immediately both visually and on our GPS nav screen. It appeared to be a white high-wing LSA (Light Sport Aircraft), either a Remos or a Flight Design. I can't recall if the tower was talking to that plane, but I'd guess not, as the traffic advisory was issued only to our own tail number, as I recall.I watched the LSA carefully as my student (via our A/P (Autopilot), in NAV mode) took us towards the VORTAC. We seemed to be converging slowly, with only a 20 or 30 degree difference in our headings, and exactly the same altitude. The LSA was rock-steady in maintaining its heading and altitude, and seemed to be on A/P, also heading for the local VORTAC.We were slowly closing on the LSA, holding a constant bearing about 30 or 40 degrees behind its right wing. As the distance between us decreased to about a mile, I instructed my student to make a serious power reduction, which he would have done anyway over the VORTAC. I thought that this would change the equation enough that we would fall behind the LSA. After half a minute (or less), I realized that we were not slowing enough to make an appreciable difference in our closure, so I told my student to put his heading bug about 45 degrees off to the left of our heading, and punch the HEADING button on the A/P, which he did. Our 185 then made a nice standard-rate turn to the left, and we passed directly behind the LSA, exactly at its altitude and about 500 feet away. The LSA never wavered - as if he never saw us.After about a minute on our new heading, I 'cleared' my student from present position direct to the VORTAC to commence the approach. We heard nothing from the LSA, nor did we see it again. The practice approach and landing were without incident.As I recall, we were always behind the wing of the LSA, so we were the overtaking aircraft. I fault myself for waiting too long before starting the turn to break the slow-motion convergence with the other airplane. There was no chance that we were going to collide with it - I never stopped watching it, and I am an experienced formation pilot, good at judging closure rates and angles, etc. But I did not allow for the possibility that the LSA might make a sudden sharp turn towards us, or that its pilot might look out to his right rear and be unpleasantly surprised to see us there. If such a situation were to arise again, I would make an earlier turn or altitude change to get a good resolution, and try to keep a mile away from the converging traffic. It makes more sense, doesn't cost any more, and sets a better example for my student pilot.
ASRS:1805411.s: An instructor and student in a Cessna 185 experienced a slow convergence with a Light Sport Aircraft at 9,500 feet while inbound to the ZZZ VORTAC. The instructor delayed a left turn to resolve the conflict, passing 500 feet behind the other aircraft, and attributed the near-miss to waiting too long to alter course.

ASRS:1805426.n: I was doing an instrument approach in to CVO with a student. RNAV 35. We had made normal radio calls, 10, 7, 5, 2 and 2 miles out.There was one plane in the downwind who had called #2, landing behind my student and I on Runway 35. When we were below the LPV minimums and the student had removed the foggles, somebody on the ground holding short of Runway 35 called out 'there is about to be a mid air collision for the 2 planes on final.'My student and I both were looking out straight ahead and to the sides and saw nothing. Out of nowhere a plane [Aircraft Y] came over the top of us, from behind and to our right and almost clipped our left wingtip.To our knowledge, there was only one plane in the downwind aside from us on short final and 2 planes holding short of 35 ready to depart. My student confirms that they saw Aircraft Y land on Runway 35 and taxi off with no radio calls.We did everything right, making all the appropriate radio calls. Aircraft Y made no calls and we never saw them on ADS-B or out the window. The pilots from on the ground from two different planes both confirmed that Aircraft Y made no radio calls and that I and my student were doing everything correctly.I never saw Aircraft Y visually or over ADS-B. The student was under the foggles for the approach but when he went visual, we still never saw a plane near us.I can confirm nobody was departing Runway 17 at the time because there was already 1 plane doing pattern work for 35, and the plane who called out the near midair collision from the ground, had just completed a taxi from 17 to 35 on the ground because it was the runway in use.This was within feet of hitting our wing from above. Not only was this incredibly unsafe, but the fact that no radio call was made ever is even more concerning.
ASRS:1805426.s: A pilot and student conducting an RNAV 35 LPV approach into CVO experienced a near mid-air collision when an unseen aircraft overflew them from behind and right, nearly clipping their left wingtip. The intruder aircraft made no radio calls, was not visible on ADS-B, and landed without communication, while ground observers confirmed the incident.

ASRS:1805438.n: Initially reported to Tower my position and I was cleared to enter the right downwind. Adjacent to the Class D boundary common with the Class D airspace boundary with the adjacent airport, I was given a traffic advisory of a small aircraft inbound. I had that aircraft in sight and reported so. I was then instructed to 'Turn left and follow that traffic' I refused the left turn as that would have taken me into the adjacent airport Class D, so reported 'negative left turn, I am turning right and following the [small aircraft]'. When approaching there were three planes on the right downwind for the runway. Aircraft Y who was cleared to land short approach with a long landing, the small aircraft I was following and myself who was cleared to land number 3.Shortly after that, something caught my eye in my right peripheral vision. As I scanned it was an airplane broadside to me, northerly heading, at the same altitude as me, in a slight climb. As a collision was extremely possible, I took evasive action by chopping power and nosed over going negative G to miss the aircraft. I contacted the Tower of who was that airplane and why was he in my vicinity and not called for traffic. Controller went into meltdown about who was who and who was where. By this time the small aircraft I was following had landed. I did not follow the previously issued landing clearance to land number 3 behind the small aircraft, but rather followed this mystery plane which was finally identified as an X type plane who had been in the left closed traffic pattern doing touch and goes. Apparently, this plane made a right pattern after takeoff and went right into me on the right downwind. Controller and any supervisors should be watching that aircraft comply with the proper traffic patterns, and if there is a deviation, notify other aircraft that such non-compliance could create a traffic conflict. Due to a staffing shortage, the other two controllers in the cab were both Supervisors, which one was on Operational Supervisor and the other on Ground Control. [This was] an abnormal configuration at this time of day. Aircraft Y had been in the pattern with minimal traffic before I took the local position. Aircraft A reported inbound from the northwest. Aircraft A seemed unfamiliar and I provided him extra assistance. When Aircraft X checked on, inbound from the northwest, I had him follow Aircraft A as I preferred not to give Aircraft A more instructions than I deemed he could handle. Aircraft Z checked on inbound from the south. TRACON called with a direct for Aircraft B. I instructed Aircraft Y to extend climb straight out to a point and make right traffic to avoid Aircraft B's expected left downwind entry at a high rate of speed.The Supervisor stated that Aircraft C was inbound from the east for a hospital. I asked if Aircraft C was coordinated by TRACON or did I miss the check in. The Supervisor said TRACON had coordinated it. The Supervisor and Ground Control continued to debate with each other the intention of Aircraft C, the background noise can be heard in the background. Traffic on final needed to extend downwind, and thus, created a problem with Aircraft C's trajectory to cross the runway final. I asked the Supervisor to find out Aircraft C's intentions. Aircraft X reported a near mid-air collision with a small aircraft which was not the correct aircraft. This prompted me to verify Aircraft Z's position. Aircraft Z confirmed his position. Aircraft X mistook Aircraft Y, as Aircraft Z. It was at this time that I realized Aircraft Y had turned in front of Aircraft X. I allowed my attention to be drawn away from my pattern. I appreciate other controllers/ supervisors willing to provide assistance, but because all the information was not known it added another distraction to the operation.Aircraft C ended up entering the airspace without coordination. Aircraft C contacted MRI as he exited MRI airspace. Do not expect aircraft to fly the left and right downwind the same. Extend aircraft further if necessary. Tell aircraft to extend further out even if it extends the pattern. Do not allow others in the cab to distract you. Other controllers and supervisors' assistance is needed in the cab and appreciated. If, however, you do not have all the known information, before distracting the local controller, confirm with the appropriate facility/ sector the intentions of all aircraft.
ASRS:1805438.s: A pilot on right downwind executed evasive action to avoid a collision with an X-type aircraft that deviated from the left pattern into the right downwind. The reporter attributed the conflict to the X aircraft's non-compliance and controller distractions caused by uncoordinated traffic and internal cab debates.

ASRS:1805443.n: After an uneventful instrument cross-country flight, I listened to the destination airport ASOS, Wind 29 knot, Gusting 38, clouds OC 900 feet and Visibility 4 sm. I set up the FD (Flight Director) for the RNAV approach into the un-towered airport. I had done this approach before in marginal VFR conditions.Approach cleared me for the approach. With the autopilot coupled to the FD I passed the IAF in heavy IMC and turned inbound at the IF. Approach cleared me to switch to the UNICOM frequency, which I did. I noticed that the autopilot was not maneuvering the airplane as I had intended, it was making a climbing left turn off course. I decoupled the autopilot and hand flew the airplane while attempting to reset the FD. While being distracted trying to reset the FD I inadvertently got off altitude and heading and found myself in an unusual attitude. I recovered from the unusual attitude and got the airplane stabilized and hand flew the airplane and landed without further incident.I performed well during my recent IPC, but single pilot instrument flying in heavy IMC is not the same as being placed under-the-hood with flight instructor in the right seat. Also, emphasis should be made on (UPRT) Upset Prevention and Recovery Training. I will seek training before doing single pilot low IMC approaches in the future.
ASRS:1805443.s: A single pilot flying an instrument approach in heavy IMC experienced an autopilot deviation and subsequent unusual attitude while distracted by resetting the Flight Director. The pilot recovered, hand-flew the aircraft, and landed safely, noting a need for additional Upset Prevention and Recovery Training.

ASRS:1805450.n: Aircraft Y departed ZZZ1 airport IFR to the southeast out of the airspace, and Aircraft X was inbound landing ZZZ. Aircraft X was cleared to the IAF for Runway X at ZZZ and descended to 060. Aircraft Y was cleared to destination and climbed to 070. 2 additional aircraft departed ZZZ1 after Aircraft Y, and required more direct handling than Aircraft Y. Aircraft X mentioned that they were picking up traffic to their Northwest, and by the time I looked, Aircraft Y was leaving 061, and Aircraft X was at 072. They were separated by 2.62 miles and 900 feet vertically. During with dealing with the other departure's climbing out behind Aircraft Y, I lost the Aircraft Y's rate of climb reference the descending jet traffic. I immediately stopped Aircraft X 's descent, and stopped Aircraft Y's climb and descended Aircraft Y. Due to COVID protocol, this occurred while staffed with 4 CPCs and 1 Supervisor to work the facility until XA:00 local time.Better staffing to alleviate Controller fatigue. Our staffing has been tight, and time on position has been increased at the facility for a while, resulting in long work sessions and short breaks sometimes to produce coverage to work the traffic, which has resumed close to 90% of Pre-COVID numbers.
ASRS:1805450.s: An air traffic controller lost track of Aircraft Y's climb while managing other departures, allowing it to pass within 2.62 miles and 900 feet of descending Aircraft X. The controller immediately stopped both aircraft's vertical movements to restore separation, attributing the incident to controller fatigue caused by tight staffing and extended work sessions.

ASRS:1805455.n: I was working Local Control with our 2 parallel runways combined onto one frequency. There were 3 touch and goes, 2 on Runway XXR, and 1 on Runway XXL. There were 2 other aircraft inbound. I cleared Aircraft X to land runway XXR, sequencing them to follow Aircraft Y on a close in base. Aircraft Z called ready to go at Runway XXR to enter the traffic pattern. At the time, Aircraft Y was rolling out on the runway, so I told Aircraft Z to stand by. Once Aircraft Y became airborne, I cleared Aircraft Z for takeoff to follow Aircraft Y into the right-hand traffic pattern. I forgot about Aircraft X.Airport Ops called on frequency to inform me that he was at the localizer site on foot, and out of the Runway Safety Area. I glanced over to visually see Ops, who was past the departure end of Runway XXR. As Aircraft Z was crossing the threshold onto Runway XXR, Aircraft X was crossing over the top, intending to touch down onto the runway at the displaced threshold. Aircraft Z questioned why an aircraft was landing on the runway, which alerted me to the situation. I extended Aircraft Y downwind so they would not begin a base. I visually watched Aircraft X exit the runway, while Aircraft Z informed me he would wait for another takeoff clearance. Once Aircraft X was turned off the runway, I re-cleared Aircraft Z, and cleared Aircraft Y. I recommend the Tower controller should pay absolute attention to his active runways, and allow his pad to assist him in not forgetting about aircraft.
ASRS:1805455.s: A Local Control controller forgot about Aircraft X while managing traffic on combined parallel runways, allowing Aircraft Z to enter Runway XXR as Aircraft X crossed overhead for landing. The controller resolved the conflict after Aircraft Z questioned the landing, extending Aircraft Y's downwind leg and delaying Aircraft Z's takeoff until the runway was clear.

ASRS:1805457.n: Two different things happened. The first was a low altitude alert below the Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA). The second thing was a pilot deviation in the formation flight. The wingman climbed 700 feet higher than assigned altitude. Flight X was leaving TRACON airspace immediately following an intercept exercise to go to a restricted area. The controlling facility approach called and said that Flight X was not on the schedule and are not allowed to enter the restricted area.The aircraft was notified and they wanted to verify if they were on the schedule and that they should be able to enter. Flight X was told to expedite climb and told low altitude alert and the MIA is 10,900 feet. The aircraft entered the area lower than the MIA. The aircraft was then given another low altitude alert because he was about to penetrate another higher terrain area. Then the wingman climbed above the assigned altitude of 20,000 feet, he climbed to 20,700 feet. I asked the flight led to have the wingman maintain 20,000 feet.We had to vector the flight out of restricted facilities airspace because of a non-important reason and we put the flight crew at risk. They were concerned with getting access to the restricted area and busted the altitude for the MIA and the assigned altitude. These are single piloted fighter aircraft that are being denied entry into an area for fighter aircraft and in a high terrain area with additional civilian aircraft.
ASRS:1805457.s: An air traffic controller reported that two single-pilot fighter aircraft in a formation received low altitude alerts for flying below the 10,900-foot MIA while denied entry to a restricted area. The wingman also deviated by climbing to 20,700 feet above the assigned 20,000 feet, requiring vectors out of the high-terrain airspace.

ASRS:1805467.n: I was taking over a MAX 8 that had an MAX/MEL for Pressure Fueling System XX-XX-XX. The outgoing Crew just had this MEL applied by MX on the Flight they finished. I had a similar MEL on an NG twice in the last few weeks that required a 'repetitive write up' so I assumed that this one would require a repetitive write up also. I looked up the MAX 8/MEL and it has a MUCH different format than the NG MEL but it lists repetitive write up in the beginning column instead of in the 'plain text' part of the MEL. The outgoing Crew who just had the MEL applied by Maintenance in ZZZ said there was no repetitive write up required, so I called Maintenance to inquire because I believed that a repetitive write up WAS required. Maintenance was also a little confused as if a repetitive write up was required. So based on my reading of the MEL and after talking to my Dispatcher I elected to do the repetitive write up on the three flights we did with that aircraft.I am writing this as I see there is some confusion on the repetitive write up in the MAX MEL as opposed to a similar MEL in the NG. I could be reading this wrong but I believe a repetitive write up is required for MAX MEL XX-XX-XX. The Dispatcher also wrote his supervisors to look into this.
ASRS:1805467.s: A pilot assumed a repetitive write-up was required for a MAX 8 fueling system MEL, differing from the outgoing crew's advice. After consulting maintenance and a dispatcher, the pilot performed the write-up on three flights due to confusion over the MAX MEL format compared to the NG.

ASRS:1805497.n: Ramp Service personnel are required to work outside in the elements while wearing a face mask as per the Government mandate. It is heating up very quickly in ZZZ. While we understand the importance of the mask mandate it is time that someone revisit the mandate and make some adjustments as far as wearing face masks outside. It is literally becoming more difficult to breathe while wearing a face mask in the extreme heat. Our Company's flight schedule and work load in ZZZ are just about pre-pandemic levels. Today, I was on a crew that had to go across the field to the Company hangar and tow an aircraft back to the terminal gates. Upon returning from the hangar, I observed employees from two other major airlines working the ramp without face masks along with an entire construction crew working on the field for the XXXX County Aviation Authority and not one was wearing a face mask. If the mandate is not being enforced out on the Ramp, then why is the mandate still in place?
ASRS:1805497.s: Ramp service personnel in ZZZ reported difficulty breathing while wearing mandated face masks in extreme heat during aircraft towing operations. The reporter noted that employees from other airlines and a construction crew were working on the ramp without masks, questioning the mandate's enforcement.

ASRS:1805505.n: Tug Dispatcher reported that when towing an aircraft to its gate a Garbage Services truck cut them off by continuously driving on the Vehicle Service Road.
ASRS:1805505.s: A Tug Dispatcher reported that while towing an aircraft to its gate, a Garbage Services truck cut them off by continuously driving on the Vehicle Service Road.

ASRS:1805515.n: Aircraft was dispatched with MEL XX #2 ENGINE COWL A/I VLV pos MNTR SYS-ENG 2 VLV-A/I MANF FAIL (DUCT BRST DET) -VLV OPEN. During climb out from ZZZ received a level 3 ENG 2 A-ICE alert. Retarding throttle to idle cleared alert. The climb was stopped at FL230. QRH checklist, consultation with dispatch and Maintenance resulted in an engine shutdown, [advising ATC] and air turn back to ZZZ. The return and landing at ZZZ were uneventful. My suspicion is that we probably did not have a bleed air leak in the Eng 2 ice duct, but rather a higher than normal temp in the area around the duct due to the anti-ice valve being secured open due to the MEL and high power settings during the climb in relatively high ambient temperatures. Although we did follow the QRH and shut down the engine as if it were a duct leak. I am sure I will receive feedback from my event report on whether or not that is correct after Maintenance has had time to inspect the aircraft.
ASRS:1805515.s: The crew dispatched with an MEL-secured open anti-ice valve received a Level 3 ENG 2 A-ICE alert during climb, prompting a shutdown and return to ZZZ. The pilot suspects the alert resulted from high duct temperatures due to the open valve and high power, rather than a bleed air leak.

ASRS:1805557.n: Near the end of the cruise phase of flight we briefed the arrival and the approach to the landing runway. During the brief of the arrival we had noticed that the crossing restriction at the first fix (DARAN) on the arrival (DARAN1A) was incorrect as compared between the approach plate and the arrival selected out of the FMC. The DARAN1A arrival is FL210 to FL230 at the DARAN, the altitude from the FMC showed FL250 to FL280 (DARAN1B). At this point we both cross checked the date on the approach and discussed when we had both done our last update. We concluded that we had both updated just before the flight and the dates were correct on the approach chart. We then had thought that maybe we had incorrectly loaded the wrong arrival into the FMC. We proceeded to monitor each other as we reloaded the landing runway approach and the correct arrival. After reloading the FMC with the landing runway approach and the DARAN1A for arrival we noticed that the crossing restriction at DARAN remain the same FL250 to FL280. Due to congestion in Mexico City our flight and another flight were told to hold 20 miles north of DARAN. When told to continue our plan was to question the crossing restriction at DARAN, but we were descended in the hold to FL210. After arriving at FL210 we were cleared to DARAN and the rest of the arrival landing on Runway 5R [was] uneventful. I have previously been into Mexico City and number of times and the DARAN1A crossing restriction at DARAN has been correct as depicted compared to the FMC. NOTE: All other fixes and crossing restrictions on the DARAN1A were correct except DARAN at FL250 to FL280. The FMC loaded DARAN1A is incorrect. Please check the FMC database is correct to make sure the DARAN crossing restriction between FL210 toFL230 is correct.
ASRS:1805557.s: Pilots discovered a discrepancy between the approach chart and FMC database for the DARAN1A arrival into Mexico City, showing incorrect crossing altitudes at the DARAN fix. Despite reloading the correct procedure, the FMC retained the error, but the crew descended to FL210 in a hold and completed an uneventful landing after questioning the restriction.

ASRS:1805558.n: On a day, VFR approach to RNO just to the north of waypoint URATE as depicted on the RNAV (RNP) Y to 16L, EGPWS alerted 'Caution, obstacle.' The FO as pilot flying altered his flight path, yet we then received 'Obstacle, pull-up!' which the FO did. Both the hill and obstacle at 5,101 feet MSL were in sight the entire time. We then continued for a normal uneventful landing. Enroute, we had discussed extensively the challenges of RNO, including terrain, single runway, engine failure considerations, and higher than typical descent rates and true airspeeds, and were comfortable with our position and closure rate with the hill and tower.Cause - EGWPS will alert for terrain or obstacles for either proximity or closure rate sooner than I expected. By being carefully studied on the terrain and obstacles in the vicinity of RNO prior to arrival, we were well aware of the tower and hill located at the location of the EGPWS alert.Suggestions - Give a wider avoidance to high terrain or obstacles both horizontally, vertically, and with respect to closure rate. Cleared visual approach 16L RNO. Turned to intercept extended final near FAP WORTH. Had briefed and set up for RNAV (RNP) Y 16L and using it as backup to visual. Dialed in 6,400 and began descent to FAP altitude turning base to final. EGPWS alerted 'Caution, Obstacle'. As PF I verified obstacle in site and continued turn to final away from it. Soon after alert 'Obstacle, Pull up' occurred. I disconnected the AP and initiated a climbing turn away from obstacle that we had kept in site the entire time. Alert ceased very quickly and we continued an uneventful and stable approach and landing. Approach briefing had included a good discussion on RNO hazards including single runway operations, EO considerations, mountainous terrain, high descent rates and TAS. We knew where the obstacle/ hill was on the approach and felt comfortable with our position relative to it on the visual approach.Cause - The preceding aircraft was denied the instrument approach. Visuals in mountainous terrain create unique challenges. Being cleared to follow proceeding aircraft and maintain spacing may have also caused a more square pattern than desired which brought us closer to the obstacle.Suggestions - Maintain the practice of following IAP ground track even on a visual approach if not intimately familiar with the terrain. Also, be cognizant of how EGPWS tracks descent and closure rate. The warnings certainly came quicker than we expected. I would give high terrain an even wider berth.
ASRS:1805558.s: Pilots flying a visual approach to RNO 16L received EGPWS obstacle alerts due to high closure rates near a known hill. They executed a climbing turn away from the terrain and completed a normal landing, attributing the alerts to EGPWS sensitivity and a square pattern caused by spacing behind a denied instrument approach.

ASRS:1805583.n: Departing DTW [Runway] 3L on the HHOWE3 RNAV departure we had a wake turbulence encounter. ATC cleared us for takeoff behind an A320. We completed a normal takeoff profile. Autopilot was engaged at 600 feet AGL and flap retraction was completed on schedule. We were at approximately 1,800 feet AGL (2,450 feet MSL) accelerating when the aircraft abruptly rolled 35 degrees right and pitched up. The autopilot disconnected automatically and the shaker activated momentarily for around 1-2 seconds. Having a hand defensively positioned for the yoke, I immediately pitched down and rolled the wings level. Once the aircraft was sufficiently under control and at a safe airspeed, autopilot was reengaged and the rest of the flight was completed without incident. We checked on the Flight Attendant to ensure she and the cabin were safe. She confirmed everything was ok. We lifted off prior to the preceding aircraft and flew according to our profiles. ATC should have given more separation between us and them. ATC needs to better separate aircraft, especially with loads increasing. There is no need to push aircraft out so closely spaced.
ASRS:1805583.s: The crew departed DTW Runway 3L behind an A320 and encountered wake turbulence at 1,800 feet AGL, causing a 35-degree roll and autopilot disconnect. The pilot manually recovered control, and the reporter attributed the incident to insufficient ATC separation.

ASRS:1805641.n: I departed BQ1 on Runway 31 and announced my attentions to return for an approach to Runway 13. After maneuvering to final for 13 I started my approach. I noticed an airplane pull out on the runway and start to back taxi. Since I was already low and approaching the numbers on Runway 13, I added full power to accelerate and began a climb before reaching the other aircraft. I also side stepped to be over the parallel grass runway. I passed above and to the left of the other aircraft by a few hundred feet.Although the winds were light and approaches had been made in both directions within the hour, it was not a good choice to depart one runway and then perform an approach to the opposite runway.
ASRS:1805641.s: The pilot departed Runway 31 and approached Runway 13, but another aircraft was back-taxiing on the active runway. The pilot executed a go-around and side-step to pass safely above the other aircraft, attributing the conflict to the poor choice of using opposite runways for departure and approach.

ASRS:1805648.n: Me and my student are on a cross country training flight from ZZZ to JWG on clear VMC day with light and variable winds. We are coming in from the east to enter the traffic pattern at JWG by flying over head the airport and entering the right downwind for Runway 17 as that runway is right traffic. Approaching overhead I notice that there are multiple aircraft taxiing on the ground on the parallel taxiway. We make multiple position reports on local CTAF about our position on each leg of the traffic pattern and me nor my student hear any other radio calls for our destination. The student is flying the entire traffic pattern and was doing a normal approach and landing. Our last radio call was on short final about one half to one mile final. As soon as we touched down on Runway 17 about 500 feet from the threshold, both me and my student notice that an aircraft [Aircraft Y] had pulled onto the runway from what appeared to be a taxiway that was at the midpoint of the runway and had turned to face north as if the aircraft had intentions to takeoff or back taxi on the runway. As soon as me and my student noticed the aircraft facing directly at us, about two seconds after touching the ground, my student executed a go-around and immediately climbed our aircraft away from the runway and made a slight turn to the left so that we would not overfly the runway. We then exited the traffic pattern back to ZZZ without further incident. This airport is a class G airport so there is no requirement for use of radios in that airspace, but there seemed to be little vigilance on the part of Aircraft Y for noticing an aircraft on short final with strobe and landing lights operable and on.
ASRS:1805648.s: A pilot and student executing a landing on Runway 17 at Class G airport JWG observed Aircraft Y entering the runway from a midpoint taxiway immediately after touchdown. The student performed a go-around to avoid a collision, attributing the incident to Aircraft Y's lack of vigilance despite the landing aircraft's active lights.

ASRS:1805663.n: After my runup at Runway XXR, I proceeded to hold short of Runway XXR at Taxiway 1. I announced on CTAF 'Grumman Tiger is taking Runway XXR for left downwind departure'. Having heard no response, I entered on the runway and started my roll. I was airborne before passing Taxiway 2. About 30 seconds later I heard 'Cessna [...] clear of Runway XXR at taxiway 3'. I assumed someone was crossing the runway and just forgot to announce entering it.I landed about 40 minutes later. After stopping by my tiedown, I was approached by the airport ops gentleman who advised me that during my take off there was another airplane still on the opposite end of Runway XXR.According to the airport ops gentleman (he stated he had already spoken with the other pilot), this plane had landed Runway XXR just before I started my runup and had been sitting on the runway for 4 minutes before finally exiting at the opposite end (Taxiway 3). He also mentioned this plane had some communication problems talking to another plane while still airborne prior to his landing.I didn't hear any radio announcement and I didn't see any traffic on my ADS-B In screen.I don't believe I would be able to discern a small tail light of that plane given the distance (8,000 ft runway) and the airport lighting (ZZZ has lots of lights now, new taxiway lights, under construction lights, etc.). At no point there was any danger of collision since I never even saw this airplane but I will have to be more vigilant and take into account that technical difficulties may prevent other pilots from hearing me or responding to me.
ASRS:1805663.s: A Grumman Tiger pilot departed Runway XXR without hearing a Cessna that had landed and remained on the opposite end for four minutes due to communication issues. The pilot reported no collision risk as the other aircraft was unseen, attributing the oversight to the Cessna's radio problems and airport lighting conditions.

ASRS:1805685.n: Prior to making the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, I met with my Flight Instructor to review my flight plan and briefing which I created. All parameters were within the confines of my limitations for my student pilot endorsements for a student solo, cross-country operation. This was my first cross-county solo flight in the aircraft. I was to make two full-stop landings at ZZZ1 as part of the flight, then return to ZZZ. Takeoff from ZZZ and cruise to ZZZ1 were uneventful. I flew at 5,500 feet and reported transitioning the airspace above a non-controlled airport along the way. Immediately after reporting this transition, and well prior to entering the Delta Airspace of ZZZ1, I switched my COM2 radio to ZZZ1 and got the latest automated weather report. I do not recall what the letter designation for the report was at the time, but the weather was clear with good visibility of 10+ miles, winds relatively calm, and a clear sky. I then radioed the tower at ZZZ1 on their frequency and identified myself as a student pilot solo flight along with my relative position west of the airport and requested a full-stop landing while approximately 15nm away.The Tower answered saying they were having difficulty hearing my transmission and to restate my position. I spoke more loudly and clearly, identifying my position as west at about 14.6 miles. They advised me to re-contact them when less than a mile from the runway. I began a descent appropriate to arrive at pattern altitude prior to radio contact. When I got within a mile I radioed the tower and the tower advised me to turn for my base and that I was cleared to land. I executed turns to base and final without issue and extended full flaps incrementally. Upon entering final approach with full-flaps I was just high of the glideslope as indicated by the PAPI system. I entered my flair and 'ballooned' slightly. When I came back down from ballooning, I came down hard and in the process, experienced prop strike, front gear collapse, and damage to my right wing before coming to a stop on the grass to the left of the runway with the help of the grass to arrest my momentum. The plane came to rest in a nose-down fashion at an approximate 45 degree angle to the edge of the runway and in the direction of the landing. After announcing over the radio that they have a crash on the runway, the tower radioed me to ask my condition and I replied that I was fine. I then noticed fuel leaking from my right wing and elected to shut down electrical items as a precaution. When the airport firetruck arrived, the operator sprayed foam on the area leaking as a precaution for the fuel leak. After several minutes, the responding airport staff strapped the nose wheel to the fuselage and were able to pull the plane to a storage hangar with a tractor by keeping the plane on the main landing gear and tugging the plane via the tail tie-down.
ASRS:1805685.s: A student pilot soloing a cross-country flight in a single-engine aircraft experienced a hard landing with prop strike and gear collapse at ZZZ1 due to ballooning on final approach. The aircraft came to rest nose-down off the runway with fuel leaking, but the pilot was uninjured and the plane was later towed to a hangar.

ASRS:1805744.n: [We were] cleared for the visual approach. Pilot in Command hand flew the visual approach. Switched to Tower and was cleared to land. During the descent to land Pilot in Command got too low. Second in Command informed Pilot in Command to climb as aircraft was too low and almost hit terrain Pilot in Command said he was good, Second in Command advised Pilot in Command to immediately climb. Pilot in Command was reluctant to climb. Tower informed us that we were too low for that sector of the approach and to Immediately climb. Pilot in Command climbed back up to 3,100 feet from 2,000 feet, then landed normally. Pilot in Command lost situational awareness during a visual approach. Pilot in Command initially did not react and did not listen to advice from Second in Command that the aircraft was too low on the Approach. It was not until the ATC Tower Controller told crew to immediately climb to 3,100 feet, did the Pilot in Command react and then climb back up to 3,100 feet. Suggest that the company discusses and better trains flight crews in performing visual approaches at day and night and to somehow incorporate improved Crew Resource Management Training so that if a Second in Command tells the Pilot in Command to climb or descend Immediately, he or she will listen and react immediately, and then ask questions later when the risk factor has been mitigated.
ASRS:1805744.s: During a visual approach, the Pilot in Command descended too low and ignored the Second in Command's warnings until the Tower controller ordered an immediate climb to 3,100 feet. The incident resulted from the Pilot in Command's loss of situational awareness and failure to heed crew advice, though the aircraft landed normally after recovering altitude.

ASRS:1805763.n: Flight ready early. Pushed back 15 mins early with OPS Controller approval. Also notified controller of 2,000 lb extra fuel. Preflight push back and taxi went smoothly. After accepting takeoff clearance we received a ACARS message from OPS asking if we had received DG (Dangerous Goods) paperwork. First Officer and I agreed we thought we did. Uneventful flight and landing. After level at cruise we inspected DG envelope and found it to be empty. We did have DG manifest signed with employee numbers and DG position summary showing Lithium Ion [Battery] at 12L. ACARS this info to Operations Center and he asked us to complete an ASAP. In summary everything was running super smoothly. Inaccessible DG seems to be every flight and we just assumed ULD DG manifest was in envelope we were given. Will check from now on! The cause of the event Assumed required paperwork was in DG envelope we were handed [was empty.] Uneventful and smooth preflight, startup, and taxi to Runway XX at ZZZ. After receiving takeoff clearance and approaching the runway threshold we received an ACARS message asking if we had received the DG (Dangerous Goods) paperwork. We both agreed we had and continued to take off. At cruise we discovered that the DG envelope was empty and did not have the Aircraft ULD DG Manifest. We did have the signed Aircraft DG Manifest and the Aircraft DG Position Summary showing lithium battery in position 12L. The ramp agent had placed the DG envelope in the yellow pouch. Poor coordination between flight crew and ramp agent with DG paperwork. [Going forward have] all eyes, flight crew and ramp agent or DG Specialist, must see and account for all DG paperwork.
ASRS:1805763.s: Flight crew and a ramp agent were involved during preflight and cruise when the DG envelope was found empty due to poor coordination. Although the crew assumed paperwork was present and took off, they later discovered the missing ULD manifest while holding the signed DG manifest and position summary.

ASRS:1805782.n: Enroute to ZZZ1 at 12,000 and 300 kts with AP on, I saw the flap indicator appear on ED1 and momentarily display flaps extended before returning to zero. Approx 1-2 seconds later, the aircraft pitched nose down slightly and descended about 200 feet before leveling off and returning to our assigned altitude. We notified Dispatch and Maintenance, and decided that the best course of action would be an air return to ZZZ. We flew back to ZZZ and landed without further incident.Cause - The FO and I initially both suspected a momentary uncommanded flap movement due to the indication and the pitch down moment we experienced. We discussed the situation with Operations and they requested we return to ZZZ, a decision that we agreed with. Later discussions with Maintenance brought up the possibility that an erroneous sensor indication may have caused the auto trim system to trim the aircraft nose down.
ASRS:1805782.s: The crew en route to ZZZ1 at 12,000 feet experienced a momentary flap indication and a 200-foot descent, likely caused by an erroneous sensor triggering auto trim. They returned to ZZZ and landed safely after consulting with Operations and Maintenance.

ASRS:1805789.n: At XA:55Z the master caution light, auto pilot disconnect aural warning and IRS annunciation light activated. The FO was the PF and immediately began to hand fly the aircraft. As PM, I verified the aircraft was stable and performed QRH XX.X IRS fault. After completing the required items and discussing all of the impact items, I sent ATC a CPDLC message as to our loss of navigation equipment and inability to remain in RVSM airspace due to the loss of the auto pilot. ATC instructed to remain at FL370 due to traffic. We called dispatch via SATCOM and relayed our current situation and reiterated our need to use the ILS RWY XX into ZZZ due to the loss of RNAV capabilities. After a conference call with Operations and Maintenance, we continued to ZZZ and landed uneventfully via the ILS RWY XX.We split the flying duties to avoid fatigue (30 minute intervals). ATC was given 2 hours to plan our arrival to the opposite runway, and they did an exemplary job. ZZZ1 was built in route 2 as our primary divert airport.
ASRS:1805789.s: The First Officer hand-flew the aircraft after an IRS fault triggered master caution and autopilot disconnect warnings at FL370. The crew diverted to ZZZ for an uneventful ILS landing after losing RNAV capabilities and RVSM approval.

ASRS:1805793.n: As I was leveling off at my assigned altitude of 6,000 ft just above the base of a scattered layer of clouds I saw a large black and silver object in my peripheral vision. I was able to catch a quick look at the object as it passed off my left wing. I would estimate the distance as having been approximately 10 ft from my wingtip. I had just exited a cloud when the object appeared, so there would have been extremely little time to take evasive action if it had been a bit further to my right. The object appeared to be a quad-copter style drone, and as previously mentioned it was black and silver/chrome. I immediately reported the object to ATC, and a nearby law enforcement aircraft went to investigate the area. The object did not strike my aircraft and the flight was completed with no further issues. Recommendation: Stricter enforcement of drone operation rules, perhaps drone manufacturers should include a pamphlet in each box describing the dangers associated with busy airspace.
ASRS:1805793.s: A pilot reported a near-miss with a black and silver quad-copter drone while leveling off at 6,000 ft just above scattered clouds. The drone passed approximately 10 ft from the left wingtip, but no collision occurred, and the flight was completed safely after the pilot notified ATC.

ASRS:1805802.n: While landing in ZZZ it was the worst turbulence ever experienced on landing. The aircraft had shifted on a sharp tilt aircraft left and sharply right. The door to the Portable Oxygen Bottles (POBs) opened and when the wheels/aircraft touched down with excessive velocity and force it catapulted the POB's forward into the isle of the aircraft. But, the grace of GOD, and physics, no one was injured! The latched locked failed. Passenger X was one of many witnesses, his kids were sitting in aft as well! I don't know how but lord I'm so thankful that no one was hit by the catapulted POB bottles. The landing was furious and as the gusts were up to 35 MPH and flaps and speed were notable not in conjunction of safety. It was clear on a not so perfect hard landing the locks failed easily. A very dangerous situation at the very least. As stated thank the lord no one was injured! The locks on cabinet failed and the brackets also failed to keep the POB's secure. It needs complete checks for the safety of the passengers and crew members alike.
ASRS:1805802.s: During a turbulent landing in ZZZ with 35 MPH gusts, a hard touchdown caused the Portable Oxygen Bottle cabinet locks and brackets to fail, catapulting bottles into the aisle. The reporter states that despite the dangerous situation, no passengers or crew were injured.

ASRS:1805820.n: I taxied from the southeast ramp intending to use Runway XXR for takeoff. When exiting the ramp Taxiway Alpha has an unmarked entrance at the very southeast end of the airport. While holding at the entrance line to Alpha ground cleared me to the Bravo run-up area just ahead of me. I did so crossing two separate dash lines on the pavement and then turned 180 deg facing back at the ramp. I saw no sign for the Bravo Taxiway nor for Runway XXR. The Tower cleared me for takeoff, but did not say to use Bravo to get to the runway which was behind me. Once cleared for takeoff I crossed both sets of dashed lines thinking I was on Runway XXR but later realized I was aligned with a taxiway.The contributing factors were entering Taxiway A at an unmarked intersection and then crossing two sets of dashed lines to the run-up area that had no marking signs. Once at the run-up area I did not see any signs for Taxiway Bravo or [Runway] XXR. Perhaps another contributing factor was not flying for seven months prior to this flight because of COVID.In retrospect during flight planning, I should have gotten an enlarged airport diagram and studied it thoroughly, anticipating my route to the assigned runway and noting any potential issues in advance. I would then zoom in on satellite maps to clarify what it actually looked like on the ground. If that didn't clear it up I would call Ground Control and discuss it with them before arrival. If I'm ever uncertain when actually taxiing I can always ask for progressive taxi instructions from Ground Control. Aircraft X was issued a takeoff clearance for Runway XXR and departed on Taxiway 'A' which runs parallel to the runway. The Local Controller was issuing traffic to other aircraft and did not see the Aircraft X rolling on Taxiway 'A'. By the time we caught it I told the local controller not to cancel the takeoff clearance as it was heading directly for Aircraft Y that was taxiing opposite direction on Alpha and the departing aircraft would not have had the space to stop before a collision would've ensued. The departing aircraft passed what I estimate to be 70-90 feet above Aircraft Y on the taxiway.Recommendation - Continuation by the FAA to inform and educate pilots on the hazards associated with wrong surface departures.
ASRS:1805820.s: A pilot departed on Taxiway Alpha instead of Runway XXR due to unmarked intersections and lack of signage, exacerbated by recent inactivity. Air Traffic Control detected the error and allowed the departure to avoid a collision with an opposing aircraft, resulting in a 70-90 foot separation.

ASRS:1805825.n: Landed Runway XX. Wind was right quartering 4-6 knots. Landed using a wheel landing, after slowing to about 20 knots or less the tail lowered and the aircraft veered hard right. Unable to counter with rudder and brake. Result was a ground loop to the right. Aircraft stayed on the runway and partially exited onto Taxiway 1. Left tire was blown. Left wing tip made ground contact. Quarterly tailwind was contributing, afternoon hot conditions.
ASRS:1805825.s: The pilot landed an aircraft on Runway XX in hot conditions with a quartering tailwind. After slowing below 20 knots, the aircraft veered right, ground looped, and exited onto Taxiway 1, causing a blown left tire and left wingtip contact.

ASRS:1805826.n: I departed out of ZZZ for a flight back to ZZZ1. We climbed up to 7,500 ft and asked for flight following from approach, which we got. After passing ZZZ2 we cancelled service and descended to 2,500 feet. After a while I noticed the voltage was lower than normal and the alternator charge indicator was showing a discharge. The low voltage light never came on. I got out the POH and went through the procedure to attempt the reset the alternator. It did not reset. I reviewed the manual gear extension procedure just in case I needed to use it. I shut off all nonessential radios and electrical equipment as called for in the POH. I wasn't sure if I would have communication with a weak battery so to preserve what was left in the battery, I shut off the master switch. I doing that, I got to thinking, I didn't have the ADS-B output normally required. I continued on the ZZZ1 as planned, avoiding controlled airspace and any airports along my path. when I got within about 15 mins of ZZZ1, I turned the battery master and Avionic master back on. I extended the landing gear and called ZZZ1 tower, explaining I had an alternator failure and requested clearance to land. They offered runway XXL which I declined. (Major tailwind, gusts to 20 knot) flew a normal pattern and landed on runway YYR without incident.I continued on to ZZZ1 because of the knowledge of the area, traffic flows and airports if I could not talk to ZZZ1 tower. If this would have happened at night, I would have landed at the first airport with lights.A broken alternator field wire at the connector was found the next day.
ASRS:1805826.s: A pilot experienced an alternator failure at 2,500 feet while en route to ZZZ1, causing low voltage and discharge indications. After conserving battery power and avoiding controlled airspace, the pilot landed safely on runway YYR; a broken alternator field wire was later identified as the cause.

ASRS:1805836.n: Take-off clearance referred to 'KOA Antenna'. I saw antennas off the end of the runway, and thought they were the intended landmark. Climbing straight out towards the antennas, the controller got upset that I wasn't 'remaining west of Parker Road', so I initiated a turn to the left to try to remain west of Parker Road (a prominent highway), but this upset him more, so I turned right and flew southeast, west of Parker Road. I later determined that the 'KOA Antenna' refers to a 672 foot AM radio tower located southwest of the town of Parker. I was given a number, and I called the Tower upon landing. I was told 'no deviation would be filed', and had a discussion about not accepting a clearance when I was unclear about the instructions. This was my first time flying into Centennial Airport. It was very busy. Take-away: Don't accept a clearance based on local landmarks when operating at an airport for the first time. The KOA tower is not charted on the TAC chart or the FLY chart, or the sectional. It is also not discussed in any web pages associated with APA. I had researched the destination, but was caught flat footed when they gave me the clearance, and assumed the antennas I was looking at were the intended landmark. Bad assumption.
ASRS:1805836.s: A pilot departing Centennial Airport misinterpreted a "KOA Antenna" take-off clearance as visible runway antennas instead of an uncharted radio tower, causing a deviation from the required west-of-Parker Road route. The controller expressed frustration, but no deviation was filed after the pilot landed and discussed the error.

ASRS:1805857.n: I completed a run-up at departure end penalty box and observed an airport vehicle depart the same place. As I was preparing to taxi, a jet called my aircraft identifying by location to request my intentions. I stated 'run up complete but he can start a back taxi.' I started the taxi to the active runway. He declined in favor of my departure. I called 'taxi and departure Runway X, VFR to the east.' I rolled on to the runway displaced threshold while checking for traffic on final. I observed the jet had not moved but he called and requested if anyone else was inbound to land, to no response. I checked the plane was secured, and after rolling some of the displaced threshold, checked instruments and passengers, and applied full power. After reaching rotation speed, I observed the airport vehicle cross the runway in front of me. It appeared he was playing chicken. I considered rejecting the takeoff but could not be certain the power changes and braking would help avoid the collision. Thankfully the vehicle cleared the runway and I was off the ground moments later. I think safety can be improved by having ground vehicles at uncontrolled airports stating their intentions. A simple call of 'crossing the active runway' would have improved safety as I could check and delay my takeoff. I called on CTAF during departure that the ground vehicles crossing was 'not good' and another voice agreed. I met the driver later and he was the voice that replied. As pilot in command, I will improve by maintaining situational awareness of aircraft and NORDO ground vehicles. It was a busy time with other traffic and that is a good reminder to double check your aircraft and intended path.
ASRS:1805857.s: The pilot of a departing aircraft at an uncontrolled airport observed a ground vehicle cross the active runway during takeoff roll. The pilot rejected the option to abort due to uncertainty about braking effectiveness, but the vehicle cleared the runway before the aircraft became airborne.

ASRS:1805890.n: Coming in on the OHSEA2 arrival we requested the visual to 20R into SNA. Passing over BHEAR waypoint we were asked if we had an arriving aircraft in site that was inbound from the east, I believe on the Disney4 arrival. We visually acquired the aircraft and was told to descend to 4,000 feet MSL just to the east of BHEAR. We were then told to turn right heading 030 and asked if we had the aircraft in site and we said 'yes, in site. We were told to continue the right turn to 120 and then told we were cleared for the visual approach Runway 20R. When we were coming around at 4,000 feet MSL I realized we had been vectored inside of LEMON. I had to make an aggressive descent in order to capture the Glide Path to be stabilized by 500 feet AGL in order to have a normal descent rate with approach power and approach speed captured. During this aggressive rate of descent to capture glide path (estimated over 2,000 feet FPM), Tower made an advisory call 'low altitude warning, check altitude;' we were actually above glide slope and coming down onto Glide path when Tower made this call but the steep descent rate triggered their warning system and they made a radio call for a 'low altitude warning;' we were never below glide slope/glide path.The most important take away is that this whole scenario started because SoCal approach vectored us high and turned us tight inside of LEMON. This high and tight turn is very hard to capture a stabilized approach. I would recommend that SoCal gives additional downwind distance prior to turning base leg if the requirement is to stay above 2,500 feet MSL when turning near LEMON or HUKEM."
ASRS:1805890.s: Pilots on an OHSEA2 arrival into SNA were vectored high and tight inside LEMON by SoCal Approach, forcing an aggressive descent to capture the glide path. This steep descent rate triggered a tower low altitude warning, though the aircraft remained above the glide slope.

ASRS:1805892.n: I was the instructor with a student training for a private pilot check-ride. The runway in use was Runway 30. My student entered mid-field left downwind for Runway 30 and made all appropriate calls. For example 10 miles out, 5 miles out, entering mid-field left downwind, left base, and final on the CTAF frequency. As we turned base another aircraft took off and was climbing out as we turned final. When my student was coming in, student was preparing to do a soft field landing. There was also active parachuting going on. When we were extremely short final the plane holding short of the runway made a call to say they were departing Runway 30 as we were coming down crossing over the threshold. They immediately started rolling toward the runway and I said 'Wait! Wait!' on the frequency. My student was starting the rounding out process and they immediately came to a stop just across the hold short line and said something about stopping on the frequency as we were touching down. I do not recall the call sign of the airplane that caused the runway incursion. We full stopped and taxied back and they departed. The aircraft was clearly not paying attention to our calls and either did not see us on final or did not look.
ASRS:1805892.s: A student pilot and instructor on final approach for Runway 30 experienced a runway incursion when another aircraft began departing without acknowledging their CTAF calls. The departing aircraft stopped just across the hold short line after the instructor intervened, though the reporter attributed the incident to the other pilot's lack of situational awareness.

ASRS:1805907.n: This report does not involve a specific incident but is submitted as a suggestion to improve safety for aircraft operating in the area of FLL Class C airspace. I am recommending a change to the MIA Class B airspace to include a new section of protected airspace to provide a sterile section of airspace for arriving aircraft on the FLL 10L and 10R instrument approaches. Arriving aircraft into FLL typically are crossing PIONN at or above 2,500 feet descending to cross NOVEA at 1,800 feet on the ILS 10L and RNAV Z 10L approaches, as low as 2,200 feet on the RNAV Y approach from ZIRLA to SIYOL (which could be raised to 2,500 feet to coincide with the minimum altitudes on the ILS 10L and RNAV 10L Z approaches). Aircraft arriving on the ILS 10R and RNAV 10R approaches are crossing BLAIM at or above 3,000 descending to cross the FAF LORII at 1,800 feet. If a new wedge of class B airspace from 2,000 feet to 7,000 feet where added where currently there are no restrictions to inbound and outbound traffic utilizing HWO and OPF safety would be greatly enhanced. FLL has extensive inbound traffic and operations at HWO and OPF are significant. Air carrier passengers deserve the added protection and as a general aviation pilot the changes would have minimal impact.
ASRS:1805907.s: A general aviation pilot suggested modifying MIA Class B airspace to create a sterile zone for FLL arrivals on ILS 10L/10R and RNAV approaches. The proposed 2,000 to 7,000-foot wedge aims to enhance safety for inbound traffic and operations at HWO and OPF with minimal impact on general aviation.

ASRS:1805908.n: I landed on the newly-resurfaced and painted Runway XXR at ZZZ, although this runway was closed by NOTAM.I was returning to my home airfield after three weeks away. Although I checked NOTAMs for the several stops enroute home from the west coast, I failed to check the NOTAMs for ZZZ, a very familiar airport, for the final leg of this trip. I also failed to catch the note on the ATIS that advised Taxiway 1 was being used as Runway XXR. The 2-3 minute ATIS transmission contained extensive information about no IFR operations and multiple taxiway and access closures.I was cleared to land on 'Runway XXR' and cautioned about the strong and gusty winds. The landing was uneventful and posed no risk to personnel in the airplane or on the ground. There were no workers or service vehicles in the area. I was able to back-taxi on the closed runway under tower supervision and exit at the normal point to my rented hangar on the northeast side of the field.I understand that the runway was closed for good reason--the yet to be completed lighting systems--and that such a landing is always a potential risk to pilots and ground crew. I hope (and believe) I would have noted and aborted the landing had any people or equipment been on or near the runway I landed on.I attribute this incident to complacency on my part. I expected a clearance to land on Runway XXR, based on the winds, and when I saw the newly-resurfaced runway, I went for it. I am embarrassed by the fact that I would make such an error after XX+ years of flying.
ASRS:1805908.s: A pilot landed on closed Runway XXR at ZZZ due to complacency, failing to check NOTAMs or ATIS regarding the closure for incomplete lighting. The landing was uneventful with no ground personnel present, and the pilot back-taxied under tower supervision to the hangar.

ASRS:1805918.n: I was training on Local Control and Aircraft X was switched to me from Approach. As soon as Aircraft X checked in, I issued traffic 11 o'clock 2 miles northwest bound 2,700 feet climbing to 3,300 feet. I then called over to Approach and informed them I was climbing the IFR Aircraft X to 3,300 feet. Aircraft X said how that's nice of them they are going underneath. The other aircraft had climbed to 3,000 feet and Aircraft X was leaving 3100 feet. I'm not too knowledgeable on getting new procedures, but something where planes don't cross [over] final Approach fix without talking to Approach or the Tower.
ASRS:1805918.s: A Local Control trainee issued traffic information to Aircraft X regarding a climbing aircraft while coordinating a climb to 3,300 feet with Approach. The pilot reported Aircraft X would fly underneath the traffic, but the trainee noted a potential procedural violation regarding aircraft crossing the final approach fix without proper coordination.

ASRS:1805938.n: The lead Flight Attendant was so uptight with a passenger not complying with the Mask policies, [Flight Attendant] thought it was prudent to chime the cockpit during landing rollout and advise the flight crew to notify a Supervisor to meet the aircraft. This was a direct violation of sterile cockpit procedures. Because flight crews repeatedly experience chimes from the cabin while in simulator training, they are most associated with fire or critical aircraft issues. This is never a good time to chime the cockpit unless it is an emergency. Especially for a mask compliance issue.Relaxed emphasis from Leadership on the tattling on passengers for improper use of masks (never saw this type of behavior from FA when it came to early seat-belt releases. Reissued sterile cockpit etiquette with a bulletin on scenario that are and are not acceptable for chiming the cockpit during landing rollout.
ASRS:1805938.s: A lead Flight Attendant violated sterile cockpit procedures by chiming the cockpit during landing rollout to report a passenger mask violation. Leadership reissued a bulletin clarifying acceptable chiming scenarios to prevent non-emergency interruptions during critical flight phases.

ASRS:1805952.n: Once on final for [Runway] XXR, we got a TCAS RA event from what appeared to me an (other carrier) aircraft that overshot the final for XXL. We did not have the transponder in TA mode because we were never given a Traffic Advisory from ATC, and did not have the aircraft in sight as instructed by our guidance. The RA instructed us to Adjust Vertical Speed. It commanded approximately 1500 FPM descent. We were at flaps 10 and 1,500 feet AGL. As we descended per the RA we continued to configure the aircraft. We were below 1,000 feet by the time we got to flaps 30. The aural glideslope warning sounded. We knew we needed to go-around but couldn't because of the aircraft above us. When I looked at the ND (Navigation Display), I saw the red square showing the intruding aircraft right above us at +5. It was at 800 feet when we got the clear of conflict aural message and elected to go around.The (other carrier) aircraft, in my opinion, went through their intended final for XXL. A contributing factor was the lack of notification by ATC. While descending through approximately 2,000 feet AGL on the visual approach and on the ILS glideslope to Runway XXR in ZZZ, we received a TCAS RA Descend. The conflicting traffic was slightly above and behind us on Runway XXL. We believe the Descend RA extinguished at approximately 800 feet AGL (although a review of the FRM (Fault Reporting Manual) afterwards says it should be inhibited 'below approximately 1,100 feet radio altitude'). After following the Descend command and by the time the command extinguished, we were not in a stabilized position to land. We executed a go-around. We were not informed about the traffic by Approach and therefore did not meet the requirements to switch to TA Only for Runways XXL and XXR in ZZZ. We were vectored around for a normal landing on XXR. As we switched to ZZZ Tower, another aircraft in front of us also experienced a go-around for the same situation.Presumably the conflicting traffic met the requirements to switch to TA Only because they keyed up on the MIC and said they didn't overshoot and we should/can switch to TA Only. However, we didn't meet the requirements to switch to TA Only. ATC never asked us to report them in sight, presumably because they were behind us! So, what happens to our RA resolution when the conflicting traffic is in TA Only and transgressing on us? Presumably they can't be offered an RA resolution (which would likely have been for them to climb). If they had climbed the Descend RA 'pressure' on us could have been alleviated sooner. Instead we were forced lower and lower. And all of this was close to the ground. Even though the RA inhibits reaching 'approximately 1,100 feet radio altitude' the conflict with the other aircraft still exists, and we were pretty sure we were below 1,000 feet before the RA extinguished (as evidence by being already slightly into the 1,000 feet white tape). When the RA finally went away we executed a go-around from about 600-800 feet, but the traffic conflict doesn't magically go away.This event occurred right as we were configuring to land, so we never had a chance to fully configure prior to 1,000 feet AGL, as maneuvering for the RA was taking up our attention. The time in the RA resolution mode was more than momentary. It seemed long and sustained enough that it felt like it would just RA us into the ground. As I now knew a go-around was imminent there was a slight moment in my mind I thought about going around right then and there, but the RA continued. I can see where a Crew may be spring loaded to go-around even though the Descend RA is still present.The FO recognized that the traffic showed '+500' on the MFD display. The FAA defines a Near Midair as 'an incident associated with the operation of an aircraft in which a possibility of collision occurs as a result of proximity of less than 500 feet to another aircraft...' We were likely very close to meeting that definition.There was a slight tail wind at altitude for aircraft joining final from left base to runway XXL allowing for increased potential for overshoot. Maybe a very slight overshoot by the other aircraft and the tight sequencing by ATC created this incident, but we can't be sure. It's possible ATC was sequencing aircraft too tight.
ASRS:1805952.s: Pilots on final for Runway XXR received a TCAS RA to descend due to an overshot aircraft on Runway XXL, which was in TA-only mode. The crew descended below 1,000 feet AGL, became unstabilized, and executed a go-around at 800 feet, citing lack of ATC traffic notification as a contributing factor.

ASRS:1805954.n: Climbing out of ZZZ in moderate rain and passing through about 18,000 feet, with the FO flying, we got an airspeed disagree and altitude disagree on our displays, a Master Caution for Engine, autopilot (B) kicked off, and VNAV disappeared all within a few seconds. We compared instruments and determined that the Standby and Captain's displays matched with airspeed at 280 and close to the same altitude still climbing. We transferred aircraft control and ran the airspeed unreliable checklist/altitude unreliable checklist. After reporting our difficulties with ATC, we leveled at FL250, to finish checklist and run checklist for EEC alternate mode. At that time the FO instruments showed an airspeed of 130 KIAS and 25,500 feet. It took a while to get through checklist, but we were able to get autopilot-A back. We talked about the bad weather at ZZZ and decided to continue to ZZZ1 due to VMC conditions there. On descent passing through 15,500 feet, FO instrumentation appeared to recover. Approach and landing were uneventful. Priority handling was requested to ensure ATC was aware of our indication problems.
ASRS:1805954.s: The crew experienced simultaneous airspeed and altitude disagree warnings, autopilot disengagement, and VNAV loss while climbing through 18,000 feet in moderate rain. After executing unreliable airspeed and altitude checklists and leveling at FL250, they diverted to ZZZ1, where instruments recovered during descent for an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1805959.n: The hydraulic reservoirs have a big red caution label. It reads, 'CAUTION DO NOT OVERFILL HYDRAULIC RESERVOIR. FILL TO APPROX. 2/3 BETWEEN REFILL(RFL) AND FULL (COCKPIT PANEL SHOULD READ 92% FULL) REFER AMM 12-12-00.'Below the caution label there is an ATTENTION label. It reads, 'ATTENTION Do Not Overfill the RESERVOIR. Overfill can Cause Hydraulic Fumes To Enter the Flight Deck and Passenger Cabin'Some years ago I had an air return when the cabin filled with acrid mist causing eyes to sting and some to choke. The flight attendants thought we were on fire! The Captain and I used goggles and oxygen to safely return. This event was caused by both hydraulic reservoirs being filled to capacity. I believe the cockpit panel read 107%. If I'm recall correctly this is the most that will register.Although I have not since had visible or detectable odor, I believe crew and passengers are breathing atomized hydraulic fluid whenever the reservoirs are over serviced. The leg noted in this report from ZZZ-ZZZ1, started with both reservoirs reading 100%. At shutdown they were at 92%. Where did the difference go in a three hour operation? The day before, my aircraft had 107% in system A and 92% in system B. I alerted Maintenance of the over service. The Technician proceeded to move System A to B. The result was both reservoirs at 100%.I have dealt with this issue individually before. I find a small portion of our technicians understand the significance. Sometimes I meet with great resistance.[Recommend] a notice for Aircrew to remind them of the placards and similar or more specific training for all our Maintenance Technicians and Maintenance Control.
ASRS:1805959.s: A pilot reported that overfilled hydraulic reservoirs caused acrid fumes to enter the cabin on a previous flight, forcing a return with oxygen and goggles. The pilot observed reservoirs reading 100% at departure and 92% at shutdown, attributing the discrepancy to atomized fluid consumption and criticizing maintenance for overfilling.

ASRS:1806099.n: When cruising at 8,000 feet direct to ZZZ1.The flight attendants called us stating they smelled a burning smell coming from somewhere in the cabin. The Captain also stated he smelled something and we immediately ran the immediate action items and the QRC for smoke/fire/fumes.
