Donning our oxygen masks, the Captain delegated the flight controls and radios to me and told me to notify ATC and he would run the checklists and talk to the flight attendants. I notified Approach giving them souls and fuel on board. We were so close to the airport they gave us a vector for the approach into Runway XX. At that time the flight attendants told the Captain that the smell had gone away but for per cautionary reasons we elected to keep the masks on and the fire trucks on standby as we continued the approach. After landing we taxied to the ramp and stopped short of the gate for the emergency vehicles to inspect the exterior of the aircraft. After confirmation that nothing was smoking outside we canceled the emergency and taxied to the gate. Emergency personal came on board inspecting the inside of the aircraft deeming it safe we deplaned. The flight attendants did an excellent job in paying attention to everything going on in the aircraft. They informed us in the flight deck immediately allowing us to take action and get on the ground quickly and safely. Maintenance found that an electrical outlet had short circuited and started to smoke in row XX. The aircraft's systems worked and the circuit breaker tripped and the fire was never fully ignited. As soon as the flight attendants notified us in the cockpit the Captain called for the immediate action items for smoke fire flames. This reaction was precautionary but notifying ATC and donning oxygen masks was the safest solution when we did not know if something was on fire or even where it was. Great communication is key in emergency situation. Our crew worked together perfectly and shows how our training has paid off. The only suggestion I have through this experience is to regularly clean the oxygen masks because you never know when you will need them.
ASRS:1806099.s: During cruise at 8,000 feet, the crew responded to a burning smell reported by flight attendants, donned oxygen masks, and executed smoke/fire procedures. Maintenance later identified a short-circuited electrical outlet in row XX that tripped a circuit breaker before igniting, allowing for a safe landing with emergency services on standby.

ASRS:1806131.n: Level at 11,000 feet MSL in cruise for about 2 min when CAS (Crew Alerting System) alert sounded and left MAP (Manifold Absolute Pressure) went to 58'. Props remained at cruise setting. CAS messages were 'Hi MAP and Hi fuel pressure'. I reduced the left throttle lever to stabilize the engine to about 70% power which brought the lever to 60% or more towards idle. I descended to 7,000 feet to see if engine would stabilize back to normal without success. I then returned to ZZZ. The throttles remained split until landing where they matched at idle with both engines at idle. Returned passengers to the gate. None of passengers seemed distraught or concerned.
ASRS:1806131.s: The pilot reported a Crew Alerting System warning for high manifold pressure and fuel pressure on the left engine while cruising at 11,000 feet. After descending to 7,000 feet without resolving the issue, the pilot returned to ZZZ with split throttles until landing, then returned passengers to the gate.

ASRS:1806166.n: While descending into ZZZ we were given a vector to the right of the arrival. Later, we were given direct ZZZ1 VOR. The First Officer, and pilot flying put ZZZ in the FMS and executed the change. I thought I saw him select LNAV, but I began looking at the approach plate to review our arrival. A minute later I noticed we were still in heading. I immediately told him to turn to ZZZ1 VOR and select LNAV. ATC contacted us at that time and gave us direct ZZZ1 again. I told them we were in the turn.This was both our first flight in the 737 Max and we were a little distracted at some of the newness of the aircraft. Attention to flying the airplane when given a clearance even while Pilot monitoring is necessary at all phases of flying airplanes.
ASRS:1806166.s: During descent into ZZZ, a 737 Max crew missed a direct clearance to ZZZ1 VOR due to distraction from the new aircraft. The Pilot Monitoring corrected the error by instructing a turn to the VOR and selecting LNAV after noticing the aircraft remained in heading mode.

ASRS:1806178.n: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) when we initiated takeoff from Runway XXR at ZZZ. Flex power was set and prior to the 80 knot call, we had an ECAM Caution for #1 Engine Bleed Vane Failure - or words to that effect. CA (Captain) and I recognized the ECAM and CA called 'Reject, my aircraft;' I responded 'Your aircraft', a positive transfer of control was made, the auto brakes engaged, and the aircraft was promptly stopped per SOP. Of note is the fact that this ECAM Caution was not inhibited, but the auto brakes did activate, so our speed must have been below 80 knots at the time of the ECAM caution, but greater than 72 knots given auto brake activation. During the stop, CA had difficulty advancing the thrust levers out of the reverse range and briefly pushed them significantly into the forward thrust range of travel. As the engines accelerated in forward thrust, I advised CA of the position of the thrust levers and he promptly retarded them to the forward idle position. We made a quick assessment of the situation and CA proceeded to exit the runway at the first available forward high-speed taxiway, with me advising ATC of the situation. While doing this, CA advised the FAs to remain seated via the PA. As we exited the runway, CA noticed the ECAM Caution directed us to place the #1 Engine Master in the 'Off' position. CA instructed me to do this and I promptly complied. CA then brought the aircraft to a complete stop and assessed brake temperatures and other factors. Correctly judging that we were in a stable and safe situation, CA checked with the FAs to ensure they and the passengers were safe and to advise them that we had experienced a low speed rejected takeoff and he would contact them to advise of the next steps. CA and I then consulted the QRH to see if there was an ECAM Exception or Follow-Up to our ECAM Caution. There was no further guidance in the QRH, so CA advised me to inform ATC we would be contacting Maintenance and then getting back with ATC to advise them of our intentions. CA contacted Maintenance, who said they definitely wanted us to return to the gate, I advised Operations and Ramp Tower of our need to return to the gate and they assigned us gate X. I subsequently coordinated with Ground our return to the gate while CA advised the FA's and passengers of the situation. We returned to the gate without mishap, deplaned, and continued the flight on a different airplane.I have no idea why the ECAM Caution appeared. Other than a brief excursion into forward thrust due to the mechanical difficulty of moving the thrust levers out of the reverse thrust range, this rejected takeoff followed SOP and was unremarkable.Increased training and guidance for low speed rejected takeoffs would be helpful. Perhaps a section in the QRH with emphasis that it is the sole source for immediate guidance following a low-speed reject.
ASRS:1806178.s: The Pilot Flying and Captain rejected takeoff below 80 knots due to an Engine Bleed Vane Failure ECAM caution. After a brief thrust lever excursion, they followed SOPs to stop, shut down Engine 1, and return to the gate for maintenance.

ASRS:1806186.n: We checked in at ZZZ for flight to ZZZ1. Walking onto aircraft to preflight and get ready the FA's (flight attendants) commented that they smelled a strong fume odor in the rear of the cabin. The prior crew had left the APU running and that was providing the air to the cabin. We were not immediately sure what it was but the longer we were inside the aircraft the more it seemed to smell all over the aircraft. One flight attendant soon commented that she had been in a fume smell diversion and that she felt it now smelled exactly like what she had experienced before. As I was contacting Dispatch and Maintenance Control, the ZZZ station without our knowledge or consent had sprayed the entire aft cabin with some kind of disinfectant spray to cover up the smell and had begun to board passengers. When I was made aware of this I radioed them to stop spraying the aircraft, halt the boarding, and remove the passengers that were onboard. Maintenance Control had called a contract Maintenance Tech to investigate the odor. Meanwhile, we had shutdown the APU and connected the ground air. When the Maintenance Tech arrived, he had a bunch of paperwork for items to check, and mentioned that he was going to inspect the APU. He did not seem to know what to check or how to check it. Ultimately he handed me the pile of papers and ask us to run the engines. In an effort to help we did so. We could not specifically determine the source of the smell, but it seemed stronger with the APU providing air. We were unable to isolate the source and could not fly the aircraft or do a maintenance ferry flight. Afterward, Maintenance Control then informed us that the residual contamination in the air ducts would have to be cleaned and tested with special equipment, and that they would have to send a road crew down from ZZZ to perform those functions. So Maintenance Control knew from the start that this type of contamination issue required special procedures and equipment to deal with and withheld that critical information unnecessarily exposing us to who knows what kind of long term health hazards instead of just informing of this up front. After we officially could not use the airplane, it was around XA:30pm. We were assigned to fly another aircraft for the flight now departing at XG:15pm. We then spent the next few hours trying to get a day room so we could get a meal and away from the airport before the later flight. Each time were verbally told we had a room from Crew Tracking, Hotel Desk, etc., we called the hotel and were told there were no such rooms available for us. After wasting a considerable amount of time on this effort we were finally given rooms and arrived at the hotel just after XF:00pm. I walked down the highway from the hotel to find something to eat after having nothing for several hours. Finally sitting down to eat a sandwich, I realized that I had a dull headache from trying to determine if the fumes were no longer present in the aircraft when isolating certain ducts for Maintenance Control. It dawned on me that I was fatigued and I reported this to Crew Tracking. The cause was Maintenance, fume smells, lack of timely day room. [Captain suggested] better communications with Maintenance and Dispatch.
ASRS:1806186.s: The crew encountered a strong fume odor from the APU at ZZZ, leading to a cancellation after Maintenance failed to isolate the source and withheld critical cleaning procedures. The incident caused fatigue and health concerns due to the fumes, delayed boarding, and a lack of timely day rooms.

ASRS:1806189.n: We departed the gate and were instructed to taxi to Runway 28 via 'D, A, A1 to the Runway 28 holding point.' Upon glancing at the taxi diagram, referencing the our Airway Manual (AM), to verify our taxi route, I quickly realized a discrepancy between the instructions we were given and the chart -- there was no A1 taxiway that reached the runway. Before we could inquire about these instructions, the controller gave us a 'follow the aircraft ahead' instruction. Digging a little farther, I began to notice that this discrepancy was worth a report submittal because the 10-9 Chart for MMGL differs from the AM, and neither the 10-9 Chart nor the AM agrees with the airport in reality. Upon your own review, you will discover that there is a difference in taxiway names between the 10-9 chart, and the AM, specifically as it relates to the A taxiway. Additionally, in reality there is an A1 taxiway, properly signed, that parallels the A taxiway toward the approach end of Runway 28. There is also an additional taxiway, A2, that connects the A taxiway to the runway, prior to the approach end of Runway 28 which is not charted on either chart. The airport NOTAMS reference a change in taxiway naming convention, however, the NOTAMS do not make sense with either the current charts, or with reality, and in fact lead to more confusion. I believe that by paying attention to aircraft position with reference to the published chart, I was able to help the Captain remain in the green, and hopefully trap this threat from snaring other crews. In deliberating whether to submit this report, I concluded that since this threat affects the broader aviation community, the report would be more appropriate for resolving this discrepancy to the benefit of everyone.
ASRS:1806189.s: The flight crew identified discrepancies between ATC taxi instructions, the Airway Manual, and the 10-9 chart regarding taxiways A1 and A2 at MMGL. The pilot used situational awareness to verify the actual airport layout, preventing a potential runway incursion despite confusing NOTAMs and conflicting charts.

ASRS:1806199.n: Shortly after commencing the initial descend from 40,000 on the ISVA3E for SKBO and no weather indicated on the radar, we hit turbulence causing the airplane to rapidly climb and then descend. I observed from the FC seat +/- 800 feet and +/- 10 knots of airspeed. The autopilot was engaged with LNAV/VNAV and VNAV PATH indicated on the FMA. The seatbelt sign was on. After the unexpected turbulence was over, the Captain asked me to call the Flight Attendants. #1 FA stated that it appeared two FAs were injured and that he would call back with the final assessment. A few minutes later #1 FA called back and stated two FAs and a passenger were indeed injured and required medical attention. I briefed the Captain and he directed me to have medics meet us at the gate. Upon arriving at gate, the medics boarded the airplane and only took the FAs to the local hospital.Cause - This was unexpected turbulence. Perhaps now in the summer months with convective weather in the area of SKBO, I will suggest to the Captain ask the FAs to remain seated from descend to landing.Night flying into SKBO could hide weather disturbances not shown in the radar, perhaps have the FAs finish service early and sit from descend to landing.
ASRS:1806199.s: During descent from 40,000 feet into SKBO, unexpected turbulence caused rapid altitude and airspeed changes while the autopilot was engaged. Two flight attendants and one passenger were injured, requiring medical attention, which the pilot attributed to undetected convective weather not shown on radar.

ASRS:1806205.n: Some really troubling events unfolded on our flight, ZZZ-ZZZ1. After ground power failed and the high pressure air carts were removed to be repositioned for a gate start (APU is on MEL) the cabin environment was no longer safe or acceptable to have nearly XXX passengers onboard. I had the FO call ZZZ Operations on the radio to have them send an agent to open the cabin door and deplane the passengers. The jetway was still attached to the aircraft but nothing was being done to get the passengers safely off the jet. I turned on my cell phone and called the ZZZ ramp manager's phone number and requested immediate assistance. After further needless delays several flight attendants came to the flight deck to tell me they could see the agents standing in the jetway but there were doing nothing, my request to begin the deplaning was being ignored. I next called the flight office and requested a Chief Pilot and a manager to come ASAP to gate XX to assist. I have attached several photos to include the air synoptic of the excessively hot cabin temperatures after the air start units were removed and the jetway power failed! It gets much worse, and I will provide the whole narrative as it unfolded.When I arrived at the gate 50 minutes or so before departure I was informed that only the first officer had arrived and was onboard. The gate agent had just received a call that the cabin was very warm and ZZZ Operations wanted us to start the APU (why did Operations not know the APU was placarded). I assured them that the FO was most likely already addressing the matter. When I arrived at the flight deck I saw the FO had the air synoptic pulled up and I noted the aft cabin temp showed 102F. The FO pointed out that the APU was placarded inoperative. Air start units were being connected at this time to power the air conditioning pacs. During the FO's walk around he had taken a picture of the way the ground crew had connected the PCA hoses. How long had the PCA even been hooked up is unknown, the jet arrived at this gate at XA:00 in the morning, but regardless, it was all to evident the PCA air was not making it into the cabin do to the improper connection. The FO joined me and we returned to the terminal, I spoke with the gate agents and told them it would be a fairly long delay waiting for the cabin to cool. I asked them to keep the flight attendants from boarding the hot jet when they began arriving at the gate area. After the ground crew had finished hooking up the air start carts, the FO and I went to the flight deck to check that the air conditioning was functioning. Nearing the schedule departure time we were finally getting the cabin temp to where boarding could begin. After boarding was complete and the cabin door closed the ground crew checked in and cleared us to start the right engine. I informed them that on this aircraft, per the manual, the left engine is started first with ground air start. The ground crew had positioned the air start units incorrectly to start the left engine. I told them to let me know when the left engine was clear for starting. The crew then shutdown the air start, even though they did not have a tug hooked up to reposition the equipment! We no longer had ANY cooling airflow into the cabin. A couple of minutes later the electrical power from the jetway fails. The ground crew begins fiddling around but can't get the power restored and there are no portable power units near this gate. I later learned, after speaking with a facilities manager, that this jetway power supply had a service tag hanging from the power panel and should not have been used do to erratic 400HZ service. So with only battery power on the airplane, recirculating fans have shutdown, there is no cool air being provided, you can see [on] our air synoptic the cabin temps quickly were above 95-98 F. In the interest of safety for the passengers it should be obvious why I requested an immediate de-planning of the passengers. Unsatisfactory that ZZZ station was delaying opening the cabin door and safely removing the passengers. I even resorted to threatening a ground evacuation after a repeated request for help to draw their attention to the seriousness of the issue at hand. Passengers are wearing face coverings in a cabin approaching 100 F with all the cabin and cargo doors closed. Still the gate agents would not open up the cabin to begin deplaning the passengers until some passenger service manager gave the go ahead, why?After the passengers had begun deplaning the ground crew finally located a portable electric unit and began reconnecting the air start carts so we could operate the air conditioning. The ramp supervisor was now on the flight deck with us with along with some other manager in tow. They were questioning why I had their ground crew shutoff the air start units and have them moved. I said that is not what I told them to do. I only stated that per this aircraft manual the left engine is to be started and to let me know when the area was clear to start the left engine. While discussing the horrible failings and going over the situation I looked up and noticed the ground power had only been restored to the PRIMARY GRD source. This aircraft requires two ground power feeds or one from the ground and the APU, our APU was still placarded INOP! There is a risk of overheating the eclectic connection the way they had provide power (see PIC). I pointed this out to the manager. I also asked him that when they provide the correct ground power and air conditioning and we can get around to re-boarding the passengers are we going to have a ground crew available so we can start and pushback as quickly as possible. The manager assured me they would have a crew there for us. He lied! After we had closed the cabin door with our original passengers minus 20 or so that chose to not fly with us, I called the ground crew to get the go ahead to start. No ground crew at our gate! The FO called ramp to ask where our ground crew had gone? Twenty seven minutes later a crew arrives at the nose but does not check in on the headset. I have the nose camera on so I can see them as they fiddle around with connecting a tow bar and what not. I had flashed the nose taxi light to get their attention and made many interphone GND crew alert chimes, all of these signals were ignored. When they did finally get on the headset I expressed some frustration that we could have been starting the engine while they prepared for the pushback. They were quick with the excuse that they had just arrived and were unaware of the situation. When we were cleared to start the left engine the air start units were not running in the high flow position and the duct pressure has only 16 PSI, 25 PSI is minimum to start. I asked them to check the start units were set correctly. This ground crew had no idea how to operate their equipment. The AutoStart of the left engine failed on the first start attempt. The second start attempt reached idle and stable barely.Almost three hours late and somewhere about half way to ZZZ1 from ZZZ I noticed that ZZZ1 had us arriving to gate XX, even though the APU was on placard. ZZZ1 gate XX is a tow in only gate with engines shutdown per the ZZZ1 airport pages. FO wants to send a message to dispatch right away. I say lets just give them a little more time to do the right thing and see if they get it sorted out. Sure enough about an hour from arrival we send for the changeover info for ZZZ1 and they still have us arriving gate XX! I sent dispatch a message to ask if ZZZ1 is really planning for us to use gate XX with an INOP APU? Dispatch calls ZZZ1 Operations and they finally get around to changing our arrival gate.Ground crew not following procedures and failing to correct errors. Station management not supporting a safety culture to support flight operations in the interest of passenger safety.Attention to details in preparation for supporting an operation with a aircraft that has an MEL placard affecting normal ops, in this case the APU inoperative. When the PIC Captain of the flight, after all the doors closed and ready for flight, calls and radios the station that the passengers need to be immediately de-planned due to safety concerns, then this decision needs to be supported and executed without delay!
ASRS:1806205.s: The Captain of flight ZZZ-ZZZ1 reported that ground crew errors, including improper air start connections and power failures, caused unsafe cabin temperatures while the APU was inoperative. This forced an emergency deplaning and resulted in a three-hour delay due to station management's failure to support safety procedures.

ASRS:1806206.n: On STAR into ZZZ I was high and was not going to make a mandatory crossing altitude. Prior to it I asked the controller if I could be relieved of that restriction and he said yes.I had not been into ZZZ since COVID and as such didn't realize that ZZZ, being a large International hub, was still operating way under capacity compared to domestic airports, meaning vectors to final were fast. I was hand flying without autopilot or auto throttles which I do typically once a trip to stay in practice. After I was given the arrival clearance the First Officer, not being familiar with ZZZ couldn't find frequency to talk to once on the ground and was asking me to help him find it. As I was flying and looking over my iPad to find the frequency I then realized I was high and requested relief from one of our crossing altitudes which was given prior to that crossing restriction.I should have just waited until on the ground to look up frequency or turned automation back on.
ASRS:1806206.s: The pilot, hand-flying a STAR into ZZZ, realized they were high for a mandatory crossing altitude and requested relief, which the controller granted. The situation occurred because the pilot was distracted by helping the First Officer find the ground frequency while flying without automation.

ASRS:1806219.n: After intercepting the glideslope it was noted by both pilots the aircraft was not slowing down normally. Despite lowering the gear and deploying speedbrakes we were having a difficult time getting 10 knots below the next flap speed to continue to configure a variable tailwind was noted between 5 & 10 knots which helped explain what we were seeing. Continuing to investigate however both pilots thereafter realized we were abnormally low and the PF disconnected the AP and leveled off. Tower called with a low altitude alert shortly after that and we acknowledged it, configured normally and were stable by 500 feet AGL. Landing and roll out was normal. There were multiple approach NOTAMs that day and we miscalculated the effective times on the one stating the ILS XXL was unusable. We were an hour off and were arriving inside the last 30 minutes of the effective time. It turns out NAVAIDs maintenance was manipulating the glide slope signal at the time, causing the glide slope to appear lower.The ILS to XXL was OTS and NAVAIDs maintenance was transmitting a lower than normal glidepath. It would have been helpful if ILS status had been repeated on the ATIS, as it normally is, but it was not. During the low altitude call from tower they were even quick to add to the call that it 'was in the NOTAMs'. Further investigating with my prior position with FAA Flight Inspection it is still in their guidance that NAVAIDs maintenance is not supposed to transmit a localizer signal if they are going to manipulate the glide slope signal to avoid this hazardous, misleading, information. The localizer and glide slope both were transmitting, with a proper ID, at the time of the incident, we even crossed ZZZZZ at the appropriate altitude of 3,000 and showed on path. It was after that when the aircraft would no longer slow, as it was chasing a depressed glide path. In the end we missed the NOTAM but then multiple holes of the swiss cheese lined up, thankfully it was day VFR and we saw the solution with our own eyes in time. The other layers of protection normally there (ATIS, maintenance procedures) would have helped overcome our oversight.
ASRS:1806219.s: Both pilots intercepted a manipulated ILS glide slope at XXL due to a missed NOTAM regarding NAVAID maintenance, causing the aircraft to track abnormally low and fail to slow. The crew disconnected the autopilot after a tower low altitude alert, stabilized by 500 feet AGL, and landed safely.

ASRS:1806222.n: Unexpected last minute change of runway from RNAV Runway 29R to ILS runway 11L. Winds were calm forecast to pick up out of the west at our arrival time. No digital ATIS, didn't find active runway until listening to ATIS on radio well into the arrival. On downwind vectors advised of pair of military aircraft we would follow on approach. Turned base and cleared for visual approach to Runway 11L. As we turned in towards the airport, we crossed a knoll just north of the final approach course. We were descending and crossed over the top of the knoll at about 1,400 feet AGL. The GPWS activated and announced pull up terrain, the FO (First Officer) executed an escape maneuver as he had been trained. With autopilot off speed quickly accelerated and still in the flaps 2 configuration we exceeded the limit speed by about 5 knots for 5 to 10 seconds before speed reduced back into normal range. We advised TUS that we were missed approach and were vectored around to another visual approach and landing.Cause - Higher than normal workload, changing runways, keeping traffic in sight and terrain awareness.On calm wind days be prepared for approach from either direction on smaller airports with only one primary runway. Study terrain areas to plan for visual approach altitude you want to be at crossing them.
ASRS:1806222.s: The crew experienced a GPWS terrain warning while descending over a knoll during a visual approach to Runway 11L after a last-minute runway change. The First Officer executed an escape maneuver, briefly exceeding flap limit speed, leading to a missed approach caused by high workload and terrain awareness issues.

ASRS:1806251.n: After parking at gate, flight crew were informed of damage to left horizontal stabilizer. It appeared to have been struck by a tall ground vehicle. I considered the aircraft inoperable after reviewing the damage. The FO noted no damage during his external inspection, and felt that he would have easily noted the damage had it appeared during that time. We concluded the damage was likely caused by a catering truck at ZZZ, after the walk around was already complete. The crew was not informed of the damage and continued the flight to ZZZ1. We had no idea.A failure on the part of service crew in ZZZ to notify the flight of damage when it occurred. This resulted in the flight continuing when not air worthy. The flight and landing went without incident, until ZZZ1 reported the damage to the flight crew after arriving at the gate.It is impractical for the flight crew to perform an external inspection after all external service equipment is removed and the cabin door is closed. The last opportunity to look over the aircraft is the push back crew. Perhaps wing walkers could walk all the way back to the tail on their respective sides and examine the airplane for anything unusual. This information could then be forwarded to the tug driver, who would in turn forward to the flight crew. Something like 'external equipment clear, inspection complete, no damage noted.'
ASRS:1806251.s: The flight crew discovered left horizontal stabilizer damage from a catering truck at ZZZ only after arriving at ZZZ1, as ground services failed to report the incident. The aircraft was deemed inoperable, though the flight and landing occurred without incident despite the crew being unaware of the damage.

ASRS:1806271.n: On flight into MSP. I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) and at 1,200 feet AGL was told by ATC to look for a helicopter at 10:00 o'clock and 600 feet below. I did not see traffic and responded with 'looking'. The helicopter reported us in sight and they were told to pass behind the aircraft and he repeated that request. Shortly after, we got a TA and traffic was 200 feet below and close by at 11:00 o'clock. Captain deviated slightly from glide path and localizer but not to full scale deflection. At this time we looked to the left and the helicopter was only 200 feet away and banking hard to the right. It seemed as if he only just saw us. We continued and landed with no further incident. There's not much we could have done different, I believe the helicopter saw different traffic as he should have never been that close to us. Helicopter reporting us in sight and not providing adequate separation.
ASRS:1806271.s: The Pilot Monitoring on an approach to MSP reported a helicopter conflict after ATC instructed a visual scan. The helicopter, which claimed sight but failed to maintain separation, triggered a Traffic Advisory and required a slight glide path deviation before landing safely.

ASRS:1806415.n: Aircraft X was scheduled to have a THSA (Trimmable Horizontal Stabilizer Actuator) oil inspection complete which it failed due to a leak. The THSA was then replaced by 1st and 2nd shift on Date. After installation the THSA failed the operational checks. The aircraft was then turned over to 3rd shift. 3rd shift changed parts but the ops checks were still failing. The corrective action ended by stating no fix and that position transducer on the THSA was suspected to be faulty. The aircraft was then turned over to 1st shift on Date 1. 1st shift signed the non-routine off without addressing the no fix statement. The operational checks were also stamped in the job card as being completed by a mechanic and an inspector. I came in for my 3rd shift last night Date 1 and was curious what 1st shift did to fix the problem. I found that nothing was documented on the non-routine addressing the no fix statement. another mechanic went to the aircraft and went through the ops checks in the cockpit and the checks failed exactly as they did the night before. Management was notified and the aircraft was brought back to the hangar from the gate. I was informed that the mechanic and inspector would be asked about it but the aircraft was never removed from service. Please have another mechanic and a different inspector run through the operational checks per the THSA replacement job card. the stab control wheel does not return to zero after being placed in 13.5 up position and sec 1 is reset. The THSA stops at .4 when .3 is the limit.
ASRS:1806415.s: A mechanic and inspector signed off a failed THSA replacement without addressing a "no fix" status, allowing the aircraft to remain in service despite the stabilizer control wheel failing to return to zero. The reporter found the operational checks still failing with the THSA stopping at .4 instead of the .3 limit.

ASRS:1806477.n: I was doing training with the Aircraft X in the right hand seat as flight instructor, left hand seat occupied by experienced skydive pilot. During the final of the first touch and go of his session of 3L heard the Aircraft Y on the frequency asking landing information. I gave him 3L in use with right hand circuit and 2 aircraft doing touch and go training. When coming in right downwind again Runway 3L we got a traffic warning on the GPS screen. Traffic appeared to be head on 200 feet above. PIC didn't see it but I spotted the traffic head on almost same altitude and called the conflicting traffic to warn him being opposite in the downwind head on. He replied to join right downwind 3L. As PIC still couldn't see the traffic and a collision was going to happen I took the yoke and turned the aircraft to the right with a slight down input. Conflicting aircraft never saw us neither did any avoidance maneuver.PIC had back the controls and we did a second touch and go. Meanwhile the Aircraft Y joined the right downwind 3L and landed when we where again end of downwind. Turning on final for full stop ( final call was done) the Aircraft Y reported entering back track 3L. Being surprised as we where already on final I saw he could however vacate heaving 3 taxiways ahead. Nevertheless the pilot of the Aircraft Y called us that we better did a go-around as they would not be able to vacate in time. I replied that his behavior was very unprofessional, first positioning his aircraft opposite ours in a downwind leg and then entering and blocking the active runway with an aircraft on final. After we landed and shut down the aircraft I expected at least that the PIC of the Aircraft Y would come to apologize, but no one came to us. When checking the airport register I also noticed he never registered his inbound nor outbound flight. When checking FlightRadar24 you can clearly see that the Aircraft Y flew opposite the downwind descending through 1,700 feet of the 03L to do a 180 turn to join his opposite track. The Aircraft X is at the same moment at 1,500 feet flying correct downwind position for the 3L. Closing speed was around 250 kts.
ASRS:1806477.s: A flight instructor in Aircraft X avoided a head-on collision with Aircraft Y during downwind training by taking control and turning right after the PIC failed to see the conflicting traffic. The incident occurred because Aircraft Y flew opposite the downwind leg and later blocked the active runway while Aircraft X was on final approach.

ASRS:1806478.n: On our flight to ZZZ1 from ZZZ we just crossed the shore of the Delaware Bay from ZZZ, about 11 nm east of DONIL intersection at 16,000 ft, XA:30, we flew past a drone that appeared to be stationary. The drone, quad type, looked to be approximately 500 feet below our left wing. The encounter was reported to Washington Center.
ASRS:1806478.s: A flight crew en route from ZZZ to ZZZ1 encountered a stationary quad-type drone approximately 500 feet below their left wing at 16,000 ft, 11 nm east of DONIL. The crew reported the incident to Washington Center.

ASRS:1806490.n: Working ILS final into Runway 13R at SAT. Moderate volume, so the final was out around 15 miles, in the vicinity for 5C1. Aircraft X on roughly a 14 mile modified left base, approximately heading 240, descending from 4,000 to 3,000 feet. A VFR target pops off of 5C1, climbing rapidly, right into the face of Aircraft X opposite direction. As soon as I noticed, I gave Aircraft X a traffic call and an early turn to final. Before Aircraft X could start his turn, the 2 were 3,200 feet, nose to nose, less than a mile, Aircraft X descending and the VFR climbing. On the scope, it appeared that the 2 aircraft got less than 1/2 mile and 200 feet apart. A traffic alert was issued, and Aircraft X called traffic in sight. The VFR never called SAT ATC, but I continued to observe the aircraft climb northeast and become traffic for 2 other air carriers around 8,800 feet. One GOBBY Departure also needed a traffic alert for the same aircraft. This is far too common of an occurrence. We need to make it compulsory for aircraft departing 5C1, climbing above 2500, to contact SAT Approach Control. Due to the location of 5C1 and its vicinity to the 13R final approach course, to not do so is to jeopardize the safely of aircraft on the instrument approaches into our most commonly used runway.
ASRS:1806490.s: An air traffic controller issued a traffic alert when a VFR aircraft departing 5C1 climbed rapidly into the path of Aircraft X on ILS final to Runway 13R at SAT. The controller attributed the near-miss to the VFR pilot failing to contact Approach Control and recommended mandatory contact for departures climbing above 2,500 feet.

ASRS:1806491.n: Two similar sounding callsigns on frequency: Flight ABCD and Flight AECD. Both aircraft were being vectored to the final approach course into SNA airport. Flight ABCD was in front of Flight AECD. I issued and altitude of 4,300 feet to Flight ABCD and Flight AECD responded at the same exact time. All I heard was Flight ABCD reading it back. I then observed Flight AECD descending below the 5,200 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude and issued a low altitude alert, stop climb, and climb back up. Need to be more observant of similar sounding call signs and should have issued the phraseology to warn both aircraft. Lesson learned.
ASRS:1806491.s: An air traffic controller vectored two aircraft with similar call signs, Flight ABCD and Flight AECD, to SNA airport. The controller mistakenly issued an altitude clearance to ABCD, but AECD responded and descended below the 5,200-foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude, requiring a low altitude alert and climb instruction.

ASRS:1806496.n: I was working Position X. Position Y was feeding me the arrivals. I was not talking to Aircraft X. He was getting close to ZZZZZ the fix prior to approach. I think Position Y was having a hard time because ZZZ1 sector was busy and not shipping all the aircraft. I pointed to the Aircraft X and told Position Y to give Aircraft X FL190 because I was not talking to that aircraft and he had needed to start down. Consequently, I was not talking to the aircraft in time to get him down. And working without a D-side to make the call, I handed the aircraft off high to ZZZ2 Approach. He should have crossed the boundary at 120 but he was more like 170 crossing. They took the hand off and I switched the aircraft. My recommendation is more D-sides. I know there is COVID and we seem to work with fewer controllers and not have the numbers in the control room as usual. And everyone needs a break. We try to have a good work break balance. Talking to the aircraft in a timely manner would help also. As controllers to do our best in switching aircraft in a timely manner. Maybe a better, faster way to get in touch with the pilot. I think I went through company, the last controller, guard frequency, the supervisor. I think it was another company airline that got a hold of him, or that could have been another instance. Yesterday was busy with weather and the situations are all blurring together. And a D-side could have helped to make the call. I kept my eyes on the other air traffic situations to keep them flowing smoothly as well. Thank God approach took that hand off. The sector would have been 10 times more difficult if I had to spin that aircraft to get him to 120 by ZZZZZ and concentrate on the other issues by myself.
ASRS:1806496.s: An air traffic controller at Position X handed off Aircraft X high to ZZZ2 Approach because they could not contact the pilot in time to descend from FL190 to the required 120 feet. The controller attributed the delay to a lack of a D-side controller and staffing shortages, noting that Approach accepted the aircraft despite it crossing the boundary at approximately 170 feet.

ASRS:1806517.n: While on the ENDEE 6 Arrival to MDW we encountered a near midair collision and the following is a narrative of that event. Time stamps are from 'Flightaware' app and may not be 100% accurate. I added these to recreate the event to the best of my knowledge.I was the Pilot Flying on this leg. At about XX:26Z ATC began to vector us off the arrival for spacing. During these vectors we were cleared to descend to lower altitudes. I had even made the comment jokingly that we were being 'over-controlled' by ATC after several heading, altitude and speed changes. At approximately XX:45Z we were cleared to descend to 5000 feet. Our flight path at the time was approximately over top of Morris Muni airport (C09) about 6.6 miles southwest of STKNY on the arrival. Crossing altitude at STKNY is published is 6000 feet. We were then cleared direct to ALQUE for the ILS 4R at MDW. While still level at 5000 feet at approximately XX:47Z we had a TCAS TA (solid amber) showing an aircraft in front of us and +100 feet above our altitude. I do not remember the scale set at the time on my navigation display but it was very 'close'. This was this first time we had seen a Traffic Advisory of any kind on the display (no open white diamond) and had not been advised of traffic from ATC. One second later ATC told us we had 'glider traffic' ahead and to 'deviate as necessary' to avoid the traffic. I immediately began a right hand descending turn. About two seconds later we received a Resolution Advisory RA to descend and the First Officer told ATC we were responding to an RA. At about 4500 feet, I saw the glider slightly higher and to our left. Once clear of the conflict, ATC cleared us to descend to 4000 feet and stated he was not in contact with the glider and asked if it was clear of clouds. ATC warned aircraft behind us on the arrival about the glider and it's altitude. We estimated the distance from the glider was 150-200 feet as it passed to our left. The event happened in the proximity of Channahon, IL Glider Club (IL59) south of STKNY on the arrival.The takeaway from this event:The TCAS did not operate as we would expect in time regarding a TA caution providing 40 seconds warning and an RA providing 25 seconds warning. It's hard to tell if the glider had just turned on its transponder or if the slow speed of the glider had an impact on our TCAS. The glider was in Class E airspace and outside the 30 mile equipment requirement (transponder) from the ORD Class B. What rules apply to gliders here, to me, is unknown to be honest.ATC had vectored us off the arrival and was assigning altitudes lower than published crossing restrictions by 1000 feet (5000 feet abeam STKNY).Vectors took us almost directly over a glider airpark with no warning about that on any chart we would ever use readily available. Some warning symbology or quick access information would assist considering the low altitudes we fly over these areas.In hindsight, I would have made clear to ATC we experienced a near mid air collision in that language as described in our FOM.
ASRS:1806517.s: The Pilot Flying on an ENDEE 6 arrival to MDW experienced a near midair collision with a glider while vectored to 5,000 feet below published crossing restrictions. The conflict occurred because ATC provided no traffic warning and the TCAS issued late advisories, forcing an immediate descending turn to avoid the glider passing 150–200 feet away.

ASRS:1806534.n: Climbing through FL180 I engaged CMD (Command) A autopilot. When I pressed the button the airplane instantly had a loud banging noise, jolted very aggressively, nosed down, and started oscillating. It was almost to the point I thought I was going to accomplish upset recovery procedures. I was quickly able to level the airplane off and safely hand fly. We contacted Maintenance and unanimously agreed that the airplane was safe enough to continue to hand fly the plane for the duration of the flight. Maintenance asked if we tried autopilot B. The jolt and aircraft response was significant enough that we did not want to try arming the autopilot again. We safely hand flew the aircraft back to ZZZ1. In our debrief we discussed that for a split second we initially thought it was so severe that we were losing aircraft control. We were greatly startled and hands were shaking for a good 5-10 minutes after the event happened. We were scheduled to fly to ZZZ2 after the flight, arriving the next morning. We hit an emotional lull after the flight and we both determined we were not emotionally, nor physically, fit to continue our pairing. We called in fatigued and were given hotel rooms immediately. We were climbing through 180 out of ZZZZ. The CA (Captain) went to engage CMD (Command) A and the aircraft made a loud bang and had a violent nose down control input. It was so severe that we thought the flight attendant could have been injured. It was so bad for a moment I thought that we might have hit something mid-air. I was completely shaken up and so was the Captain. We refused to attempt to re-engage any autopilot. We were just about to divert but we had Dispatch run the numbers for us at non-RVSM altitude. We calculated 6.0 remf on this 700 so we opted to hand fly it. We worked in 30 minute shifts. The arrival was busy with many changes enroute. We were both shaking at the initial event and were completely calmed down enroute but we both started to feel drained after the adrenaline started to wear off. We were both obviously not fit for our next leg which was scheduled to arrive after midnight into ZZZ1. We both got a hotel at ZZZ even though I could have commuted home that evening, I was toast at that point and just went to bed.
ASRS:1806534.s: During climb through FL180, engaging CMD A autopilot caused a loud bang, violent nose-down jolt, and oscillation, leading the crew to hand-fly the aircraft to ZZZ1. The pilots refused to re-engage the autopilot and terminated their pairing due to fatigue and emotional distress following the event.

ASRS:1806547.n: Approach control cleared us for visual approach to [Runway] 14R. I turned right, towards ZATAR, the final approach fix, and started descending from 4,000 to the final approach fix altitude, 2,400. We observed the 2,500-foot tower and passed several miles to the north of it. The tower is approximately 5 nm east of OMA.The transition from the Pawnee City arrival to a visual approach to 14R places the aircraft in a position where the tower is difficult to locate and is in a location where the pilot will naturally be descending towards. Our Jepp pages do not highlight this as a potential problem.Our Jepp page that shows how the tower interferes with a right traffic pattern to 14R. The tower is at a normal traffic pattern altitude where a downwind to base turn would be made. When arriving on the Pawnee City arrival, and landing 14R, a preferred route around the tower for a visual landing should be shown. Also, approach control could vector the airplane safely North of the tower before giving the clearance for the approach.
ASRS:1806547.s: The pilot reported that while descending for a visual approach to Runway 14R after the Pawnee City arrival, the aircraft passed north of a 2,500-foot tower that was difficult to locate. The reporter attributed this risk to charting omissions and suggested preferred routes or vectors north of the tower to ensure safe clearance.

ASRS:1806555.n: There is a group of towers on right downwind/base to 14R and 14L that are a potential hazard when visual approaches are in use. As shown on the approach plates, at least one of these towers is 148 feet higher than the glide slope intercept altitude for these runways. Although the VFR traffic pattern for both runways is left, the PAWNEE CITY 1 and HOWRY 2 arrivals set IFR traffic up for a righthand pattern with the towers situated between them and final. Unlike the approaches, these towers are not charted on either arrival.When flying a righthand traffic pattern, such as from PAWNEE CITY 1, HOWRY 2, or on a visual missed approach, pilots are susceptible to colliding with the 2,548 feet towers while attaining the glide slope intercept altitude of 2,400 feet.1) Add a page in Jeppesen for OMA which calls attention to the towers. 2) Provide easier access to traffic pattern altitudes and directions in Jepp in the event of a visual missed approach. As of right now, this information is buried in a 4,000 plus page document. 3) Obstacles and terrain that are considered significant to approaches should also be charted on arrivals. 4) Pilots should thoroughly review significant obstacles and terrain depicted on procedures and enable ownship on Approach in Jeppesen for increased situational awareness. 5) ATC should ensure pilots see these particular towers, not just the airport, when clearing pilots for the visual from the west. Alternatively, pilots should be vectored well clear of the towers before being issued a visual.
ASRS:1806555.s: A pilot reported that uncharted towers near Omaha pose a collision hazard during right-hand visual approaches or missed approaches from PAWNEE CITY 1 and HOWRY 2 arrivals. The towers exceed the glide slope intercept altitude, prompting recommendations to chart obstacles on arrivals and improve ATC visual clearance procedures.

ASRS:1806569.n: Upon taking off out of ZZZ at a couple hundred feet I got a CAS (Crew Alerting System) message alerting me that the RH Crew Door was open and unlocked. When I got a second to check it, it appeared closed securely to me with the handle all the way down and the door tight. Given the fact that until that moment the door was indicating closed and locked and my own observation seemed to confirm that, I believed it to be a sensor issue and elected to continue the flight. I had no further issue until I was less than a minute from landing. At this point the door came open. The door was still tight against the air frame due to the wind forcing it closed but it was clearly unsecured. I landed with no further incident and taxied to the gate.
ASRS:1806569.s: The pilot reported a false Crew Alerting System message indicating the right-hand crew door was open shortly after takeoff from ZZZ. The door subsequently unsecured near landing but remained sealed by wind pressure, allowing for a safe landing and taxi to the gate.

ASRS:1806599.n: During walk around, a ground crew man informed the Captain of need to push prior to darkness as ground crews have difficulty seeing. Pushback happened after dark due to weather delays. Initially, the tug driver wanted to drop the airplane with a minimal push which would have resulted in a max pivot turn. We felt we were unable to have wingtip to wingtip and/or tail to tail clearance so we asked the tug driver to pull us out further telling him it was too tight. He complied. The right wing walker seemed confused as he walked in front of the engine and not at the right wing-tip, the closest point of potential impact. Walking in front on an engine had no value to us as an aircrew. Once we were released from the tug, taxiing was extremely difficult due to several factors. These were narrow alleyway, very poorly unlit alleyway, at least 1 heavy jet parked on low D gates, construction on the south side of the alley way, no hazard O4 lighting for the construction fence, ramp and construction vehicles parked outside the fence on the ramp, and poor surface markings. Taxiing out was extremely slow and challenging and we notified an inbound aircraft to be careful. Poor visibility due to rain and the glare from wet added or exacerbated the taxi out difficulty. Poorly lit area, poorly marked area, new operational area, construction. Our first warning came from the ground crew when they express difficulty with completing the pushback after dark. If not for the interior lights of the terminal, I feel we would have struck the aircraft parked at gate. Our second clue was the attempted drop spot which showed us the degree of difficulty these crews were operating in. Better training for wing walkers. Better lighting in this area. Better surface markings to assure wingtip clearance in this area. Hazard lights on construction fence. Removal of all equipment and vehicles on ramp parked up against the fence. Reevaluation reflective paint stripe/J line coming from this alley. Until at least some items are addressed, all night operations should be towed to the top of the alley with lighted vehicles to protect rampers and cover far distance as wing walkers. I feel this is an aircraft damage event waiting to happen, even without the low light low visibility conditions.
ASRS:1806599.s: The Captain and ground crew experienced a difficult night pushback and taxi due to poor lighting, construction, and a confused wing walker. The crew requested a longer tow to ensure clearance, but the pilot warned that aircraft damage was likely without improved lighting, markings, and training.

ASRS:1806605.n: Winds were calm at ROA. ATIS called Runway 24 as landing and departing using RNAV (RNP) Z RWY 24. ATC asked us if we wanted the visual. Given terrain and having never been to ROA I elected to stay with the RNAV approach. ATC had us cross STEFN at 5,400 feet which had us 400 ft high. We attained VNAV PATH and 150 KIAS approximately 3 miles after STEFN. Since we could see the terrain and visibility was greater than 5 miles we planned to maintain 150 KIAS until 5 miles prior to the airfield. Between DBERD and WILHE there is depicted terrain with a spot elevation 2,058 feet. Just pass that terrain, still on LNAV and VNAV PATH at 150 KIAS Roanoke Tower gave us a low altitude warning. We verified both our altimeter settings and altitude. We advised Tower that we could see both terrain and the airfield. Tower acknowledged and advised us that they could see us clearly, and that they were required to announce the low altitude alert anytime it is activated. Otherwise, the approach and landing were normal. Of note there was no GPWS alert with flaps 20 and gear up. After block-in, I requested a phone number to discuss the event.I spoke with [ATC] and inquired about the altitude alert call. He indicated they sometimes get an altitude alert activation, but usually on vectors to visual Runway 24. He also indicated he was not as familiar with the Tower sector. I asked him to look into it a bit more given that the only difference between what I flew and what I would have flown in IMC is I would have been 25 KIAS slower which would have resulted in a descent rate difference of just 133 FPM given a constant wind. The wind in this case was a light headwind during the approach.Had I been in IMC and/or could not immediately determine by visual reference terrain clearance, the approach would have terminated with an immediate climb and terrain escape maneuver.Recommend the altitude alert system be de-conflicted to ensure aircraft on FMS glide path for the RNAV Z RWY 24 do not get erroneous alerts and/or note on company chart outlining requirements for speed on the approach or other requirements to successfully complete the approach in IMC.No deviations noted by Tower or aircrew. The low altitude alert system may need to be adjusted or approach procedures may need to be adjusted to avoid erroneous low attitude warnings.De-conflict low altitude warning with proper approach lateral and vertical guidance.
ASRS:1806605.s: The flight crew flew an RNAV (RNP) Z RWY 24 approach at ROA and received a low altitude warning from Tower while on VNAV PATH at 150 KIAS. The crew verified terrain clearance, and the reporter attributed the alert to a system de-conflict issue rather than an actual deviation.

ASRS:1806679.n: I departed from FXE in Aircraft X for a training flight with a CFII that was supposed to consist of commercial maneuvers. I noticed an aircraft about 20-30 feet below me on a collision course with us passing from our left to right. The aircraft looked like some kind of Learjet with wing tip fuel tanks flying northwest bound. The aircraft was not talking on the 123.45 which is the frequency all VFR flights make position reports on within the ALERT AREA A291A.As pilot flying I had to abruptly maneuver away from the aircraft. A few seconds later I contacted FXE Tower to report the incident.
ASRS:1806679.s: A pilot flying Aircraft X during a training departure from FXE observed a Learjet on a collision course 20-30 feet below while the intruder failed to communicate on the required ALERT AREA frequency. The pilot executed an abrupt maneuver to avoid the aircraft and subsequently reported the incident to FXE Tower.

ASRS:1806685.n: I was flying VFR cross country to ZZZ from JZI flying direct with a planned northern deviation towards HYW to avoid MYR airspace. Altitude was 3,000 AGL due to moderate turbulence. As I was nearing MYR airspace the GPS encountered interference and the aircraft indicator on the moving map was blocked (later determined to be ADS-B shadow). When the GPS self corrected, I realized that I was near or touching the outer ring below the 4,000 upper limit and above the 1,200 lower limit. I immediately executed a 180 degree turn and then turned north and skirted the outside ring as planned. I did possibly touch the airspace but did so for only the minute it took to turn away. The certified GPS never gave the warning that it usually does when class airspace is entered, I had to range the GPS out near maximum to even see the touching of the outer ring, so I do not know what the ATC radar would have shown. I do not expect a re-occurrence as I better understand how the ADS-B shadow sometimes disguises the aircraft symbol. I have been flying nearly 40 years and have never had a violation or an airspace incursion.
ASRS:1806685.s: A VFR pilot flying at 3,000 feet AGL likely entered MYR Class B airspace due to GPS interference from an ADS-B shadow that obscured the aircraft symbol. The pilot executed a 180-degree turn to exit the airspace immediately after the GPS self-corrected and displayed the position.

ASRS:1806687.n: I was making a precautionary return to the airport after experiencing a decrease in fuel pressure on my left engine. In the descent phase to ZZZ the left engine began running worse and worse as I descended. I activated low boost on the left engine to keep it running. I was able to keep the engine running until landing by a combination of low and high boost and manipulating the throttle. On roll out, my right engine idle was low and in an attempt to keep it running I hit low boost and pushed the throttle up, but it died anyway. Managing asymmetric thrust and keeping the left engine running so I could clear the active runway and not shut the airport down, took my full attention. I did not turn the little boost off of the right engine until I had cleared the runway and by then the system was pressure charged and porting fuel overboard.In retrospect I should have feathered and secured the left engine and concentrated on landing and clearing the runway. This would have reduced my workload.
ASRS:1806687.s: The pilot experienced decreasing left engine fuel pressure during descent, requiring boost manipulation to maintain operation. Post-landing, the right engine failed while the pilot managed asymmetric thrust to clear the runway, later admitting that feathering the left engine earlier would have reduced workload.

ASRS:1806698.n: Just after liftoff from a touch and go, the engine failed with a loud squealing noise. I lowered the nose and easily landed on the remaining runway. There was no sign of fire, I accomplished the shutdown procedures and got out of the plane. I visually checked the pattern and did not see any traffic, nor did I hear any on the CTAF the last two times around the pattern. I pushed the plane about 50 feet to the next taxiway and got it clear of the runway. What I forgot to do was make any announcements on the CTAF after my engine failed. If it was busy, I am pretty sure I would have made a call that I had landed again and would be occupying the runway for a few minutes, and then another call to say I was clear. Even so, I should have made those calls in case there was some traffic I was not aware of.
ASRS:1806698.s: The pilot experienced an engine failure with a loud squealing noise just after liftoff during a touch-and-go and landed safely on the remaining runway. The pilot acknowledged failing to make CTAF announcements regarding the emergency landing and runway occupancy, though no traffic was observed or heard.

ASRS:1806744.n: ORD was on a very busy east flow arrival push. The weather was severe VFR and there were numerous aircraft on 1200 codes flying underneath the ORD finals. I was working the north final. A VFR aircraft who I believe departed ZZZ1 climbed up to 3900 feet which is 100 feet below the base of the Class B. I did not see the aircraft approaching my final because of all of the overlapping data blocks from the south two finals. When the conflict alarm sounded, I saw the traffic and issued a traffic alert to Aircraft X who climbed 800 feet to avoid a collision.The Class B airspace around ORD does not match the current arrival/departure procedures. On East Flow, the low-side runway is required to turn final at 4000 feet in accordance with the facility Standard Operating Procedure. The floor of the Class B airspace is 4000 feet, so there are constantly conflicts with VFR aircraft climbing up to 3500 feet or higher in that area. When doing simultaneous approaches, there is nowhere to go when there is a conflict. The floor of the Class B airspace west of ORD should be 3,500 feet until 25 miles west of ORD.
ASRS:1806744.s: An air traffic controller at ORD issued a traffic alert to Aircraft X during a busy east flow arrival when a VFR aircraft climbed to 3,900 feet below the Class B floor. The controller attributed the conflict to overlapping data blocks and a mismatch between the 4,000-foot Class B floor and arrival procedures requiring turns at that altitude.

ASRS:1806767.n: On date, I was informed that I flew an aircraft with un-reported tail strike damage. The flight in question was Aircraft X. I don't remember very many specifics from my walk around. I showed up to the airport in ZZZ a little early that day because my spouse had traveled to ZZZ with me on the overnight and she was leaving on a slightly earlier flight. The Captain and I ended up meeting up at KCM [Known Crew Member] to begin our day. I was slightly delayed getting through security due to no one attending the KCM station and then being selected for random screening. I don't recall feeling rushed though as a result. If I recall correctly, it was a sunny or partly cloudy day, and I almost always wear sunglasses during daylight hours. One threat that occurs is due to Airlines mask wearing policy. While wearing a mask and sun glasses on a walk around, the lenses become fogged often-creating a visibility issue. I am constantly battling this issue on clear, sunny days. Performing multiple walk around a day and per trip, I am having a tough time recalling what the ramp conditions were like with regards to belt loaders and ground equipment around the airplane. I do recognize the threat that dodging ground equipment and vehicles and other equipment around the airplane opens the door for distractions and the potential to miss important items on the walk around. I was notified by flight operations that the aircraft I flew on this flight had experienced a tail strike 2 flights prior to this flight that subsequently went unnoticed for a total of X additional flights including this flight. I did not perform a walk around inspection on this flight but the First Officer did. I do not recall a rushed departure as evidenced by the fact that we pushed 8 minutes prior to schedule but the First Officer did get selected for random additional screening that morning upon going through KCM [Known Crew Member]. I stopped on my way to the aircraft to get something to eat. The delay from the random screening as well as the fact that I did not arrive at the flight deck until approximately 25 minutes prior to scheduled departure may have caused the F/O to feel rushed when he did the walk around inspection, I am not sure.
ASRS:1806767.s: The Captain reported that the First Officer conducted a walk-around on Aircraft X in ZZZ, which had unreported tail strike damage from two flights prior. The Captain suggested the First Officer may have felt rushed due to random security screening and a late arrival, potentially contributing to the missed damage.

ASRS:1806784.n: DG [Dangerous Goods] was planned and loaded without enough mail / bags / ballast. I realized my mistake once I noticed most of my weight in the AFT was cargo and not enough mail / bags as I couldn't close the flight. I also didn't receive a notification prior to closing out the flight. Aircraft pushed early and was returned to the gate as I was contacted by load planning and realized my mistake. DG was removed from pit 4 and placed to pit 3 and secured with bags. Once DG was secured load planner was contacted for pilot notification to be sent. DG (Dangerous Goods) was planned by Ramp Lead without enough weight to secure it. Load Planner called station to stop push because DG was not secured with adequate amount of weight. Lead had to move DG item #1 from pit 4 to pit 3 to secure DG.
ASRS:1806784.s: A Ramp Lead loaded Dangerous Goods without sufficient ballast, causing the aircraft to be returned to the gate before pushback. The item was moved from pit 4 to pit 3 and secured with bags after the Load Planner intervened.

ASRS:1806836.n: We refused aircraft for improper logbook documentation.The aircraft arrived in ZZZ with a write up that the aft, right service door light illuminated in cruise flight. I spoke to the inbound captain face to face who told me that the light illuminated twice in flight and per QRH procedure he directed the cabin crew to push the door handle down which extinguished the light.Maintenance applied MEL 52-XXX which is for the door warning light system. This MEL applies if the door warning light system is malfunctioning. It is my judgment that the warning system was functioning properly. This function was tested again in ZZZ. When the door handle was lifted the light illuminated, and with the door handle fully closed the light extinguished. In other words, the malfunction was likely within the door itself and not the warning system.I discussed this with two B737 check airmen via telephone who agreed the MEL was inappropriate. I also spoke with a representative of the ZZZ chief pilot office and the duty pilot and told them I would gladly take another aircraft or accept the current aircraft if the door/sensor could be adjusted or if a different MEL or sign off could be applied to the logbook.The flight eventually cancelled.The cause of this event was the application of an MEL which did not address the actual maintenance issue.Perhaps this MEL could be written in a matter to include other malfunctions of the door system.
ASRS:1806836.s: A maintenance technician refused a B737 in ZZZ after the crew applied an inappropriate MEL for a door warning light issue, which testing showed was caused by the door itself rather than the warning system. The flight was cancelled because the applied MEL did not address the actual maintenance problem.

ASRS:1806849.n: On initial climb at about 1,000 feet we got a TCAS resolution advisory when an aircraft crossed our departure path. We maintained vertical speed in a climb to comply with the RA. Aircraft almost crossed our departure path only about 100 feet below us.
ASRS:1806849.s: During initial climb at 1,000 feet, the crew received a TCAS resolution advisory as another aircraft crossed their departure path. The crew maintained vertical speed to comply, resulting in the other aircraft passing approximately 100 feet below them.

ASRS:1806914.n: Upon landing long, student without instruction, decided to do a takeoff , without retracting full flaps, carb heat hot, unbeknown to instructor, instead of power he pulls forward mixture that affected partial RPM (was set for high altitude operation) with about a 1,000 ft runway left and not enough speed I (CFII) regain control pulled power, Mixture and deviate to right pass the runway, gravel into short vegetation where I aggressively turned right 180 degrees to preventing hitting airport boundary fence (10 feet away). The plane made a stop without structural damage, there were no physical injuries, the only sustained damaged was to left main wheel brake caliper pressure release nipple and a flat right hand tire.
ASRS:1806914.s: A student pilot attempted a takeoff with full flaps and incorrect mixture settings, causing insufficient speed. The CFII regained control, veered off the runway to avoid a fence, and stopped with minor damage to the brake caliper and a flat tire.

ASRS:1806926.n: Two flights ago in flight training my instructor had taught to keep fuel in mind and to switch tanks periodically during flight as well as when following the checklist. The next flight an engine failure was simulated and upon switching fuel tanks my instructor restored power to the aircraft. Both lessons were among the flight training lessons I had learned were in mind during this flight. I had rested well the night before, had eaten a good breakfast, was not on any medication, and all my paperwork was current. After taking off with full fuel tanks, the plane flew normally during VOR practice and soft field landings at ZZZ1 airport and the fuel tanks were switched about every 15 minutes. Upon returning to ZZZ, I followed the checklist and in doing so switched fuel tanks again. I then completed two landings and take offs. On the third my instructor initiated another simulated engine failure abeam the numbers on downwind. I thought of the previous lessons and decided to switch fuel tanks again after establishing the glide speed and planned to land on runway X. Once I was set up to land and on final for runway X my instructor allowed me to add power as I deemed necessary. The landing was successful and since we were doing touch and go's I set up the aircraft and added power for takeoff. After successful rotation I established the initial climb. About 50ft above the runway surface the engine lost power. My instructor took the flight controls then and landed back on runway X. We rolled off the runway threshold into the grass along the center line. The plane stopped before hitting the fence. The engine was still running at idle at that point, so my instructor radioed ZZZ Tower and they gave us clearance to taxi off the grass and onto the ramp but no further. After looking at the fuel selector switch my instructor and I determined that it was past the left fuel tank mark between it and the shutoff position. The stop that prevents pilots from going past the left fuel tank was not there. I was the instructor giving instruction on a training flight to a student in an airplane owned by a flying club. The student is a member in good standing with the club, and is nearing completion of his Private Pilot training. We were in the process of prepping for his Practical Test by practicing VOR navigation, short field takeoffs and landings, and soft field takeoffs and landings. We were returning from ZZZ1 to ZZZ after practicing on a sod runway. We had entered left traffic on runway X per ZZZ tower instructions, and were remaining in the pattern for the option. Tower had switched us to right traffic on runway X, which is normal procedure at ZZZ. After several touch and goes, the student applied power, initiated rotation, started the climb and the engine lost power. I took the controls and successfully landed on the remaining runway, but was unable to stop prior to running off the end of the runway and rolling out into the grass. Fortunately, the aircraft was able to come to a complete stop prior to the boundary fence.In the past week leading up to this flight, I had to keep reminding the student to switch fuel tanks, stressing that it is most likely going to be the cause of an engine failure if he doesn't. I had the opportunity to reinforce that during another subsequent flight prior to this one. He was in the habit of not utilizing the checklist - not sure why, as it is something I mention on every flight. Today's flight, I again had to remind him when to use the descent and before landing checklists. Both of which call to verify that fuel is on the fullest tank. We have previously discussed having a designated time to switch tanks on numerous occasions. For some reason, he has never accepted any of the instruction I have been giving him. Perhaps now he will.I noticed he was very busy on final this last trip around, and it appeared at this time he was switching tanks. I have never instructed him to switch tanks on final before. For some reason, he continues to do things in the airplane that were not taught, or are in direct opposition to what was being taught. Most of them are minor, but fuel is something I'm very passionate about having on board.After the landing was completed, I looked over at the fuel selector valve which is hidden from my view in the right seat. 'Right' is at the 3 o'clock position with the plastic frame to guard it from going further. 'Left' is at the 12 o'clock position with the spring loaded stopper at the 6 o'clock position so you feel a 'click' when it is in the detent. Off is at the 9 o'clock position, requiring the stop button to be depressed before it can be selected. It was evident the stop button had broken off at some point. When I examined the physical position of the selector switch, it was at the 10-11 o'clock position. Not fully 'Off', not fully 'Left.' An engine run performed by us after being towed back to the FBO ramp verified the engine ran fine. That's when we discussed the broken fuel selector valve.As the instructor, I monitor my student's preflight actions, but never really perform the preflight myself to verify the students actions unless I notice they miss something. I have no reason to doubt my student did anything wrong during the preflight. During the debrief, we reviewed the importance of a thorough preflight and proper maintenance. We also performed an engine run per Maintenance's request. There was nothing noted on engine performance, but while switching the fuel tanks, it was discovered that there was no 'click' when the Left tank was selected.My student may have felt a need to hurry things along with his training since he is leaving the area at the end of this semester. Perhaps some basic knowledge was missed, he may have been stressed with school coming to a close, or any number of things that distracted him from truly paying attention to flying.I believe with the debrief we had, my student will now pay attention to appropriate times to switch fuel tanks rather than being so focused on one thing at a time.
ASRS:1806926.s: During a student pilot training flight, the engine lost power shortly after takeoff because the fuel selector was positioned between the left tank and off due to a broken stop. The instructor took control, landed the aircraft, and rolled off the runway into grass before stopping safely.

ASRS:1806940.n: Received ATIS and requested taxi clearance with VFR Flight Following. Instructed to taxi to runway 35R via the ramp and cross Runway 35L. Started the taxi and received the VFR Flight Following instructions on the taxi. During taxi I was looking for the ramp taxiway lines, unable to see them due to fading. Entered Runway 35L, with no knowledge of crossing a hold short lines. There is no difference between ramp and Runway 35L concrete and the ramp was covered in weeds. Cleared the runway at 35L and asked for instructions from Tower to Runway 35R. Was instructed to taxi down Runway 35L to Taxiway G then holdshort of Runway 35R.
ASRS:1806940.s: The pilot entered Runway 35L while taxiing to 35R because faded markings and weeds made the ramp and runway indistinguishable. After clearing the runway, Tower instructed the pilot to taxi down Runway 35L to Taxiway G and hold short of Runway 35R.

ASRS:1806942.n: FL290, approximately 45 nm south of ZZZ, SIC (Second In Command) noticed oil streaming across the left side of the right engine. Immediately after the master caution illuminated and both crew members noticed the right engine oil pressure in the yellow range indicating 65 PSI. Shortly after the engine oil pressure dropped to the red range and the crew received a master warning oil pressure low light. Crew immediately referenced the checklist and conducted the engine shut down procedure for the right engine. Crew then advised ATC and diverted to ZZZ. Crew completed a single engine landing that was uneventful.
ASRS:1806942.s: The SIC and PIC flying at FL290 observed oil streaming and low pressure on the right engine, triggering a master warning. They executed the shutdown checklist, diverted to ZZZ, and completed an uneventful single-engine landing.

ASRS:1806949.n: While visiting out west, I planned a short, low altitude flight for a view of the lake, and to take some footage and photos. It was sunny, no clouds. A resident agreed to let me take off and land. From the takeoff location, I called Leidos Flight Service to get a flight briefing and asked about weather conditions and for any TFRs. Everything seemed in order for a flight, although he did suggest calling the airport. I said we should not call anymore, that if it was in such an area they now have LAANC (Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability). He said he was not sure, that they keep changing the procedure. About the same time, I checked my EFB, iFly GPS, which has a Quick View Popup window with advisories for an immediate location. The controlled airspace advisory button was dimmed, but I clicked it anyway to be sure and it said 'No Airspaces found here'. I took that to mean no controlled airspace was where I was, at my AGL (0 ft). I should have checked against the LAANC system. I am sorry about that. The iFly GPS sectional also referenced svc times for the surface extension, which was confusing to me, since the popup window said no controlled airspaces were found. I should have spent more time pouring over the sectional and have recognized the meaning of the magenta dashed lines.
