Although I also found out today they are on reduced service hours, so not sure if this applies. But I should have been aware. It was not until today, that I happened upon the LAANC for the area. Recommendation: To avoid this, remote pilots should always check against the LAANC system for controlled air space, especially if relatively unfamiliar with an area, as I was. Remote pilots should not rely on general aviation EFBs that may or may not call out things that are significant to remote pilots. I have taken some manned pilot flying lessons. Again, I am sorry. I am definitely going to be more diligent, and take extra precautions in unfamiliar situations to watch for controlled air space. I will pore over the sectional closer, and check the LAANC system. Thanks.
ASRS:1806949.s: A remote pilot conducted a low-altitude flight near a lake and inadvertently entered controlled airspace due to relying on an EFB that failed to display the restriction. The pilot admits the cause was failing to verify the area against the LAANC system or properly interpret sectional chart markings.

ASRS:1806950.n: I was on a mapping mission for a housing development at this [location]. As I was beginning to take the photographs and was hovering at 400 ft. AGL I noticed a fighter jet performing a banked turn just beyond my UAV. I am not sure whether it knew I was flying there or not. It showed up on my photo so I knew it had to be pretty close. Based on my sectional chart I did not believe I was in Lake AFB SATR (Special Air Traffic Rules). I immediately descended and landed my aircraft to avoid any other conflict in the area.
ASRS:1806950.s: A UAV pilot conducting a mapping mission at 400 ft AGL observed a fighter jet performing a banked turn in close proximity. Believing the location was outside Lake AFB SATR, the pilot immediately descended and landed to avoid conflict.

ASRS:1806968.n: The Autopilot A was engaged. The RNAV ZZZZZ3 Arrival and the RNPZ XXL were programmed in the FMC. The approach was not connected at ZZZZZ, as we were not cleared for the approach. Approximately five miles prior to ZZZZZ1 [fix] we were told to expect vectors for the ILS. We selected the ILS XXL in the FMC, and upon executing the selection, we received an Autopilot Disconnect message, and an A/P Disconnect Caution light. The aircraft went into Control Wheel Pitch. I, the Pilot Flying, immediately selected Vertical Speed to keep the aircraft in a state towards the impending crossing restriction. I also reset the Altitude Alerter for X;000 feet, as we now were in Vertical Speed and needed altitude protection at ZZZZZ2 [fix].A few seconds later we passed over ZZZZZ2. The Autopilot Disconnect Caution light illuminated, and the Autopilot Lateral Mode switched to Control Wheel Steering, and the aircraft didn't turn and follow the still illuminated and displayed LNAV PATH. I immediately engaged heading mode, and turned to rejoin our intended course. Approach gave us a heading, as the minor deviation from our path was most likely noticeable. The rest of the flight proceeded uneventfully. We assumed we programmed the FMC incorrectly, in some way, and we needed to be more vigilant. ZZZ to ZZZ1 [airport], we were on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV, Autopilot B engaged, on PATH. We were given an intercept heading to join final for [Runway] XX. Heading mode was selected. The aircraft flew heading and was in VNAV. The final approach course was entered into the FMC, and upon executing, the Autopilot B Vertical mode disengaged, with the A/P Caution light and the aircraft descended in Control Wheel Pitch. We selected a pitch mode and proceeded without further incident.My concern: I don't know why these disconnects happened. If they are normal for the -800 MAX, I am unaware of this. I thought all of our fleet types were programmed and responded to Pilot programming the same, in this scenario. I've never experienced [other model] aircraft revert to CWS Pitch or roll, even with faulty Pilot programming. We both assumed that perhaps, since neither of us had flown a MAX in a few years that we missed some training, or company notice. We assumed that the error was a Pilot programming error. I called the Chief Pilot on Call and told him of the occurrence the first time, and he was unaware of such a thing happening normally. We confessed that we actually had more experience than him in the MAX. He indicated I should call later and talk to the MAX programming expert and he perhaps could explain why the MAX behaves in this way. That is why we flew the aircraft a second leg with the anomaly, I assumed it was Pilot programming error. A few days later, I was contacted by a Chief Pilot, who informed me that our experience was a malfunction, and that a logbook entry and maintenance resolution should have taken place. I assumed it was a MAX anomaly, but it was a malfunction.
ASRS:1806968.s: Pilots on a Boeing 787-8 MAX experienced two autopilot disconnects during arrival and approach phases when selecting ILS and final approach courses in the FMC. The aircraft reverted to Control Wheel Steering and Pitch modes, which the crew initially attributed to programming errors but was later confirmed by the Chief Pilot to be a malfunction requiring maintenance.

ASRS:1806979.n: Severe turbulence encounter on climb after departing. We conducted a full and normal briefing in operations prior to the flight. During that briefing we identified a threat of possible turbulence around 20,000 feet based on a PIREP. Upon arriving at the plane, I briefed the lead Flight Attendant. That briefing included a discussion on turbulence. I directed that the Flight Attendants stay seated for the departure until I call. Ground operations through takeoff and climbout were normal and uneventful. Departure cleared us to 17,000 feet. We leveled there awaiting hand off to Center and were in light turbulence. After a short delay we were cleared to climb to approximately 25,000 feet and to contact Center. I initiated the climb via VNAV. Almost immediately we encountered severe turbulence. The airspeed was fluctuating and the plane banked +-25 AOB (Angle of Bank). The autopilot remained engaged and made appropriate corrections. However, I put my hands on the controls in anticipation of needing to take control. The ride was so violent that my First Officer could not get his hands on the radio knob to change frequencies. By 18,000 feet the ride eased to moderate turbulence. When I deemed it safe, I then picked up the PA and asked 'Flight Attendants check in.' They checked the cabin and reported all passenger, crew and plane were safe. The First Officer made the check in with Center, reported the severe turbulence.At an appropriate time, I notified dispatch of the event. He published our PIREP. Later we submitted the log entry for maintenance. Further down line ZZZ1 Station was notified and I discussed with them an appropriate response upon landing. The remainder of the flight was uneventful, not even a ripple of turbulence. Once blocked in and checklists completed, I greeted passengers in case any were still concerned. They all seemed very appreciative, and thankful. Many even commented on the smooth landing and offered thanks for a safe trip. Customer Service, Maintenance and Flight Operations and met us at the gate. I provided full debriefs to each. The flight operations manager said we did a great job but also advised we submit a safety report. I want to offer that I believe the system, Standard Operating Procedures, and tools made available work. While I could not foresee the severity of the turbulence that awaited us, we knew a rough ride would be encountered in that area and took precaution. The result was no injuries to crew or passengers or damage to the plane. I offer this report mostly to help improve the system. And I am happy to answer any questions if necessary. WSI (Weather Service International) indicated a narrow band of turbulence on our route from roughly 17,000 to 20,000 feet due to shear below a jet stream. Larger jets reported moderate (PIREP symbols) turbulence on WSI so the Captain had the flight attendants remain seated after takeoff until we called them. At the time of the event the seat belt sign was ON and everyone on the plane was seated. As we climbed through 17,000 feet the turbulence worsened from moderate to severe. Large and rapid airspeed deviations of +/- 25 knots and sharp rolling moments of roughly 25 to 30 degrees occurred for roughly 2 minutes, all estimates. As Pilot Monitoring it took me awhile to tune the ATC radios for a frequency change as I couldn't grab the tuning knobs in the turbulence. I believe ATC instructed us to climb from 17,000 to 19,000 feet and that put us into the worst of the turbulence. Once we were cleared to climb higher (above 19,000 feet) the ride improved quickly. I believe a hand off from TRACON to Center caused much of the delay but I am not certain.Again, the seat belt sign was on and all flight attendants were seated per the briefing. No injuries and no damage. We did not make the 'be seated immediately' announcements as everyone was still seated since takeoff. We were focused on getting a higher altitude and a better ride. Once we were clear of the turbulence we asked the flight attendants to 'check in' per our turbulence training. We filed a PIREP with ATC and notified Dispatch.
ASRS:1806979.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence while climbing from 17,000 to 25,000 feet after departure, causing rapid airspeed fluctuations and bank angles up to 30 degrees. The event was attributed to shear below a jet stream, but because all crew and passengers were seated per pre-flight briefings, there were no injuries or aircraft damage.

ASRS:1806995.n: After getting our clearance to depart SEA via the Mountain Departure 16L, the airport switched runways to north departure on 34R. ATC [then] gave us the Seattle 7. After looking at the FMS it appeared that it coded a 345 heading after departure but no intercept of the 341 radial off SEA as shown on the plate. Thus I used raw data and flew the departure with heading select and tracked the radial manually. I believe there is an error with this departure because a 345 initial heading diverges away from the 341 radial instead of towards it. This may be why the FMS does not show an intercept because it is not possible to intercept on a 345 heading. This should be 341 or something similar to the Mountain Departure which is basically the same.
ASRS:1806995.s: The pilot reported a potential FMS coding error on the Seattle 7 departure from SEA runway 34R, where the programmed 345-degree heading diverged from the required 341 radial. The crew manually flew the departure using raw data, suspecting the FMS failed to show an intercept because the initial heading made interception impossible.

ASRS:1806998.n: We were cleared to taxi out for takeoff on Runway XXR via [Taxiway] 1, hold short of [Taxiway] 2. After stopping as directed, we were told to continue to Runway XXR on Taxiway 2. Around [Taxiway] 2X, a Regional Jet pushed back without warning from around gate XX or XY just in front of us. I made an abrupt stop. My guess is they saw us stop before [Taxiway] 2, assumed we were going to stay there and prepared to push back without looking at us again. I called back to the purser to ensure everyone was okay. She stated that a Flight Attendant had hit the wall hard but was okay. We continued taxiing for takeoff.
ASRS:1806998.s: While taxiing to Runway XXR, a Regional Jet pushed back without warning from a nearby gate, forcing the flight crew to make an abrupt stop. The reporter attributed the incident to the jet crew assuming the aircraft would remain stationary, resulting in a Flight Attendant hitting the cabin wall.

ASRS:1807000.n: Started descent for the ZZZZ 1 arrival into ZZZ from FL400. At approximately FL330 we received an IAS DISAGREE message. I checked all 3 airspeed indicators and mine matched the standby while the Captain's showed 10 KTS slow. Captain ran the appropriate checklists. Shortly after finishing the checklist we got an ENG master caution. I looked up and saw the Electronic Engine Control (EEC) had both reverted to ALTN. Captain ran the checklist. At approximately FL200 we got the ALT DISAGREE message, again ran the checklist. As we descended the Captain's airspeed indicator got as low as 40 KTS slower than my airspeed indicator and the standby airspeed indicator. We continued to descend via the arrival and shot the visual approach to Runway XXL with no other issues or incidents.
ASRS:1807000.s: The crew experienced IAS, EEC, and ALT disagree messages during descent from FL400 for the ZZZZ 1 arrival, with the Captain's airspeed indicator showing up to 40 KTS slow. After completing checklists for these discrepancies, the flight continued safely to a visual approach and landing on Runway XXL.

ASRS:1807015.n: While in cruise phase at 35,000 feet the Captain who was the Pilot Monitoring at the time noticed a small crack in the left windshield. Upon recognizing the situation the Captain immediately took the aircraft controls, instructed me, now the Pilot Monitoring, to advise ATC that we are executing a descent. I complied with the Captain's instructions and we told ATC that we were descending to 10,000 feet and diverting to ZZZ which was approximately 40 miles away at the time. At this time the Captain continued to fly and talk to ATC while I called operations at ZZZ to let them know we were coming. After this we set up for the ILS XXL to back up the visual since the weather was VMC at ZZZ. We executed all normal checklists and the Captain executed an uneventful approach and landing. We taxied into the ramp and the Captain shutdown and inspected the exterior in the vicinity of the window and passenger door on the left hand side to ensure it was safe to deplane. ZZZ fire rescue also confirmed that we required no further assistance. Passengers were deplaned and aircraft was secured. Cause unknown. Suspected micro crack and heat/cool cycles.
ASRS:1807015.s: During cruise at 35,000 feet, the Captain noticed a crack in the left windshield and diverted to ZZZ for an uneventful landing. The cause is unknown but suspected to be a micro crack exacerbated by heat and cool cycles.

ASRS:1807023.n: Cruising at FL250 due to limitation of PACK 2 deferred. CA (Captain) noticed smoke in cockpit and we ran smoke in cockpit procedure backed up by checklist. Informed flight attendant and she said no smoke in cabin. Performed an immediate descent to 3,500 feet as directed by ATC for visual to Runway X at ZZZ. Vehicles escorted us to Gate X. Fire services performed a sweep for hotspots and found none. Deplaned aircraft and a ferry flight was sent to retrieve passengers.Not sure [of cause] at this time. Could have been avionics or a PACK leak.To make it easier for crew to hear each other and ATC, microphone and oxygen masks should be improved to reduce oxygen noise over ICS (Inter Communication System) and reduce workload due to excess noise.
ASRS:1807023.s: The crew encountered cockpit smoke while cruising at FL250 with PACK 2 deferred, prompting an immediate descent to 3,500 feet and a safe landing. Fire services found no hotspots, and the cause remains unknown, though the pilot suggested avionics or a PACK leak and recommended improved oxygen masks to reduce noise.

ASRS:1807029.n: Due to smoke in cockpit at cruise we requested priority handling, ran smoke in cockpit checklist and memory items, landed safely. After landing I determined we were not in a fully developed active fire, so elected with the escort of the ARFF vehicles to head to a gate, deplaned without incident, fully shut down the plane. Potential fire from avionics or pack system.Suggestions - Improve the o2 mask microphone and reduce o2 noise in the system so that it is easier to hear your crew and ATC.
ASRS:1807029.s: The flight crew encountered smoke in the cockpit during cruise, executed emergency checklists, and landed safely. They attributed the potential fire to the avionics or pack system and suggested improving oxygen mask microphones to reduce noise.

ASRS:1807048.n: Upon departure from Runway XXR, just as we reached acceleration altitude I received an emergency PA from the flight attendant informing me there was smoke in the cabin. I immediately shut off the gasper fan, the recirc fan, the packs, and the APU bleed. I inquired as to the severity and was told 'it's bad.' My First Officer and myself did not see or smell anything resembling smoke. I immediately informed ATC we would like priority handling and requested vectors for an approach back into ZZZ. I asked the flight attendant if the passengers were in danger and if I needed to drop the oxygen masks. I was told at this point 'no' and was informed that the smoke had stopped. I asked the flight attendant to remain on the PA and to inform me the instant any more signs of smoke appeared.We were given vectors around to shoot the ILS to Runway XXR. I told the flight attendant we would be landing soon and to plan for a normal landing and taxi back assuming the smoke remained stopped. After a successful overweight landing, we exited the runway and taxied into the ramp. We had fire trucks follow us into our gate. They informed us they saw no heat signatures on our aircraft. The aircraft was successfully deplaned without injury or incident. Contract maintenance arrived a short while later and found a panel light in above seat X had shorted out and burned through the contact casing.Hindsight 20/20 I wouldn't have requested priority handling. In the moment, given the information I had to work with, I made a decision based on the fact that I thought there was a fire in the cabin and wanted to get the aircraft on the ground as quickly and as safely as possible. Crew Resource Management was almost nonexistent during this event. There was a very big language barrier between myself and my First Officer. During normal operations I often struggled to understand what he was saying. I took the lead on the radios, navigating, the communication with the flight attendant, and piloting the aircraft.
ASRS:1807048.s: The flight crew diverted immediately after a flight attendant reported cabin smoke during departure, shutting off air systems and requesting priority handling. Maintenance later found a shorted panel light caused the smoke, and the aircraft landed safely with no injuries, though the pilot noted significant language barriers with the First Officer.

ASRS:1807082.n: IOE FO (First Officer) was performing a visual approach into RNO Runway 16L, backed up with RNAV X 16L. We were outside BADPE and were visual with the runway, check airman was monitoring FO and said 'You are too low, shallow out your descent rate.' FO proceeded to do so but not aggressively enough of a correction, Check airman was about to correct him again and we got a single EGPWS aural of 'OBSTACLE.' Under guidance of check airman, FO disconnected autopilot, added power, and climbed a few hundred feet. We were then back on profile and still outside final approach fix of BADPE so continued on approach with FO hand flying. The EGPWS Aural occurred at about 6,500 feet altitude about 4 miles outside of the BADPE fix. Check airman believes terrain clearance was safe, we were observing one white light and three red lights on PAPI, but the EGPWS disagreed with me. We were too low on a visual approach. Check airman had asked for a correction but was not insistent or urgent enough to get through to the FO. Busy arrival with many configuration changes, radio calls, etc. And it was a first day of flight with this particular FO, check airman did not realize that this FO was perhaps a bit overloaded and behind the aircraft, may have overestimated his skill level at this time.Check airman (Me) should have been more insistent about tolerances, as in not accepting one little bit low per arrival altitude guidance on RNAV plate.
ASRS:1807082.s: A Check Airman and First Officer experienced an EGPWS "OBSTACLE" warning at 6,500 feet during a visual approach to RNO Runway 16L. The event occurred because the First Officer descended too low and the Check Airman failed to insist on immediate correction, leading to a manual climb to regain profile.

ASRS:1807149.n: While descending into ZZZ, my student elected to make a midfield entry into the downwind. We briefed the approach and announced our position on CTAF at about 4 miles outside of the airport. Following our call, another aircraft asked our location in relation to the airport. We attempted to reply, but severe radio congestion prevented a response. The student and I began scanning for traffic, but it appeared that no other aircraft were in our area. Just after crossing midfield, we began our turn to downwind when the previous aircraft announced a midfield downwind. We spotted the traffic 100 to 150 feet below us and passing underneath us to our left. We took evasive action and initiated a climb, then rejoined a normal downwind behind the aircraft. No evasive action was taken by the other aircraft and it seemed he was not aware of the near miss. The rest of the flight occurred without incident.I believe the cause of the near miss was a result of extreme frequency congestion in the area. Communication in the area was encumbered by heavy usage and several radio calls we made were blocked due to other transmissions, leading to confusion over aircraft positions at the airport we were using. A review of the chart showed a large number of airports with 50NM operating on XYY.Z and several of those airports were surrounding the busy nearby metro areas. My recommendation would be to evaluate the airport usage of that area and assign unique frequencies several busier airports in the area.
ASRS:1807149.s: A pilot and student descending into ZZZ experienced a near miss with another aircraft due to severe radio congestion on CTAF. The congestion blocked position reports, causing the other pilot to unknowingly pass 100 to 150 feet below, forcing the reporting crew to climb and rejoin downwind.

ASRS:1807158.n: I was not present when the event occurred. I am the instructor who signed off this student for solo. The winds were calm, the student was proficient, and to my knowledge, the aircraft was well maintained when I provided instruction to him the previous day. The following is what the student told me. After touch down, the student attempted to make an early exit, and allowed the stick to return to neutral and applied brakes. This caused the tail wheel to lift off the ground and he lost control of the aircraft. He told me that his wingtip touched the ground and there may have been damage to one of the wings. He stated that he will have the aircraft manufacturer or other qualified mechanic inspect, repair and return the aircraft to service. To my understanding, the cause of the event was the student's failure to keep the stick in the full aft position, combined with excessive braking. This appears to be the result of a momentary lapse of judgement on his part. The student was highly proficient in all procedures involving taxi, takeoff and landing of the aircraft. This error was not made on any recent instructional flights. Following the procedures taught to him by his instructors (keeping the stick full aft, minimizing brake usage, and taking the next exit) would have prevented the event from occurring.
ASRS:1807158.s: A student pilot lost control of a tailwheel aircraft during an early exit after landing by neutralizing the stick and applying excessive brakes, causing a wingtip strike. The instructor attributed the incident to the student's momentary lapse in judgment regarding control inputs and braking.

ASRS:1807175.n: The rental company I operate under had asked myself and another flight instructor to return the crew car back to ZZZ and in the process of doing so, fly back the Cessna 182 that had stayed there over night. A few days ago, that C182 had a runway excursion under a renter and instructor that had resulted in the aircraft going off the end of the runway in to the dirt, stopping short of the fence at the end. This was due to a failure in the left brake. The mechanic in ZZZ had worked on the airplane over X days to inspect the condition and replace the left side brakes. Myself and another instructor were asked to fly the C182 back home to ZZZ1. Upon arriving to ZZZ, the mechanic had informed us that the C182 is good to go with no damage to the firewall and engine and had us do a static check on the ground before taxiing. This resulted in us using full brakes and full power to make sure the airplane wasn't going anywhere. After our preflight inspection and the 'OK' from the mechanic, we deemed it safe to fly back to ZZZ1. I had no issues upon landing and made the safe 20 minute maintenance flight home. Upon us returning the keys of the C182 to the office, we had asked for the airplane to be grounded regardless, for our own maintenance personnel to inspect the airplane. Our maintenance had let us know that the bottom of the fuselage appeared slightly bent and that the left brake that had been replaced still needed some work. Seeing as that we had flown an aircraft that had the potential to be unairworthy, I will be much more careful next time I take a maintenance flight and see if I can get a double check on aircraft that need to flown, with other mechanics. I do not do many maintenance flights for this reason and will be much more thorough about what airplanes I fly.
ASRS:1807175.s: Two flight instructors flew a Cessna 182 from ZZZ to ZZZ1 after a mechanic replaced the left brakes following a previous runway excursion. Post-flight inspection revealed a bent fuselage and remaining brake issues, leading the pilots to ground the aircraft and resolve to verify airworthiness more thoroughly before future maintenance flights.

ASRS:1807201.n: On ground Controller warned of incoming storm from the south. I suggested that I remain in pattern and just do some full stop landings ahead of the storm. Controller said storm was not moving quickly and likely could get in at least one practice instrument approach. Controller said Approach was busy that day so I said I would vector myself. Flew ILS XX approach. Vectored self successfully and joined the localizer. Encountered light rain at ZZZZZ [fix] but maintained VFR. Inside of ZZZZZ rain stopped. Cleared for landing on Runway XX and had very nice, smooth landing. Use Beta to slow aircraft down and left runway for taxiway without incident. Controller advised re: taxiways back to hangar. Left turn off of runway then right turn onto Taxiway 1. At end of Taxiway 1 left turn at Taxiway 2/3 intersection. Plane facing west. Braked, trying to stop at the intersection to confirm controller instructions. Plane would not stop and would not go straight. Very unusual and had not encountered that situation before. Plane veered off taxiway to left, went off into grass and down a slight hill, doing a 180, facing east. Then came to a full stop. No plane damage and no injuries. Passenger who had much difficulty fitting into the passenger seat. He was a big man and was quite cramped. He asked if seat would go back further but it would not. Not sure if his feet interfered with brakes/rudder pedals. Personnel showed up and provided tow vehicle. Had plane towed back to hangar. Aircraft to be inspected.
ASRS:1807201.s: The pilot and a large passenger experienced a ground incident where the aircraft veered off the taxiway after failing to stop at an intersection. The pilot suspected the passenger's feet may have interfered with the brake or rudder pedals, resulting in no injuries or damage but requiring a tow and inspection.

ASRS:1807244.n: I was working Sector 18 Woodstown, but not actually Woodstown (sitting at Sector 17). I was to be only working the Compton and Reading military airspace, which had Aircraft Y's and a Aircraft Z in it at the time. I witnessed the Aircraft Y refueling with the tanker at FL256 with out communicating that to me. Shortly there after, Aircraft Y separated from the tanker without communicating to me, and what I assume was descending back to the fighter cap altitudes of FL230-FL240 of which he was initially cleared to be at. Aircraft Y turned at the southern portion and descended, and then I saw him at FL227 below his assigned altitude. Aircraft X, was at FL220 right underneath him. I immediately asked the pilot if he was FL230-FL240, he responded that he was. At the same time the altitudes on the data block went back to FL230-FL240. The Sector 19 Controller, who was working Sector 18's airspace (even thought Sector 18's airspace was assigned to me sitting physically at Sector 17), said that Aircraft X was responding to an RA and descended. I immediately called the traffic to the fighter jet at that time. Filed previous reports regarding the Presidential airspace over Delaware. Procedures are not defined, there is no LOA or SOP, and the workforce was not properly briefed. There are many sited violations FAA Orders associated with this unsafe operation in addition to automation issues that can cause unsafe situations with Sector 18 not being utilized correctly. Request an LOA for the procedures, and for the boundaries, altitudes, refueling operations, and reroutes to all be negotiated with affected parties and implemented correctly in an LOA. A fighter jet got too close to an airliner jet in this situation, and the pilot did not even seem to understand the issue or care. They need to at the very least stay at their assigned altitudes, and they should be communicating with us on refueling operations to avoid situations like this. Aircraft X was level at FL220 and given the descent clearance for the PHLBO 3 arrival. Aircraft Y was a single military fighter in COMPTON Airspace. Aircraft Y descended out of the Airspace without coordination and caused Aircraft X to react to an RA alert. Traffic was issued to Aircraft X and he eventually continued his descent via the PHLBO3 arrival.There is much confusion on how the Biden airspace should be managed. Some controllers work EWR arrivals while others don't. The current assignment of airspace makes it difficult for processing hand-offs and point-outs correctly. Although this airspace confusion had no implication on the military aircraft leaving the confines of the restricted airspace, it needs to be address for clarification and safety. Point-outs and hand-offs may be missed.
ASRS:1807244.s: A military fighter (Aircraft Y) descended below its assigned altitude without coordination after refueling, causing a civilian airliner (Aircraft X) at FL220 to react to a Resolution Advisory. The controller attributed the unsafe proximity to undefined procedures, lack of communication regarding refueling, and airspace management confusion.

ASRS:1807247.n: I was providing training on Ground 1 when Aircraft X exited Runway 25R and the trainee instructed them to taxi via C, N, north route. The Aircraft X pilot read back the instruction correctly. A minute later, I heard the OS (Operational Supervisor) advise us that Aircraft X taxied up L and not N which we, the training team, had not noticed. (Background: Taxiway K & L used to be the north route, but those are now a ramp area controlled by the City of LA for pushback from the international terminal. Taxiway N is now the north route.) This situation began to present itself several months ago when the taxiway routes first changed from L & K to N & P. It does not seem to happen as often, but I've now noticed four different scenarios in the last week (two last weekday, and two this same weekday.) It still seems to be a possibly systemic problem. In addition to Aircraft X, while the OS was telling me and the trainee that our 'scan needs to be better' to prevent this situation, Aircraft Y was under tow to Gate X and began to turn on K instead of L. (Per the LOA with the city, all arrivals to the ramp must enter via L & hold short of K1.) I immediately instructed Aircraft Y to stop, called the Ramp Tower to coordinate any potential traffic conflicts, then allowed the Aircraft Y reposition to continue. I'd recommend additional signage, a change to the charts, or added emphasis in the text of the 'north route' that emboldens how N is now the north route, not K or L. Or all of the above. The above recommendations would help alleviate the issue from the IFR/pilot side. Regarding the repositions/tows: the City of LA should disseminate refresher training to every airline that repositions aircraft on the LAX airfield. This training should be mandatory for any reposition operator and clearly explain the new procedures for the ramp. The response from Aircraft Y for why they turned on K instead of L was that they 'temporarily lost communication with their tow driver.' This response is unacceptable. Unless specifically instructed, no revenue flight or reposition is ever to enter the ramp via K.
ASRS:1807247.s: An ATC training team observed Aircraft X and a towed Aircraft Y incorrectly entering restricted taxiways K and L instead of the designated north route N at LAX. The reporter attributes these systemic errors to outdated pilot knowledge and a tow driver's loss of communication, recommending updated charts and mandatory ramp training.

ASRS:1807255.n: Upon arrival to the gate we waited approximately eight to ten minutes for an agent to show to bring the jetway to the aircraft. We called twice to operations to request a jetway driver. Upon opening the flight deck door, I noticed that the provision and provo worker was already on board the aircraft and restocking items. This is while we had no jetway attached to the aircraft. Upon asking the Flight Attendants I asked them if any of the doors were armed and also asked that the provision truck be delayed and close the door. I questioned the ability to be able to evacuate the aircraft with approximately 136 passengers onboard with no jetway attached, all doors disarmed and at least one provision truck attached at the forward service door. After visiting with the Flight Attendants about this topic and also the Provo Worker, I was informed that this is a procedure approved about one year ago. I have a great concern if the need arises to evacuate at the gate while waiting for a Jetway Driver and the jetway to be attached, having one or more Provo trucks attached at a several feet up in the air that this may impede an evacuation.
ASRS:1807255.s: The pilot reported that a provision worker boarded and restocked the aircraft while no jetway was attached and all doors were disarmed. The pilot expressed concern that the attached provision truck could impede evacuation of 136 passengers, despite being told this was an approved procedure.

ASRS:1807278.n: PTKK Runway 4 PAPI out of service. Broke out at minimums and no PAPI. Asked TKK Radio and they said it was not working, but no NOTAM issued.
ASRS:1807278.s: A pilot approaching PTKK Runway 4 found the PAPI out of service with no NOTAM issued. After breaking out at minimums without visual glide slope guidance, the pilot confirmed the equipment failure with TKK Radio.

ASRS:1807279.n: Since Typhoon Yutu in Saipan, the PAPI lights have been out of service. After advising the company last year, the Jepp chart was finally changed. However, it now says there are VASI instead of PAPI (but there is no visual guidance). After I made several queries with SPN ATC, they said there is no plan to install any visual guidance lights (PAPI or VASI) on Runway 07. There is a plan to replace the PAPI for Runway 25.
ASRS:1807279.s: The pilot reported that at Saipan, Runway 07 lacks visual guidance lights following Typhoon Yutu, despite Jepp charts incorrectly listing VASI. ATC confirmed no plan to install lights on Runway 07, though PAPI replacement is planned for Runway 25.

ASRS:1807288.n: We have been made aware of the PKWA (Bucholz Army Airfield Kwajalein Island) runway being shortened from 6,668 feet to a new LDA (Landing Distance Available), ASDA (Accelerate-Stop Distance Available), TORA (Takeoff Run Available), and TODA (Takeoff Distance Available) to 6,058 feet. This is due to what has been called a 'displaced threshold' on both ends of the runway. However, I was expecting pavement from the start of the original Runway 6 with chevrons or similar markings as per the AIM. However, what I saw on final was the first 400 feet of Runway 6 is now coral, gravel, and dirt...not pavement. It is not a displaced threshold, the runway now actually starts 400 feet further down the island. There are temporary lights placed on the pavement to indicate the starting edge of the new runway edge. The approach end of Runway 24 has been displaced 140 feet and still has pavement that is repainted with a temporary threshold and is marked with temporary lighting as well. The performance on the Takeoff Data Message has been adjusted correctly. The PAPI are out of service as well to ensure you are not guided into an early landing as well. Don't expect a displaced threshold on Runway 6 per the NOTAM, expect a new start to the runway surface.
ASRS:1807288.s: A pilot reported that Runway 6 at PKWA was shortened to 6,058 feet due to the first 400 feet being replaced by coral, gravel, and dirt rather than a standard displaced threshold. Consequently, the runway surface effectively starts 400 feet further down, with temporary lights marking the new edge and PAPIs out of service to prevent early landings.

ASRS:1807324.n: Night VFR RNAV Y XXR approach. Approaching FAF ZZZ tower advised us of Cessna traffic on downwind turning base for short parallel runway XXL. Traffic in sight. As we passed our FAF, fully configured and stable we saw the Cessna pointing right at us on base and both remarked 'I hope they don't overshoot'. At approximately 800 feet AGL the Cessna was still pointing at us and I could see they were clearly going to overshoot slightly above us as they turned to final. I felt it was way too close and pushed over slightly as I estimated them to be no more than 100-200 feet above us as they crossed right over us and slightly behind. As our approach was now unstable in my estimation I executed an uneventful go-around. We advised tower of the close pass. We returned for a second, uneventful approach and landing to XXR. I called tower controller after landing and he said he would contact the Cessna pilot and talk to him about the incident. Cessna not keeping us in sight and possibly lining up on incorrect runway. Light VFR traffic maintaining better situational awareness with a large air carrier with approximately XXX people on board and all landing lights, fully configured on final approach.
ASRS:1807324.s: During a night VFR RNAV approach to runway XXR, a Cessna on base for a parallel runway passed within 100–200 feet above the carrier aircraft. The pilot executed a go-around due to the unstable situation, attributing the close call to the Cessna's poor situational awareness and potential runway confusion.

ASRS:1807350.n: Flight called approximately 10 minutes after departure stating that they had a frozen stabilizer. The crew said that the aircraft was still controllable with increased difficulty. When they called they were dumping fuel with intentions of returning to ZZZ. They dumped 82,000 lbs of fuel at X;X00 ft. The fuel jettison system failed before they could get under max landing weight. They continued to burn the remaining amount in a holding pattern. Flight [advised ATC] and landed the aircraft safely.
ASRS:1807350.s: The flight crew reported a frozen stabilizer 10 minutes after departure and attempted to jettison 82,000 lbs of fuel at X;X00 ft to return to ZZZ. When the fuel jettison system failed, they burned the remaining fuel in a holding pattern and landed the aircraft safely.

ASRS:1807355.n: Aircraft X reposition leg from ZZZ-ZZZ1. On climbout through around 10,000 ft MSL, copilot side AP Pitch Trim Fail Red CAS message illuminated once pilot flying engaged autopilot. After disengaging autopilot, PM noticed the pitch trim indication was inoperative. Aircraft pitch trim still was operational, but indication was not working. Crew referenced QRH and contacted company operations and decided to divert to ZZZ2.
ASRS:1807355.s: During Aircraft X's climbout through 10,000 ft MSL, engaging the autopilot triggered a copilot AP Pitch Trim Fail message and inoperative pitch trim indication. The crew followed the QRH, contacted operations, and diverted to ZZZ2 while the trim remained functional.

ASRS:1807364.n: On descent into ZZZ, I was the pilot monitoring, on the way we were cleared from 17,000 ft to 5,300 ft to commence our approach into ZZZ. Leaving 16,000 the plane experienced a loss of oil pressure in our #2 engine. After taking a few moments to assess the situation I had confirmed the warning message with the supporting oil pressure gauge on ED1 as it read 7 psi. From there I handed the radios over to the Captain as I proceeded to the appropriate QRH procedure for R ENG OIL PRESS. Following the steps of this procedure very carefully, I was led to shut down our #2 engine in flight through the In-flight engine shut down procedure. After which I then completed the single engine approach and landing procedure. During this time the Captain, flew and maintained control of the aircraft, alerted ATC, as well as alerting the flight attendant of the situation. We landed safely in ZZZ where we were cleared by ARFF and taxied to the gate.
ASRS:1807364.s: The pilot monitoring reported a #2 engine oil pressure loss at 16,000 ft during descent into ZZZ, confirmed by a 7 psi reading on ED1. The crew executed the QRH shutdown procedure, completed a single-engine approach, and landed safely after ARFF clearance.

ASRS:1807394.n: Flight began from ZZZ as second leg of duty day. Start, taxi and takeoff were uneventful. Shortly after reaching cruise altitude of FL280, we noticed a low oil qty (0%) and dropping oil pressure (approximately psi). I called for QRH and Captain began running Low Oil Pressure Checklist. While accomplishing the checklist, the oil pressure dropped below 15 psi and entered the Warning (Red) regime. This drove us to shutdown the #1 engine. Captain advised ATC and a gradual descent to FL 250 was initially begun. After the shutdown was completed, we elected to begin diverting to ZZZ1 as it was only 50 miles away. ATC, Flight Attendants and dispatch were all provided with necessary information to assist us as we requested Rwy XXL, but due to heavy traffic and closure of XXC, ATC requested we use XXR. Landing data was run by both crew and dispatch and stopping distance was sufficient on the shorter runway. While descending, I was momentarily distracted by the runway change and while simultaneously slowing to 200 kts Inattention caused us to slow to approximately 189 kts and we received an 'Airspeed Low' warning. I accelerated back to 210 kts and requested Flaps 5. We executed a normal approach and landing with 5 extra kts of speed due to a '10 kts of gain' on final report. Once we landed, we exited the runway and requested Fire Chief to check us out. After receiving the all clear, we taxied uneventfully to the gate and accomplished all checklists. All events were debriefed in accordance with company debrief card.
ASRS:1807394.s: The crew diverted to ZZZ1 after a low oil pressure warning forced a #1 engine shutdown at FL280. During descent, pilot distraction caused an airspeed low warning, but the aircraft landed safely on runway XXR with no further incident.

ASRS:1807398.n: FL340 approximately 160 nm east northeast of ZZZ the right engine OIL FILTER BYPASS caution annunciation flashed for 3-5 seconds then remained illuminated. We advised ATC with clearance to descend as requested to FL200 (FL223 max single engine altitude capability). Drift down profile initiated while concurrently performing required checklists, balancing fuel as needed as checklist directed engine shutdown. Declared ZZZ as the nearest suitable divert at point in time. Notified dispatch of intent for ZZZ, as well as coordinating communications with the Purser and making a PA to the passengers. Obtained ZZZ ATIS which stated winds variable at 6 kts landing Runway XX. Requested Runway XY for additional runway length. Transitioned from drift down profile to a descent profile when a 3:1 profile attained. As we approached within 15 nm of the field, we were informed that winds were gusting in excess of 20 kts from the south. We coordinated a runway change to XXL and at approximately 10-12 nm north of the field executed a left 360 degree turn descending to the sector MVA as to scrub altitude due to the much shortened landing distance to Runway XXL.Approach and landing was uneventful as was the taxi evolution to the gate for parking. Fire crash and rescue followed and informed that there was no threat heat signature emanating from the landing gear/brake assemblies. Normal passenger deplaning ensued.ATC throughout the evolution was perfect in every respect in aiding the successful uneventful outcome. A discrete frequency was assigned and that was immeasurably valuable. We were in Cruise and the 'OIL FILTER BYPASS' light illuminated for engine number two. The Captain took the flight controls while I ran the checklist. We ran the checklist which led us to shut down engine number two as the light did not extinguish. We advised ATC and requested a diversion to ZZZ, which was the closest suitable airport. We drifted down to FL 200 while preparing for the 1 engine approach. The Captain notified the flight attendants to prepare the cabin, he also made a calming PA, and we notified dispatch. ATIS for ZZZ winds were variable at six knots so we requested Runway XXL as it is the longest runway. We were less than 10,000 feet and approximately 20 miles out when the tower reported strong gusting winds from the south so [Runway] XYL was the safest option, but we were too high and had to do a left 360 degree [turn] while we prepared for the new approach. We flew a normal single engine approach and landed normally. Fire trucks escorted us to the gate as a precaution. Brake temperatures were normal and not excessive. Passengers deplaned in a normal manner. The Captain and I debriefed each other and then the flight attendants.
ASRS:1807398.s: The flight crew diverted to ZZZ from FL340 after an Engine 2 oil filter bypass light required a shutdown. They executed a drift down to FL200, adjusted for gusting winds by changing runways and performing a 360-degree turn, and landed safely with no fire or brake issues.

ASRS:1807408.n: Before landing at Sacramento we were told to expect Gate X. We briefed that we would taxi left on Y1 from C1 and then make a right into the angled gate, according to the taxi chart. After landing we taxied west on C1 and noticed a B737 that was parked just north of the Gate X jetway, according to the chart. As we made the left onto Y1 we saw that the correct entry to Gate X was from directly north of the gate, which is actually on the most northern part of the terminal. We had to cut across the RON parking spot 6 on our second attempt into the gate. When safely parked at Gate X we were facing due south, not southwest like the chart depicts. The SMF terminal chart appears to need an update.
ASRS:1807408.s: The flight crew landed at Sacramento and attempted to taxi to Gate X using an outdated chart, which showed incorrect entry directions and aircraft orientation. They had to cross a parking spot to reach the gate, concluding the terminal chart requires an update.

ASRS:1807412.n: Aircraft on Ground DG (Dangerous Goods) [document] was sent to ZZZ without DG acceptance process. There was no booking in [Cargo COMAT form].
ASRS:1807412.s: A Dangerous Goods document was sent to ZZZ without undergoing the acceptance process. The reporter noted that no booking existed in the Cargo COMAT form.

ASRS:1807431.n: I had just finished pushing back Aircraft X and as I was backing up a [ground service truck] sped by despite my wing walkers telling them to stop. He was going over the speed limit and was paying no attention to his environment. He was traveling at a very high dangerous speed. I had to slam on my brakes to prevent collision.
ASRS:1807431.s: A ground service truck sped past Aircraft X during pushback, ignoring wing walker stop signals and exceeding the speed limit. The truck driver's inattention and dangerous speed forced the reporter to slam on brakes to prevent a collision.

ASRS:1807456.n: At AVL we had been vectored across final and then back around to the final approach course, near the FREEZ intersection. Conditions were completely clear with great visibility. We had briefed the airport qualification pages, and had talked about the terrain and possibility of GPWS alerts. We were level at 5,100 feet, on autopilot, and received an audible 'terrain, pull up' and had a red 'gnd prox' appear on the PFD. I disengaged the autopilot and began to execute the terrain escape maneuver, and the warning disappeared almost immediately. I had climbed to 5,300 ft during the maneuver. We contacted ATC to notify of the alert and altitude deviation, and the controller replied that the minimum vectoring altitude in that area was 5,100 feet. I slowly returned to 5,100 ft and we continued being vectored onto the visual approach without further issue. Marginal distance from terrain set off the GPWS. It appears that the MVA takes us within 951 feet of the highest obstacle in the area, a small radio tower just north of FREEZ. Executed terrain escape maneuver, per company procedures. It appears the MVA of 5,100 may be insufficient in that area, recommend at least 5,200 feet.
ASRS:1807456.s: The flight crew received a GPWS terrain alert while level at 5,100 feet near the FREEZ intersection during a vector to final approach. The pilot executed a terrain escape maneuver to 5,300 feet, concluding that the Minimum Vectoring Altitude was insufficient due to proximity to a radio tower.

ASRS:1807459.n: Coming into IAD the errors started when we were intercepting the localizer for Runway 1R. I was the pilot monitoring and the FO (First Officer) was the pilot flying. Approach cleared us to intercept when we were basically already crossing the final approach course so we had to navigate back to the localizer on our own. At the same time we had been getting hit with some minor wake turbulence from the airplane ahead of us which Approach informed us was a Boeing 777. We were then cleared for the visual approach and advised of the caution for wake turbulence and to maintain 170 kts. until 5 miles out. At this time we configured gear down flaps 20. I had just recently had training in the sim for wake turbulence and remembered how dangerous it could be so I advised my FO to use caution and I believe I recommended maybe staying above their path since we had already hit a small portion of their wake prior when we were on downwind. He elected to turn the autopilot off and hand fly slightly above their glide path. We then continued down and around 100 ft. got a terrain warning. Our first reaction was this was because we weren't on glide path and the FO called out, 'visual, landing.' around 50 ft. we got another aural message stating 'too low terrain', at this point I realized something was wrong and quickly scanned and noticed we were still at flaps 20. At this point I immediately called for a balked landing. The FO restated in a question, balked landing? I said yes and he immediately executed the maneuver. We advised ATC of the go around and they asked for the reasoning and I stated we were unstable. We continued the go around and came back to land on [Runway] 1R after some vectoring without further incident. To add to this and to summarize, we did not complete a landing checklist, we were not fully configured and were at gear down flaps 20 degrees, and our speed bug was still at 170 kts. We received a terrain aural warning that we misinterpreted followed by a second aural warning and executed a balked landing at a medium energy state with lower power setting but high airspeed. Our attention started deviating from standard starting with the poor intercept angle of the localizer. I further complicated the situation by over concentrating on the wake turbulence from the 777 and focusing too much on the FO's glide path and what I would call tunnel focusing on his flying. I believe my statements to him about the wake turbulence also led to distracting him from normal flight operations as well. He was talking through his thought process on staying a half dot high on the glide path and I was responding with statements like I agree, not necessarily breaking sterile cockpit but also causing more distraction on both of our parts. This was the first time that I had not completed a landing checklist. It has made me realize that while being aware of threats like wake turbulence is important, it's even more important to maintain a greater situational awareness and take a step back and not tunnel focus on one threat while other threats could arise. While I am glad we did not try to force a landing. This is a mistake I never thought would be possible or would happen to me. I have definitely learned a lot from this experience.
ASRS:1807459.s: During a visual approach to IAD Runway 1R, the crew failed to complete the landing checklist and remained at flaps 20 while distracted by wake turbulence concerns. Misinterpreting terrain warnings, the Pilot Monitoring called for a balked landing at 50 feet, resulting in a successful go-around and subsequent safe landing.

ASRS:1807484.n: We received an 'expect NOTOC' ACARS message during preflight. Once the pushback crew was on the headset I asked about the NOTOC and was told that we had two Personal Parcel Shipments (PPS) with a UN1845 that were marked 'dry ice exempt' that did not require a NOTOC. I wasn't aware of any exemptions for dry ice so I called and conferred with my Dispatcher. Finding no dry ice exemption in the FOM we called the pilot HAZMAT hotline number located in the FOM (Cargo Operations Control) where it was confirmed that a NOTOC was required. A NOTOC was received in short order but it took us about 30 minutes off the gate to get a revised DG (dangerous goods) revised Load Closeout. Incorrectly labeled dry ice shipment caused the problem. Reporter suggests correct Information regarding Personal Parcel Shipment limitations be provided when shipping dry ice.
ASRS:1807484.s: The flight crew encountered a 30-minute gate delay during preflight due to incorrectly labeled dry ice shipments that were falsely marked as NOTOC exempt. After verifying with Cargo Operations Control that a NOTOC was required, the crew obtained the document and a revised dangerous goods load closeout before departure.

ASRS:1807534.n: The situation happened on leg 1 on the second day of a 4 day sequence. We departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. As the First Officer I completed both the interior checklists and performed the exterior inspection. I noticed during the walk around that one of the red navigation lights was inoperative. When I got back to the flight deck I confirmed that it was previously written up and had been deferred in the AML. No other issues were noted during the preflight. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring. We departed ZZZ on Runway XXL. The takeoff and departure were uneventful. Weather was clear with unrestricted visibility. The climb was continued until we leveled off at FL340. At approximately XA:13Z, I started to smell something. It smelled like burning plastic. At the same time I noticed the smell the Captain asked 'Do you smell that?' Before replying we both saw smoke coming from the 'FL' button on the transponder located on the center console. At this time we both we executed the items for 'Smoke, Fire, or Fumes', donned our oxygen masks and established crew communication. At that point the Captain gave me both aircraft control and the radios so he could focus on the abnormal. While I monitored the autopilot the Captain continued with the 'Smoke, Fire, or Fumes' checklist. I confirmed with him that the proper switches were being turned off in accordance with the checklist. We noticed that the smoke and fumes were decreasing and did not need to run the 'Smoke or Fumes Removal' checklist. While the Captain attempted to locate the transponder circuit breaker to isolate the problem he noticed that the 'ELEC PANEL LIGHTS AFT/CENTER' circuit breaker located at the base of the front of the center pedestal was popped. We were confident the problem had been isolated and the Captain informed me that he was about 90% sure we were going to divert but he wanted to check with company to see if we were missing anything. We quickly realized that a step in the checklist had us turn off the internet and he would be unable to use the crew phone app to communicate with the Dispatcher. The Captain then took the radios back and attempted to get phone patch with the Center Controller. The controller was unable to give us the phone patch but was able to relay information. After communicating through the controller and using ACARS, it was decided that we would divert to ZZZ2. The Captain notified ATC and informed Center we wanted to divert to ZZZ2. The controller asked if we want ARFF (aircraft rescue firefighting) and the Captain said yes. The Captain then gave me back the radios so that he could run more checklists. The Captain continued with the checklists the controller asked what runway we wanted to land on. The Captain and I agreed that we wanted the longest runway due to the fact we would be landing overweight. I then requested Runway XXR. I got the airplane set up for an ILS approach to XXR. I started the descent into ZZZ2 while the Captain finished checklists and briefed the passengers and Flight Attendants. Then the Captain told me that he ran the 'Non Routine Landing Considerations' checklist and that the passengers and flight attendants had been briefed. He talked about the heavy weight landing and did a landing assessment. He asked if I had anything to add or could think of anything else we might need to do before landing. I told him that I think we had covered everything and I had nothing else to add. He then briefed the approach and took aircraft control. We completed both the descent and before landing checklists. After landing we cleared the runway at taxiway. I relayed to ARFF that unless they see anything abnormal from the outside our plan was to continue taxing to gate. They informed us that they did not see any unusual readings on thethermal scan. ARFF followed us to the gate. The Captain had me make a PA to the passengers that we would be taxing to gate and they would be accommodated after deplaning. The taxi and engine shutdown at the gate was uneventful. At the gate we were met by a member of the company Flight Office and he asked if we needed to be checked out at the hospital. We both said we did not require medical attention and that no more than a few seconds went by that we breathed in fumes before getting on oxygen. He then told us that he was pulling us off the remainder of the trip and could positive space home. The Captain completed writing up items in the AML. We then debriefed when it was just the two of us left on the airplane. I told him I thought maybe I could have done more to help. He said I did what he needed by flying the airplane and communicating with ATC while he ran the appropriate checklists and backed him up in his decision making process. We both agreed that we handled the situation in the way we are trained to handle abnormal at the school house. The cause was smoke coming from the 'FL' button on the transponder located on the center console.
ASRS:1807534.s: During the climb to FL340, the First Officer and Captain detected smoke from the transponder's 'FL' button caused by a popped 'ELEC PANEL LIGHTS AFT/CENTER' circuit breaker. The crew executed smoke checklists, diverted to ZZZ2 with ARFF support, and landed safely without injury.

ASRS:1807543.n: On the RNAV Visual 31 L between fixes WEMIR and CEKMA, SOCAL Approach witnessed a target (aircraft he was not talking to) pop up that was a threat to us. He instructed us to stop descent immediately, the First Officer did a great job of arresting the descent, then Approach told us to immediately climb as TCAS instructed us to descend. We followed TCAS and saw the single-engine turboprop pass over us by about 400 feet and in front of us by about one-half mile. The FO re-established us on the approach and we landed without incident.The beautiful weather in Palm Springs and general aviation aircraft not talking to ATC was THE factor in this TCAS RA. ALWAYS follow TCAS.
ASRS:1807543.s: The crew received a TCAS Resolution Advisory during the RNAV Visual 31 L approach when a non-communicating single-engine turboprop intruded. The First Officer arrested the descent and followed TCAS climb instructions, allowing the intruder to pass 400 feet above before the crew landed safely.

ASRS:1807665.n: While performing a fire cartridge change on (Aircraft Number) the #2 right hand engine squib was set off and discharged the canister. The cartridge was discharged while performing the continuity check which requires the pulling and turning of the fire pull handle. The lighting inside the cockpit was very poor and multiple glares coming through each window caused even less visibility. Handle was turned in the wrong position causing the bottle to be discharged. Both lead and supervisor were notified immediately of the situation. Once the bottle was discharged a hissing sound was heard. The cause of the bottle being discharged was lack of lighting, the AMM and task card not having enough safety measures (the C/B's for the bottles not being tested should be pulled alleviating any potential error).Radioed mechanics at the rear of the aircraft that were watching the continuity test box to make sure no one was injured and then immediately notified the lead and supervisor on shift of the mishap. The C/B's for the bottles not being tested should be pulled alleviating any potential error. A task card should be made for this job (the task card is currently just a component replace task card with no specifics other than p/n and s/n) specific to the aircraft and air carrier so that no further errors occur.
ASRS:1807665.s: A mechanic discharged the #2 engine fire bottle during a continuity check due to poor cockpit lighting and turning the handle incorrectly. The report cites inadequate task card safety measures, specifically the failure to pull circuit breakers, as the cause of the accidental discharge.

ASRS:1807687.n: We went out to the aircraft and found the slide of the L1 door resting on the entry stand. We tried to push the slide back, but there was no way to re-secure the slide and we could not pin the slide. For safety purposes we were told to pull the stand away from the airplane and the slide then fully deployed. I assigned Technician Y and Z to the aircraft which was parked in hangar to continue the cabin odor Job card. I was notified that the L1 door slide was laying on the platform on the stand. Myself and others went to the aircraft to inspect the L1 Door. After further investigation there was no way to re-secure the slide or pin the slide. For safety purposes [it was decided] to move the Stand to prevent any injuries or further damage to the aircraft.
ASRS:1807687.s: Technicians found the L1 door slide resting on the entry stand of a parked aircraft in a hangar. Unable to re-secure or pin the slide, they moved the stand away, causing the slide to fully deploy to prevent injury or further damage.

ASRS:1807696.n: Landing on Runway XX, made landing on center line and was coming to a stop and I felt a gust of wind blow the plane side ways with ground and skid off runway. Hit marker sign. I attempted to give full right rudder but tire slid in dirt. It was a Student Cross country flight. The contact happened at ZZZ.
ASRS:1807696.s: During a student cross-country landing on Runway XX, a gust of wind blew the aircraft sideways, causing it to skid off the runway and hit a marker sign at ZZZ. The pilot attempted full right rudder, but the tire slid in the dirt, resulting in the excursion.

ASRS:1807702.n: Enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1 noticed oil pressure in right engine had dropped to the low end of the green operating arc and noticed a gradual power loss. Due to this issue I decided to divert from my flight plan and land to evaluate potential oil leak. Chose to divert to ZZZ2 as it had a long enough runway, listed to have maintenance services, and other facilities on the field. Notified ATC of plan to divert and location. ATC approved direct to ZZZ2. Enroute to ZZZ2 oil pressure and engine power on the right engine had diminished significantly. Notified ATC of situation and advised ATC. I was cleared for the straight in visual approach to runway 7. As I switched frequencies from approach to tower the engine began to sputter and the oil gauge was showing in the red arc. I declared to tower that I am shutting down the right engine. Tower cleared me to land. Airplane landed safely and taxied to the FBO. No damage was caused and no injuries were sustained.
ASRS:1807702.s: The pilot enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1 diverted to ZZZ2 after right engine oil pressure dropped and power diminished. The engine sputtered and entered the red arc during the visual approach to runway 7, prompting a shutdown; the aircraft landed safely with no damage or injuries.

ASRS:1807722.n: I was cleared to land. As I came over the end of the runway, I was getting some weird wind shear that was pushing me around, but my approach felt controlled and so I went through with it. Right before I touched down, I got a strong crosswind gust of wind (from the left) that pushed my super cub sideways (nose pointing to the left) as I touched down. Being a tail dragger, the plane responded accordingly, and I began to skid sideways down the runway. I was already down and too sideways for a go-around, so I pulled the throttle all the way back, stick back and left, and rudder full right. The plane continued to skid to a stop sideways on the runway, but all three wheels remained on the runway at all times, and no damage to the runway or aircraft occurred. After coming to a complete stop, I proceeded to turn the plane around to the left, leaving the asphalt for a brief time on the left side of the runway and taxing to the exit ramp on the other side where the Tower then informed me to stop, and I was later met by a foam truck and a service vehicle. I believe that the main factors in this were the wind gusts from the side, which in turn caused me to land sideways. I could have performed a go-around, though in the moment my approach felt controlled up until the last minute. I believe that I took the correct actions on the ground, and in so doing prevented any further damage to the aircraft or to airport property. My plane did not complete a full ground loop, but rather only turned about 90-120 degrees, and the rest of the 'loop' was me taxiing out of my predicament back on to the runway.
ASRS:1807722.s: The pilot of a Super Cub taildragger experienced a strong left crosswind gust during landing, causing the aircraft to touch down sideways and skid. The pilot applied full right rudder and left stick to stop the aircraft on the runway without damage, though a foam truck and service vehicle responded after the pilot briefly left the asphalt while turning.

ASRS:1807742.n: Near miss with SR22. Non local SR22 was sightseeing around ZZZ area with ADSB turned off.This non local SR22 was seen on initial arrival on ADS-B traffic on GLSP's (Glasair's) instruments. On another flight returning to airport GLSP made appropriate radio calls and observed no traffic on ADSB within 10 mile. 1,000 feet AGL turning downwind a very close miss with the same SR22 (verified by observation of subsequent landing). Situation observed too late to apply effective evasive maneuver.SR22 had turned off ADS-B instrumentation to avoid detection from low flight. During the observed portion of flight SR22 broke no altitude restrictions however turning off ADS-B broadcast compromised flight safety in this sparsely populated area.FAA should remind pilots that ADS-B is for safety not for enforcement, and is especially effective in avoiding midair collisions.
ASRS:1807742.s: A Glasair pilot experienced a near miss with a sightseeing SR22 at 1,000 feet AGL while turning downwind. The SR22 pilot had turned off ADS-B to avoid detection, preventing early traffic awareness and making evasive maneuvers impossible.

ASRS:1807758.n: My student and I departed on a training flight to the southeast practice area where we were going to run through Private Pilot maneuvers (stalls, steep turns, engine out, ground maneuvers and landings). After climbing to 035 and completing steep turns, we set up to do power on stalls and climbed to 050. We then set up to do power off stalls. After completing 4 power off stalls, we still had significant altitude and I decided to give student an engine out by pulling the mixture. The student set up the aircraft for best glide and selected an airfield that was about three miles away and ran through the restart checklist. Every 1500 feet I would advance the mixture and push forward on the yoke to make sure the engine was staying primed. We then simulated part of the forced landing checklist (ELT, squawk codes, emergency calls) and performed the landing brief.The student chose to try to get to the airfield by going down the downwind then realized that student was too low and close to the runway to safely make it to the field. I asked student what the backup plan was and student selected a field to right of the aircraft that student could easily turn into. Student turned the aircraft to the field and I estimated that student could easily make the landing and that student had the engine back and to do a go-around. I advanced the mixture and the engine sputtered and died and the prop stopped. The student announced that I had the controls and I pointed the airplane to the field that student had selected. I checked the mixture in, shut off valve on, then attempted to restart the engine with the key. After two attempts, I determined that we were too low and shut off the fuel valve and pulled the mixture and landed the plane in the field.There was no damage to the plane, no injuries to myself or my student, and no property damage. Fuel levels were still visible and greater than half way from the top of the tanks (well over 1/2 full, I didn't have a fuel stick to check total actual levels), oil level was still at 5 qts. We were able to later restart the airplane and taxi it closer to the property owner's barn with permission.The biggest thing that I learned was that I will not pull the mixture to simulate an engine out any more. That was the mistake that I feel caused this. In the future, all engine outs will be initiated by pulling the throttle. Though this has been common in my training from private to commercial, it put us in a dangerous situation that I could have avoided. At the altitude of 4,000 feet my Instructor pulled the mixture in the aircraft to simulate an emergency landing. At that moment I trimmed the plane all the way, pulled the carb heat and pitched the airplane for 60 kts. Next I looked for a place we could simulate the landing and we were just 2-4 miles from [an] airport. We were descending approximately 500 feet per minute. The closer we got I realized that I was too low to make the obstacles. I made the error of not looking at the altitude of the field. Therefore, I looked to my right and there was a large field and I pointed to my instructor that at that moment the safest decision was to do the field on the right. My instructor said that was a good decision and I started my turn to the field.My airspeed was 60, my right hand was on the throttle, which at the time it was all in. My left hand on the controls and my feet on the rudder. A few seconds later my Instructor looked at me and said 'you would have made it' and he decided to end the simulation by putting the mixture all in. However, the engine would not work and my instructor said 'my controls' I restated 'your controls' and he took charge of the plane. He tried turning the engine on a couple times and the propeller would just not move at all. It happened in a matter of seconds. Since I had already lined up the airplane to the field, my Instructor worked hard to fly the airplane until it touched the ground where he applied the brakes after he had landed it safely. We turned all the systems off and removed the key from the starter. We opened the doors and got out of the aircraft. We called the flight school and they came to get us and to see the airplane.
ASRS:1807758.s: During a training flight, an instructor and student simulated an engine-out scenario by pulling the mixture, which caused the engine to fail to restart upon re-engagement. The instructor took control and executed a safe forced landing in a field with no injuries or damage, attributing the incident to the decision to use mixture rather than throttle for the simulation.

ASRS:1807778.n: While landing on Runway XX at approximately 70 KIAS and power pulled to idle, after touchdown, plane started to veer to the left. Plane ultimately veered off of runway onto grass, where it came to a near-complete stop. Power was added to keep the plane moving in order to avoid getting stuck in the grass. Tower asked if we were OKAY, which I responded in the affirmative.Tower instructed us to re-enter [Runway] XX, and taxi to the T-hangars (with runway crossing and holding instructions included). We inspected the airplane and there was no apparent damage to the plane, just grass stains on the wheel pants, which we cleaned up. The airport operations reported there was no damage to anything on the runway environment. And there were no injuries to me (PIC) or my safety pilot passenger.The airplane was inspected the following day and was found to be in good operating condition and has been successfully flown since, with no reported issues.I believe the cause was my feet inadvertently slipped up the pedals and activated the toe brakes after landing, with the left side braking more strongly. There were some tire marks on the runway that seem to support this, according to the ground ops personnel.I plan to go up with a CFII as soon as possible, paying special attention to my foot position on takeoffs and landings. I may also fly with the seat farther back to make it less likely that my toes will accidentally be on the brakes.
ASRS:1807778.s: The pilot reported veering off Runway XX onto grass during landing due to inadvertent asymmetric toe brake application caused by feet slipping on the pedals. The aircraft stopped on the grass with no damage or injuries, was inspected, and returned to service.

ASRS:1807787.n: I rushed my preflight and missed the tail tiedown. I dragged the tiedown weight about 50 feet before I realized it was still attached.There were several human factors which led to a hastily/poorly performed preflight. Reflection upon my day leading up to the flight should have warranted extra patience, but a perceived time frame overshadowed better judgement. 'Got to get there' syndrome got me. and extreme caution and patience will be warranted in the future. I had also not dealt with tiedown ropes in over 15 years.My take away is to calm down and double check everything and not rush anything to do with aviation.
ASRS:1807787.s: The pilot rushed the preflight due to time pressure and lack of recent experience with tiedowns, missing the tail tiedown. This caused the pilot to drag the tiedown weight approximately 50 feet before realizing it was still attached to the aircraft.

ASRS:1807796.n: While on ILS final to Runway XL under visual conditions, the right engine failed. Landing with the left engine only was accomplished after advising ZZZ tower. Aircraft was returning from ZZZ1 with X passengers aboard. It was thought that a fuel pump had failed, but further investigation revealed that I as the PIC had misread my fuel gauge. I had thought that the right fuel quantity was off by 300 pounds because I had flown this aircraft several times before and was going to report the discrepancy to maintenance.On the previous flights, I would refuel the amount of fuel plus reserve I needed for the next flight evenly distributing the fuel load. However, I did not take into account that I would start the right engine first to get air condition operating for the passengers onboard then program the Garmin 1000 for the flight. I forgot to take into account the extra fuel burned during this procedure, thus producing a cumulative effect of showing a fuel imbalance of close to 300 pounds which I would report to maintenance after this flight. I thought the engine stoppage was the result of a fuel pump failure, instead was probably due to fuel starvation due to the cumulative effect of my failure to account for the additional fuel used during start up and a misguided conclusion that the right fuel gauge was inaccurate.
ASRS:1807796.s: The PIC experienced a right engine failure on ILS final to Runway XL while returning from ZZZ1 with X passengers. The cause was fuel starvation due to the pilot misreading the fuel gauge and failing to account for fuel burned during startup procedures.

ASRS:1807804.n: Very poorly written NOTAM creating a dilemma in operations. After landing on Runway 6, Napa Tower cleared us to back taxi on Runway 6 and exit on Taxiway C. We stated that we were unable Taxiway C due to our aircraft weighing more than 30,000 lbs. There was a NOTAM 04/006 in effect stating 'Taxiway C closed to aircraft more than 30,000 lb'. Tower then stated that it was OK and reissued the clearance for us to exit Taxiway C. I was hesitant, but we complied with the clearance and exited Taxiway C so as not to create a potentially bigger problem with other traffic. But I also stated on the frequency for the tapes that we are exiting on Taxiway C in compliance with our clearance despite weighing more than 30,000 lbs per the NOTAM. I think we made the wise decision to comply with ATC under the circumstances, but the pilot should not be put into that situation of either violating a clearance or violating a known published NOTAM. Per many NOTAMs at APC, Runway 1L/19R was closed with many other taxiways closed also. We were very aware of the NOTAMs and pre-briefed our certain back taxi on Runway 6 during our approach briefing before top of descent. We were very situationally aware and not surprised except for the clearance to exit on Taxiway C (it was supposedly closed to us). I politely had a short discussion with Ground Control during taxi in to the ramp and expressed my concern about being issued a clearance that made us technically in violation of the NOTAM. He said it was OK, but he would discuss it with the supervisor. I did not mention this to Ground Control, but the NOTAM should have stated more clearly and accurately that Taxiway C is closed north of Taxiway H to aircraft over 30,000 lbs. The NOTAM for Taxiway C has been in place for a long time-- certainly before the NOTAMs for Runway 1L/19R and other taxiways were more recent. Somebody didn't review the consequences of the older Taxiway C NOTAM when they published the more recent ones. It created an operational problem needlessly.
