Napa Tower did not appear concerned, but I hope they and Airport Ops fix this situation.
ASRS:1807804.s: The pilot reported a poorly written NOTAM at Napa (APC) that closed Taxiway C to aircraft over 30,000 lbs, conflicting with a Tower clearance to exit there after landing on Runway 6. The crew complied with the ATC instruction to avoid traffic delays but noted the NOTAM required clarification to prevent future operational dilemmas.

ASRS:1807828.n: During the final minutes of a long training lesson of emergency procedures my student and I were hovering at the departure end of Runway XX. We had just finished our last emergency procedure training pattern and were ready to head back to the ramp to stop our lesson. Where we were located, we needed to cross Runway XY/XZ to get to the ramp on the east side of the airport. Since my student is getting ready for a check ride and I am very comfortable with both her flying and communication skills with ATC I left it up to her how we would reposition. Due to the light wind an air taxi crossing the field and Runway XY/XZ was both appropriate and her final decision. She keyed up the mic on tower frequency and requested the air taxi back to our ramp as she, and others at the school, normally do many times a day. Unfortunately, the first transmission was blocked by additional traffic on frequency and her request did not go through. She knew this occurred since she heard the end of the other traffics transmission, and ATC was advising that traffic that we were still on the runway. Once there was silence on the tower frequency, she made her request again. The next thing I heard was a traffic report from ATC advising her of an additional helicopter about two miles to the west and inbound to the same location we were going. My student acknowledge the advisory and advised we would be looking for that traffic as she started to proceed to air taxi to the ramp crossing Runway XY/XZ. Just as we were about to cross XY/XZ we heard an advisory from ATC that an airplane was cleared for takeoff and as the pilot was acknowledging his clearance, he inquired what the little helicopter was doing (us). I thought it was weird of the clearance for takeoff since we were in the process of air taxing and about to cross the runway. Once past the runway and starting to land, ATC inquired with my student if she requested to cross Runway XY/XZ and she replied yes (thinking her transmission was received and by ATC giving her the traffic advisory he was aware of our movement). Unbeknownst to her or I, her second transmission was also walked on and not received by ATC. My student took the coincidental advisory of traffic as ATC's acknowledgment that we were intending to air taxi and cross Runway XY/XZ. It was confirmed upon landing by someone listening to ATC that neither of our requests had gone through. ATC had not heard her first or second transmission for the request and the traffic advisory was merely coincidental looking back on it. Luckily the traffic that was advised they were clear for takeoff on Runway XY had not even started rolling at the opposite end of the runway for their takeoff and they had also seen us and not started rolling until we past the runway.Looking back on the incident I know as an instructor I CANNOT let comfort and confidence with a student lead to complacency. I need to be on top of my game 100% of the time and make sure both myself and my student is both listening to and understanding radio traffic, and if we do not, we need to make sure we completely understand and get clearances before moving. This had the potential for a worse outcome and I most definitely have learned from it. I need to keep my eyes and ears 100% concentrated on the task at hand, and looking back on it I know my mind was still partially concentrated on our last emergency procedure training and how to debrief my student about it, and not on the 'simple' task of taking the helicopter back to park it. Complacency has no place in the cockpit and this event has taught both my student and I a valuable lesson.
ASRS:1807828.s: A helicopter instructor and student attempted to air taxi across Runway XY/XZ without receiving ATC clearance due to blocked transmissions. They mistakenly interpreted a coincidental traffic advisory as acknowledgment, nearly conflicting with an aircraft cleared for takeoff that held short until the helicopter passed.

ASRS:1807834.n: While on an IFR training flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we were on an IFR flight plan at 10,000 ft. and in VMC conditions. ATC called a drone and chase plane at 11 o'clock and ten miles crossing our path left to right at the same altitude. We thought the drone and chase plane were moving back into the military airspace to the north. At five miles, the drone and chase plane turned directly into us at our altitude. The TA (Traffic Alert) warning lit up on our G1000 NXi and we visually identified the drone at our 12 o'clock at the same altitude. We disconnected the autopilot and made a gentle turn and dive to the left. The drone passed so close to our right we asked our passenger to take a picture of it, but she did not have time. I could easily identify the drone as about the same size as our aircraft. The chase plane passed above us to the left.After we got back on our course and altitude, I reported on frequency, 'Center, Aircraft X, we got a pretty good look at that drone.' ATC came back and said he was, 'trying to get them to turn several miles back'.We were exactly where we should have been on an IFR flight plan. Without our action, we would have had a mid-air collision.
ASRS:1807834.s: During an IFR training flight at 10,000 ft, a drone and chase plane turned directly into the aircraft's path, triggering a G1000 NXi Traffic Alert. The pilot disconnected the autopilot and executed a left turn and dive to avoid a mid-air collision, while ATC attempted to redirect the drone.

ASRS:1807842.n: After departing ZZZ for ZZZ1 on an IFR flight plan, at about 500 feet AGL and 2 miles from the airport I switched frequency from ZZZ Tower to ZZZ2 Center before being asked to switch frequency by the tower. I have not flown IFR for more than one year due to COVID. I recently completed a Flight Review and Instrument Proficiency Check, but this was only the second IFR cross-country flight since then (the first was from ZZZ1 to ZZZ a few days earlier), and the first departing from a towered field. This led to my improper ATC communication procedure.
ASRS:1807842.s: A pilot with limited recent IFR experience departed ZZZ for ZZZ1 and switched to ZZZ2 Center at 500 feet AGL before being instructed to do so by the tower. The pilot attributed this improper ATC communication procedure to inexperience with departures from towered fields.

ASRS:1807843.n: Private pilot instrument student was flying. I was instructing from right seat. Always scanning visually for traffic as well as the ADS-B display, while we were northbound I noticed a target on ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast) less than a mile behind us at -300 feet (we were at 3,100 MSL). Target was gaining on us and climbing toward our altitude. When target showed -100 feet and nearly merged with us on the ADS-B display (approaching from our 7:00 position), student initiated a climbing right turn to the east since it appeared the target aircraft had no idea we existed. Thankfully, that maneuver started to put some distance as well as altitude between us. However, the target started turning right as well. We continued climbing and turned further right (net 180 by then), while it appeared target was still at their previous altitude (now -700 thanks to our climb) and maintaining a roughly easterly heading but still in a right turn. After we continued our right turn (now heading west), I for the first time caught a visual on the other aircraft at roughly our 4:00 position and 700 feet below (where ADS-B said they were at that moment). They appeared to be still turning right, perhaps practicing 360s -- I don't know. In any case, we were continuing to put distance and altitude between us such that we resumed our northerly heading back to home airport without further incident other than perhaps a minute during which our altitude was 3,800 MSL -- not a legal VFR cruising altitude -- while we made sure the other aircraft was not trying to chase us. We then descended to 3,000 MSL and contacted Portland Approach for flight following for the assurance of an extra set of eyes.
ASRS:1807843.s: A flight instructor and student in a private aircraft encountered a target on ADS-B while northbound at 3,100 feet. The student executed a climbing right turn to avoid the converging aircraft, which was later visually confirmed 700 feet below, prompting a temporary climb to 3,800 feet before contacting Portland Approach.

ASRS:1807846.n: I was conducting a training flight on Airman Certification Standards (ACS) maneuvers to prepare a student for the practical test to be taken within 4 days. Initially, we conducted normal, short field, and soft field takeoffs and landings without incident. Then, we departed to the practice area and practiced unusual attitude recoveries, steep turns, slow flight, approach stalls, and departure stalls from 3,000 feet MSL. That complete, I directed the student to return to the home airport. On downwind entry, we were 500 feet above pattern altitude. I considered this a good opportunity to give my student a simulated engine failure and have him continue to the runway. On downwind, we were at an altitude lower than the student felt comfortable. He stated that he didn't feel we could make it. However, to demonstrate that the landing could still be made if the conditions (engine out) were real, I took the controls made a short approach (a banked continuous base to final turn) and lined the aircraft up with the runway in a landing attitude. Unfortunately, during the maneuver I became obsessed with monitoring our airspeed for proper glide speed and maneuvering during the turn at the neglect of ensuring the landing gear was extended. We landed with the gear retracted. The flare (round out) was at normal altitude and attitude. Overall, it was not a bad landing. The student caught the error prior to me when we heard scraping. The aircraft slid and eventually slid off the runway to a point between the runway and taxiway.One human performance consideration may have been a factor. I have been conducting training in both straight gear and retractable gear C-172s switching between the two on the same day. That was the case on this day. I had flown 0.7 [hours] practicing landings with one student in a fixed gear 172 in the morning, driven to a different airport, and flew in this student's retractable 172 in the afternoon. My mindset was fixated on making the landing and not on the differences between the two aircraft.
ASRS:1807846.s: During a training flight in a retractable-gear Cessna 172, the instructor landed with the gear retracted while demonstrating a simulated engine failure. The error occurred because the instructor, who had flown a fixed-gear aircraft earlier that day, neglected to extend the gear while focusing on airspeed and maneuvering.

ASRS:1807859.n: While in cruise flight, I began to notice undesirable engine trends and indications of an impending failure or forced shutdown. I adjusted my destination from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with ATC. Upon further evaluation and worsening engine indications, a change of destination from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 was requested with ATC and approved.As I turned toward ZZZ2, I was forced to shut down the ride engine and requested priority handling with ATC. An approach to land was made on Runway 13 with no event and no injuries to passengers or crew. We then exited the runway and parked at the FBO as if it was a normal flight. I then contacted WX Brief and asked them to contact Center, relay my phone number, and confirm I was safe on the ground. Center Controller then contacted me to verbally verify we were safe on the ground in ZZZ2. I would like to thank the professional and extremely helpful Center Controller. It helped in a truly troubling situation.
ASRS:1807859.s: During cruise, the pilot diverted from ZZZ to ZZZ2 due to worsening engine trends, eventually shutting down the right engine. The aircraft landed safely on Runway 13 at ZZZ2 with no injuries, and the Center Controller verified the crew's safety on the ground.

ASRS:1807873.n: I am a university student who is taking some drone classes, but am not an aviation student. I was walking by [a] school building (275 ft) and saw a two person UAS crew operating a small UAS below. As a licensed Remote Pilot, I stopped to look for the drone out of interest, and only saw it for a brief moment before it disappeared. I am far sighted an was concerned that the drone was being flown out of the pilot's VLOS. I assumed that they were a UAS instructor and student and did not say anything to the crew. While I have my Remote Pilot's License, I have yet to fly any missions and was not sure how high the legal limit of 400 ft. actually looks like. I brought up the occurrence to some aviation major friends and was immediately concerned to find out that the building they were flying near was 275 ft. This put things into perspective for me and I now believe they were flying well over 400 ft. AGL.I talked to my UAS professor who informed me that because our campus is in the landing pattern for ZZZ airport, the ceiling for drones is actually 100 ft. He also said that permission from the tower only grants you to fly up to 300 ft. I am reporting this because the pilot was flying the UAV at what I believe to be an illegal height in the traffic pattern for an airport that has a lot of traffic due to University's flight training.
ASRS:1807873.s: A licensed Remote Pilot observed a two-person UAS crew operating a small drone near a 275-foot building within the ZZZ airport traffic pattern. The reporter believes the crew violated altitude limits by flying well above the 100-foot campus ceiling and 300-foot tower authorization.

ASRS:1807874.n: I was flying for a video mission, circling a gasoline station at no greater than 150 ft., in an area that I thought was not regulated for altitudes less than 250 ft. I had consulted with my insurance coverage app and the DJI app in order to make sure the area was not regulated for the operation of my drone under VLOS and less than 250 ft. I was asked to report when admin within the company realized that the flying location was under regulations for no flight i.e. Class B [airspace]. I was in error by not consulting the B4ufly app to determine that my location was inside a no-fly zone.
ASRS:1807874.s: A drone pilot conducting a video mission at 150 ft. over a gas station inadvertently entered Class B airspace. The incident occurred because the pilot failed to consult the B4ufly app, relying instead on other applications that did not identify the no-fly zone.

ASRS:1807875.n: Breached 400 ft. ceiling in airspace authorization. Was on a very fast climb and was keeping VLOS (Visual Line of Sight) of the UAS in order to see and avoid all aircraft. RPIC (Remote Pilot in Command) was monitoring altitude by briefly breaking VLOS to look at GCS (Ground Control Station) screen. RPIC was briefly distracted by a member of the flight crew and the interval between checking the GCS screen exceeded anticipated amount of time. When RPIC saw the UAS exceeding altitude, RPIC immediately stopped and began descending. RPIC should have crew member read off altitude during fast climb.
ASRS:1807875.s: The Remote Pilot in Command breached a 400 ft ceiling while climbing a UAS, caused by distraction from a crew member and delayed monitoring of the Ground Control Station screen. The pilot immediately stopped the climb and descended, noting that a crew member should have read altitude during the fast ascent.

ASRS:1807908.n: We had been cleared the ILS 25L Approach while on the ANJLL Arrival and assigned 250 knots. At about 12,000 feet, we got a call from the cabin that the passenger we had called STAT-MD for earlier in the flight, was feeling worse. I asked the First Officer to call OPS for medical assistance to meet us at the gate. When he returned back to the ATC frequency, we were approaching 10,000 feet and hit wake turbulence sufficiently strong to cause the airplane to go into control wheel pitch and roll. I redirected the aircraft to KRAIN, re-engaged LNAV and VNAV, and asked ATC what we were following. I was told we were following nothing. This didn't make sense since we had just hit very strong wake turbulence. While established on final, ATC told us to slow to 170 knots. This surprised both of us, because the last speed assignment we recalled being given was 250 knots. 170 knots would be a huge speed reduction and we were still about 25 miles out. ATC then asked us if we were at 210 knots. We told the Controller no, and that we had been assigned 250 knots. He told us we had been instructed to slow to 210 knots back when we complained about the wake turbulence (approaching 10,000 feet). We were now overtaking a B777 ahead, so our approach clearance was canceled. We were given vectors for spacing and vectored back onto the localizer and then re-cleared the ILS 25L. Neither the First Officer no I recall hearing the 210 knot speed assignment. We had only heard 250 knots and read that back. The 210-knot speed assignment probably occurred about the time the Flight Attendant called us about the passenger feeling ill again and just as we hit the wake turbulence. A bunch of things happened at once which led to us missing a slower speed assignment. On the arrival to LAX, cleared the approach to 25L and told to maintain 250 knots. The flight attendant called up and said that our previous medical issue in the back (we had earlier talked to STAT-MD and gotten clearance to continue) was not feeling well again, and asked for paramedics. As the Pilot Monitoring, I called OPS at LAX, to arrange for emergency personnel - meaning I was off frequency. At the same time, we encountered wake turbulence, strong enough to knock the aircraft out of both LNAV/VNAV. The Captain, Pilot Flying, reported the wake turbulence to Approach, after getting the aircraft established on profile, apparently ATC told us to slow to 210 knots. Neither of us heard or read back the speed change. A few miles later Approach canceled our approach clearance and said we were too fast. We responded that we were assigned 250. They said no, we were given 210.
ASRS:1807908.s: The flight crew missed a speed reduction to 210 knots due to simultaneous cabin medical calls and wake turbulence while on the ILS 25L arrival. Consequently, ATC canceled their approach clearance for being too fast, vectored them for spacing, and re-cleared them for the approach.

ASRS:1807917.n: Exiting Runway 26L onto A6, the Tower Controller issued an alert for wildlife on Runway 26R. I instinctively slowed my taxi speed and came to a gradual stop on the high speed exit and began to scan for any hazards. After 20-30 seconds, with no further instructions for us, we heard the Controller send Company around. He then explained that we had not completely cleared the hold short line, then cleared us to cross [Runway] 26R and contact Ground.Improve distraction management discipline by assuring thorough completion of the task at hand, at the time of the distraction, before diverting attention to the threat. Consciously heighten situational awareness of aircraft state and location in the knowledge that situational awareness invariably breaks down in any non-normal situation. Also, actively solicit fellow Crew Member input for back up in this process. Exiting Runway 26L onto A5, the Tower issued a wildlife alert on Runway 26R. Captain then brought the aircraft to a stop while we looked for animals /hazards. After about 20 seconds with no Tower instructions, we heard Tower send Company aircraft around. He then said we had not fully cleared the runway hold short line and proceeded to clear us to cross 26R and contact Ground.Improve distraction management by assuring task at hand (clearing runway) is finished before diverting attention to the threat.
ASRS:1807917.s: The flight crew stopped on a high-speed exit after a wildlife alert but failed to fully clear the Runway 26R hold short line. The Tower Controller subsequently instructed them to hold, then cleared them to cross the runway and contact Ground.

ASRS:1807920.n: Aircraft on ATL's south runways caused Tower to divert several aircraft waiting to take off to the north side including us. Tower made several calls for aircraft to 'be ready' as he was trying to launch many in a short amount of time. My best recollection is we had cleaned up from flaps 5 to 1, and were approaching flaps 1 min maneuver speed when we hit several seconds of heavy moderate rolling motion, requiring almost full throw of the ailerons to maintain wings level attitude as we hit the wake from an Airbus that took off ahead of us. When I got to my hotel room, I looked up the event reporting requirements and realized we didn't report the incident to ATC. I did, however, make a PA above 10,000 feet to explain to the passengers what happened and why, and got positive feedback from the flight attendants who said the event concerned the customers.
ASRS:1807920.s: The flight crew experienced heavy rolling motion requiring full aileron input while accelerating for takeoff after being diverted to the north side due to south runway congestion. The pilot attributed the turbulence to wake turbulence from a preceding Airbus and later informed passengers via PA above 10,000 feet.

ASRS:1807970.n: Pilot released brakes without authorization from ground crew. The lead on the gate was located at the front landing gear and was waiting to pull chocks. The pushback tractor driver was not set in tractor and did not give okay to release brakes. The lead had to jump back from aircraft because of fear he might get run over.
ASRS:1807970.s: The pilot released brakes without authorization while the ground lead waited at the nose gear and the pushback tractor driver was not ready. The lead had to jump back to avoid being run over by the moving aircraft.

ASRS:1808024.n: FA (Flight Attendant) called as we were climbing to FL280 reporting dirty sock odor from Row 26 aft to galley. No odor in rest of cabin. No odor detected in flight deck. Asked FA to check lav, overhead bins, galley carts and storage areas. Nothing was found. Began getting data for landing in ZZZ1. Began referencing QRH for smoke procedure and overweight landing procedure. FO (First Officer) assumed Pilot Flying duties and ATC. FA (flight attendant) then informed us that occupants were becoming ill. We immediately notified ATC and requested diversion to ZZZ1. Informed ATC we had injuries. Sent ACARS to Dispatch advising of diversion. During descent completed QRH Overweight Landing procedure and began Smoke/Avionics Smoke/Fumes QRH 17-1 procedure. Stopped Smoke procedure while maneuvering for approach and assumed Pilot Flying duties. Uneventful overweight landing. Stopped aircraft on runway and called FA's to assess. Was notified that the odor had stopped. Requested taxi to gate. Taxied per ATC instructions to ramp. Ramp unaware of our condition and asked us to hold on the ramp. Attempted contact with Operations. No answer. Ramp was able to obtain gate information from company and cleared us to gate. Fire truck followed us to gate and fireman came onboard and said all was clear outside of aircraft. Requested paramedics. Waited for over 15 minutes to arrive. FA 3 and several passengers were ill and required treatment. Informed that odor had completely subsided. Passengers remained onboard to allow access for paramedics as ill occupants were blocking front galley area and jetbridge. Flight Attendants were very assertive in communicating the specifics of the odors and location including the condition of our passengers throughout the event. This played a significant role in understanding the condition in the cabin and making proper decisions. Odor events can be difficult to prevent. Preparing for these seemingly inevitable challenges can make them easier to manage. Climbing through FL240 on our way to our final FL280 we receive a call from the (FAs) flight attendants. The Captain took the call because I was responding to a frequency change to ATC. After checking in with Center I noticed the call with the FAs was taking longer than most so I decide to listen in. I overheard that the one of the flight attendants was reporting a weird smell in the back of the aircraft. After hearing a very brief snippet I pulled out my QRH and located fumes on page 17-2 just as a precautionary measure. The Captain returns from the call and informed me of what was taking place and that he was trying to receive more information from the FA's. During this time we had leveled at our cruise altitude of FL280, and our closest airport was ZZZ1. We decide to see what the weather was in ZZZ1. The weather was VFR conditions landing west. The FA calls back, I tell the Captain my aircraft, my radios so he can direct all this attention to the issue at hand. As he was talking to the FA's I overheard that they trying to figure out what the odor smells like. I look down and at the bottom of 17-2 is an odor/toxic substance checklist on 15-32. I flip to that page and hand the QRH to him. The Captain returned from the call and informed me that it smelt like a dirty sock/wet dog and that we have injuries on board, we are diverting to ZZZ1. After that the Captain hands me back my QRH and starts the smoke/avionics smoke/ fumes QRC /QRH procedure. As we start descending I notice our aircraft gross weight was at 180,200 lbs and that we are going to be landing overweight so I turned my QRH to 15-22 over weight landing. After finishing the fumes QRC I hand the Captain my QRH so he can start that procedure. Shortly thereafter ATC asked what runway we would like and after making the landing calculation the Captain determined XXR would be the safest runway to land on. I put the ILS XXR in the box and sequenced it accordingly. After the Captain finished the overweight landing QRC, he resumed Pilot Flying duties, I resumed Pilot Monitoring duties and he asked for descent checklist as we were on a base leg for XXR. We were cleared the approach, we fully configured the aircraft, ran the before landing checklist. On short final I asked Tower to have safety vehicles standing by and that we were going to stop on the runway. The Captain landed the aircraft smoothly around 179,000 lbs, 148 knots and vertical speed around 100 ft a minute. We stopped on the runway, the Captain informed the passengers to remain seated three times. ARFF told us the aircraft looked fine and we taxied to the gate. Reporter suggested Airbus needs to determine what causes these mysterious 'dirty sock' fume events and provide a fix.
ASRS:1808024.s: Flight crew diverted an Airbus to ZZZ1 during climb to FL280 after flight attendants reported a "dirty sock" odor and passenger illness. The crew executed smoke and overweight landing procedures, resulting in an uneventful landing where paramedics treated several ill occupants.

ASRS:1808027.n: I am a little rusty because I haven't flown much over the past 12 months. We had a tailwind on final, but as ZZZ frequently does, they asked us to keep our speed up and maintain 180 knots until ZZZZZ (the final approach fix on XL ILS). I had configured to flaps 10 and gear down before ZZZZZ. After we crossed ZZZZZ I finished configuring but the plane did not want to slow down after flaps 25, possibly because we hit a gust or went through a shear zone. I was so distracted by the amount of difficulty I was having getting the plane to slow down so I could call for flaps 30 that I didn't realize we were lowering the flaps to 30 just as we passed through 1,000 feet.The tailwind on final, ZZZ's request for us to keep our speed up, my relative lack of proficiency and my not paying close enough attention to our altitude were the causes for my error.I will start configuring even earlier when contending with a tailwind on final. After fully configuring the aircraft for landing, I realized that we were below 1,000 feet.A tail wind, ATC assigning 210 knots on final, and a lack of recent experience all combined played a role in my late recognition of configuring below 1,000 feet.Configuring the aircraft earlier, and paying closer attention to procedures.
ASRS:1808027.s: The pilot reported that a tailwind, ATC speed restrictions, and recent inexperience caused delayed aircraft configuration, resulting in flaps 30 being selected below 1,000 feet. The pilot attributed the error to distraction from airspeed management and insufficient altitude monitoring during the final approach.

ASRS:1808092.n: After the medical [aircraft] that brought as [us] to the gate, I ask [ed] the Supervisor who was to take the two containers of needles and sharps. They had the orange Hazmat stickers on them. The Aircraft Maintenance told me to put them the red bag waste in the trash can, at which time I told him that was a high risk to anyone picking up those bags if a cap comes off and I needed to hand them over to someone [qualified] for disposal. He told me to put them in the trash can. I pushed back again explaining that was a high risk for anyone gathering the red bag if a cap came off. At which time he told me to put them in a red bag and leave them in the wheelchair in the jetbridge. I did as I was told, putting them in a red bag waste bag and tying the top, and then did as I was told and left them in the wheelchair in the jetbridge where our passenger's were deplaning.
ASRS:1808092.s: Cabin crew reported that an Aircraft Maintenance Supervisor instructed them to dispose of two containers of medical sharps in a red bag left in a wheelchair within the jetbridge. The crew complied despite expressing safety concerns about the risk of needle exposure to others handling the waste.

ASRS:1808135.n: We are currently in the process of returning X number of 737-MAX aircraft to service following the accomplishment of an EO. When auditing the paperwork on Aircraft Y, it was discovered that the tooling required to accomplish Step XX F.X, and F.Y was unavailable. This caused a retroactive audit of previously completed paperwork on Aircraft Z. It was determined that the tasks were stamped as accomplished in spite of the lack of available tooling. The aircraft was not in service at the time, however it was due to be released. The paperwork was pulled and the required tooling has been ordered to ensure correct accomplishment of these steps on both aircraft prior to aircraft release.The reference material uses generic three digit ATA codes (XX-XX-XX, XX-YY-XX) instead of complete ATA codes to identify applicable AMM references for a given task. Additionally, the maintenance tasks are all very similar when performed and easily confused. Furthermore the job card does not include the tooling in the bill of required materials, further obfuscating the tooling requirement. Finally, the tasks all have very similar nomenclature. You can be easily fooled into thinking you've accomplished more than one task when you have, in fact, only accomplished one, or part of another task. It is also worth noting that other similar task cards for this fleet type are significantly less vague. It appears that this card was created quickly with little mind paid to details. This is also the first time this job card has been accomplished at this station.Include the full ATA code for each task. Include the required tooling on the job card bill of materials. Add a note to Step XX F.X and F.X indicating that tooling is required to complete these steps.
ASRS:1808135.s: During a 737-MAX return-to-service audit, mechanics discovered that maintenance tasks on Aircraft Z were stamped complete without required tooling due to vague job cards and missing tooling lists. The aircraft was grounded, paperwork was pulled, and tooling was ordered to ensure correct task accomplishment before release.

ASRS:1808147.n: I taxied just past the runway hold at C3 from D3 in an effort to perform run up clear of the main taxiway. The hold lines had been moved back and I was now over the hold line. I realized I was over and did a 180 back to taxiway C and called ground for instructions to taxi back to the hangar. I just completed the Runway safety course yesterday and am beginning recurrent training this afternoon. My plane was just out of annual and after an extensive preflight I wanted to do a few trips around the pattern to help verify the soundness of the aircraft before I took my flight instructor up with me. I am fairly new to DVT. It is way more complicated on the ground and in the air here than I was accustomed to so I wanted to get with an instructor before I flew around the area too much. Then Covid hit and I couldn't go up. None of this is an excuse. It is just background that I hope will be helpful.
ASRS:1808147.s: The pilot inadvertently crossed the runway hold line at C3 while taxiing from D3 to perform a run-up, noting the hold lines had been moved back. Upon realizing the error, the pilot executed a 180-degree turn, returned to taxiway C, and contacted ground control for instructions to return to the hangar.

ASRS:1808150.n: Aircraft X was arriving in from the northeast of ZZZ, was cleared for the ZZZZZ3 arrival, and had been cleared direct to ZZZZZ intersection at 8,000 feet. Company aircraft was at 8,000 feet when a small drone passed on left side just below the left wing. Pilot did report it to ZZZ Center, just prior to being handed off to Approach. The drone appeared to have four greenish colored lights on it and was maybe 50 feet to 100 feet below aircraft.
ASRS:1808150.s: A pilot flying Aircraft X on the ZZZZZ3 arrival at 8,000 feet reported a small drone with four green lights passing below the left wing. The drone was estimated 50 to 100 feet below the aircraft and was reported to ZZZ Center before the handoff to Approach.

ASRS:1808167.n: I am a Private Oilot who currently lives in ZZZ, and I was in ZZZ1 for the weekend. I am currently working on my instrument rating, and I do not have a complex endorsement. I was looking to book a plane for that day, and I decided that it would be best to look at renting a complex aircraft and hiring a CFI as PIC so I could get my first lesson in flying complex. This way, the time would count towards my 10 hour requirement for complex or TAA aircraft for my commercial license, which I plan on getting after my instrument rating. I knew that I would be required to hire a CFI as PIC since I do not yet have my complex endorsement. We arrived on the morning of Date and took off from ZZZ2 at roughly XA:00am after a preflight with the CFI, who is employed by Company. The lesson took place in the school's 172RG. Our flight consisted of an intro complex lesson where we flew down to ZZZ3 for a touch and go. Following this, we flew back to ZZZ2 and prepared for landing. We were cleared for Runway XR by Tower and made a straight in approach. The before landing checklist was completed, and we extended the landing gear as required. We noted that the light on the landing gear instrument had turned green as we were on approach, indicating that the landing gear had been deployed. There was a crosswind out of 070 with winds at 17kts, gust 22kts as reported by Tower. We performed a side slip to correct for the crosswind, and approached the runway at normal speed. The side slip was performed well and the airplane touched down straight and in the middle of the runway at appropriate touchdown speed. Once the main wheels touched down, the plane started to wobble on the left side, and it became clear that the left main landing gear had not locked in place. The left landing gear then folded back into the plane during the rollout. By this time our ground speed had slowed considerably, but the plane was supported partially by the left fuselage. While the main right gear and front gear had deployed, the main left gear was now back inside the plane, and the aircraft veered off to the left and into the grass. Informed Tower, and the airport closed the runway and deployed emergency services to come meet us.Nobody was hurt during the event, and we safely exited the aircraft where we waited for the airport personnel. I did not notice any damage to the airport, and no runway lights were hit. The only damage to the plane was minor, and from what I could see it was limited to the landing gear and possibly the left wingtip, which was touching the ground when the plane came to a stop to the left of the runway. The engine, prop, and the rest of the plane seemed undamaged.The airport informed the FAA of the event, and eventually I was dismissed after giving the airport workers my pilot certificate. I made a quick call to inspector. We briefly spoke, and I gave a brief oral statement. In my opinion this was a clear mechanical failure and was not due to pilot error. Also, this event does not fit the definition of an accident or reportable incident to the NTSB, per NTSB part 830. Take off at ZZZ2 at XA:40 AM local time Eastbound after clear ZZZ2 Delta airspace, right turn southbound direct to ZZZ3 at 1,500 feet MSL. Joined left downwind runway seven and performed one touch and go, no issues. After the touch and go, we flew out of the traffic pattern to the west and proceeded directly over the bay towards ZZZ2 at 1,500 feet MSL. At mile 10 southwest from ZZZ2 we proceed to check with ZZZ2 Control Tower and be clear to join direct final Runway XR for a full stop. Around XC:46 we performed a normal landing. After touchdown we proceeded to press brake pedals and the left landing gear slowly collapsed rearward and up. Left wing tip touched the runway's surface around 40 knots and by that time directional control of the plane was lost even with use of opposite brake, aircraft slowly slid left towards the grass and off the runway and fully stopped on the left side of runway nine right. No hard Landing, no injuries, no propeller strike, no fire.
ASRS:1808167.s: A private pilot and CFI in a Cessna 172RG experienced a left main landing gear collapse during rollout at ZZZ2 after a crosswind landing. The gear failed to lock despite a green indicator, causing the aircraft to veer off the runway with minor damage but no injuries.

ASRS:1808178.n: I was cleared for takeoff from Runway 23 (gravel runway) in Merrill Field Anchorage Alaska by the Tower of the airport. The Tower had given me the so called 'Chester Creek Departure' with the Altitude deviation across the Knik Arm of the Cook inlet, after I had talked to the Tower on the Ground frequency 121.70 about my intentions and asked for the deviation across the cold water. All normal procedures here in town! After getting cleared to takeoff I responded with repeating my clearance and that I am taking the runway for departure (on 126.00). After liftoff I climbed, as there are obstacles to clear etc. As I clear the obstacles I am still on runway heading and after clearing them I turn right about 20 degrees or so to go onto my 'Chester Creek departure' route: as cleared and as advertised by Tower and me. In this moment I notice a Cessna C172 coming at me head on, right down 'My' 'Chester Creek departure' at low altitude!!! I take evasive action by stopping the climb and banking right, bringing my flight path parallel and below to the head-on coming-at-me Cessna C172. - As I saw the Cessna C172 in time and evaded it there was no big danger but If I had not seen him it would have been head on for sure or an extremely close near miss. Had I flown a C185 it would have been head on for sure, had I been by myself or less fuel on board it would have 'fit' too!This should not have happened and it happens often in Merrill Field. There is nothing wrong with any of the airspace of the Airport or the procedures, its just that there are certain individuals on that tower that fail to warn of traffic conflicts in their airspace or they fail to warn certain flight instructors about their deviations!!! This C172 was LOW and should have been at full pattern altitude as it was on a downwind for Runway 25 !!! This is not the first close call I have had with this Tower. I am flying in Alaska and Anchorage for XX years. Depending on who is on this Tower I am either relaxed as I can trust the person I hear (and Know as known good) or I am nervous as I hear who it is ( and I know who I am talking about ) and I worry 'what will be messed up today?' again. As I am leery whenever I hear this person on the tower I do all I can to make it easy, and clear and precise and yet again this happened. How often will this continue to happen? I am pretty disgusted with the services of some (very FEW) of the controllers of Merrill Field Tower...
ASRS:1808178.s: The pilot of a departing aircraft at Merrill Field encountered a head-on conflict with a low-altitude Cessna 172 on the Chester Creek Departure route. The pilot attributed the near miss to the tower controller's failure to warn of the traffic conflict or the Cessna's deviation from pattern altitude.

ASRS:1808185.n: For years I have seen student pilots overshoot final when landing on the parallel runway at Centennial airport. More then a few close conflicts have occurred during the landing phase while I was on final approach. The recent mid-air collision at that airport was overdue, and it will happen again. During my last visual approach to APA, Aircraft Y was on base at a collision course with my Aircraft X and we only saw it at the last second while it was turning finial. A staggered spacing controlled by the tower controller would make things much safer. At least staggering small aircraft to turn base after passing traffic on final would end the inherent danger.
ASRS:1808185.s: The pilot of Aircraft X reported a near-mid-air collision with Aircraft Y during a visual approach to APA at Centennial Airport. The conflict occurred when Aircraft Y turned final on a collision course, which the pilot attributed to student pilots overshooting and a lack of staggered spacing by the tower controller.

ASRS:1808193.n: Operating flight ZZZ-ZZZ1. Myself and other Flight Attendant during taxi noticed a musty like fume smell moments after pilots turned on the engines. Followed by extremely hot temperatures in the cabin which overtook the cabin. Immediately we noticed the majority of the customers reaching for their air vents and received multiple comments about the aircraft blowing 'hot air'. We walked through the cabin and were able to identify the fumes were coming from the Air supply vents towards the FWD of the Cabin. The intensity was Level 2 Moderate. Flight Deck was notified immediately. The moment the engines turned on I immediately felt a sudden rush of heat and immediate chest pain/tightness, nausea, and the air felt very thick making it slightly harder to breath. Ones the Flight Deck was notified they immediately responded and shut off the engines. I gradually began to feel better and my symptoms eventually went away. We returned to gate and deplaned the aircraft. Maintenance requested details of the Fume Event which we provided. Maintenance deferred the P.A.C.K. located in the FWD of the aircraft which stopped the Fumes. We re-boarded and departed from ZZZ -ZZZ1.These fume events are happening more than it is being reported. The company procedure for these events are misleading crew members into reporting to the company as an ODOR (Smell) event vs Fumes event so that they don't have to report it properly. Out of fear of retaliation crew member choose to not report and ignore symptoms. These too common mechanical issues are exposing us to harmful chemical exposures and causing us to get sick at the moment and then experience more severe symptoms later. Myself and many crew members. If we can enforce and install Carbon Monoxide sensors on the aircraft which is something we have in our own homes and is not costly, we can prevent and attend to these fume events in a timely manner and prevent Crews/Customers from getting sick or worse situations that can cause a more severe safety incident.
ASRS:1808193.s: Flight attendants on flight ZZZ-ZZZ1 reported moderate fumes and extreme heat from forward air supply vents during taxi after engine start, causing crew illness. The flight deck shut down engines, maintenance deferred the forward PACK, and the aircraft departed after re-boarding.

ASRS:1808197.n: Flew on a stale license starting on Date with additional flights on Dates. I did not become aware until today. My license certificate with expiration date is in my office which has been closed due to the pandemic. I only noticed my expiration when logging into my FAA account. The physical FAA license (which I do carry on my person) does not have this expiration information printed on it. This can be prevented in the future by keeping a photo of the completion certificate in my wallet.
ASRS:1808197.s: A pilot flew multiple flights on an expired license, unaware of the expiration until checking their FAA account. The incident occurred because the physical license lacked an expiration date and the certificate was inaccessible due to office closure.

ASRS:1808202.n: On a coupled RNAV XX LPV approach to ZZZ the aircraft overshoot the turn to final. It started the turn but not fast enough to intercept. After correcting and intercepting final the aircraft began a descent as if following the glideslope. There was heavy rain between me and the airport and my attention was diverted to that and I lost situational awareness. It is obvious now that the descent was not following the glideslope when the terrain alert activated I climbed to a higher altitude and shortly broke out of the rain and landed in visual conditions. We were in contact with approach control until just before the turn to final, then switched to UNICOM. My mistakes were ones of complacency. When I had an abnormal turn to final I should have executed a missed approach. Something was not right. I allowed my attention to be diverted at a critical time from the task of monitoring the approach. I misinterpreted the weather situation. I used ASOS reports that may have been 5 - 10 minutes old in a rapidly changing weather situation. I should have requested the RNAV XY and accepted the tailwind even though the minimums were higher. The weather was moving west to east and conditions in the quadrant turned out to be much better.
ASRS:1808202.s: The pilot flying a coupled RNAV XX LPV approach to ZZZ overshot the turn to final and descended without glideslope guidance due to diverted attention from heavy rain and complacency. After a terrain alert, the pilot climbed, broke out of the rain, and landed visually, admitting to misinterpreting weather and failing to execute a missed approach.

ASRS:1808219.n: Aircraft X was cleared for the option on Runway 24. After starting departure roll for a touch and go operation, Aircraft X reported an engine sputter, and chose to abort takeoff. I was training on the Local Control position at the time, and asked Aircraft X if he required any assistance. Aircraft X responded 'no' and was instructed to turn left onto Taxiway A at the end of the runway. Aircraft Y was on final for Runway 24 at this time, and using landmarks, it was determined that runway separation was ensured for all phases of Aircraft Y's touch and go operation. Aircraft X was observed in a turn and clear of the edge of runway. At that point Aircraft X taxied to a position where the aircraft was not observed due to a newly built hangar on the airport. Tower personnel did not observe Aircraft X taxi beyond the view that was obstructed in a timely manner, and were concerned for the pilot of Aircraft X.The recently built hangar west of the Control Tower presents a line of sight issue that diminishes the ability for the Control Tower to provide service to the users of POU in a safe, orderly, and expeditious manner. The hangar is too high for Tower personnel to have a full view of all movement areas on the field. The hangar should be lowered, or the Tower should be raised. The blind spot caused by the construction of a new hanger has been an ongoing issue at POU. I was working CIC. Runway 24 was the active. Training was in progress on LC. 3 Routine touch and go aircraft were in the pattern. Aircraft X was performing T and G with Aircraft Y well behind him in sequence. As Aircraft X was on departure roll, the pilot aborted takeoff and rolled all the way to the end of the Runway 24. He said he didn't require any assistance and was visually observed crossing the runway edge line and turning off Runway 24 onto alpha taxiway. Simultaneously, Aircraft Y was observed over the approach end threshold, but we could not VISIBLY VERIFY if the pilot in Aircraft X still had forward progress when he went passed the runway edge lines at the end of Runway 24. Being unable to see the aircraft moving (or not moving) passed the hold short on taxiway Alpha off of Runway 24, limits ATC ability to make informed decisions on having to send following aircraft around or safely land. The new hanger blind spot has been creating unnecessary problems in the way ATC is conducted on BOTH Runway 6 and Runway 24.Recommendation - Build a new taller tower, add height to the existing tower, lower the hanger to eliminate the blind spot.
ASRS:1808219.s: A pilot aborted a takeoff on Runway 24 due to an engine sputter and taxied off, but a new hangar blocked the tower's view of the aircraft. This blind spot prevented controllers from verifying the aircraft's position, creating safety concerns for following traffic and prompting recommendations to raise the tower or lower the hangar.

ASRS:1808272.n: I was the First Officer and Pilot Monitoring for our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After an uneventful departure and climb we established our cruise at FL360. Approximately 15 minutes into our cruise the Captain noticed a bright light near the top of his side view window. He brought my attention to the window heat unit which was glowing. From my vantage point I initially thought the unit itself was aflame but after several seconds it became apparent that a short existed which was contained within the window panes. A glowing line similar to a light bulb's filament began snaking downwards from the heat unit between the window panes. The Captain tapped the window several times which managed to briefly extinguish the light. We both acknowledged the need to descend as soon as possible and I requested a lower altitude with ATC. ATC mentioned traffic directly in front of us and stated he would try to give us a descent after the traffic passed. During this time, around 10 seconds after the Captain tapped the glass, the short reignited and continued to grow. The Captain noted an acrid smell, unusually high heat emanating from his window, and again expressed the need to descend. I pointed out the traffic, now visible to us, at our 12 o'clock and stated that we can descend shorty after they passed underneath us. For a third time I requested a lower altitude with ATC. The window failed shortly thereafter. The Captain's side view window let out a loud bang and fractures spider-webbed its entirety. For the first time since this incident began we received a L WSHIELD HEAT EICAS message followed by another L WINDOW HEAT EICAS message.Considering the potential for smoke/fumes and loss of cabin pressure we both immediately donned our oxygen masks, ensured they were at 100%, and established communications between ourselves and ATC. As I was donning the mask I saw the previously mentioned traffic pass safely below us. I relayed this to the Captain who began an emergency descent and told me to notify ATC. I [advised ATC] and let the controller know we were beginning a descent. As the Captain was flying our descent I sent an ACARS to Dispatch notifying them of the L WINDOW failure and that we would need a diversion. The Captain noted that we were close to ZZZ2. I plugged ZZZ2 into the fixes page, identifying that we were 55 miles away and subsequently plugged ZZZ3 into the fixes page, identifying us to be 90 miles away. Our first thought was to proceed to ZZZ2 as it was so close. I requested a heading from ATC as the airplane was about to turn north towards ZZZ1 along our original route and that we would likely be diverting to ZZZ2 but were still weighing our options. ATC gave us a heading which we accepted. As we were established in our descent I told the Captain I'd notify the flight attendants. He continued to fly the airplane as I called the FAs. I provided them a brief note of what had happened, that we were diverting, and that we would make an announcement to the passengers when we knew where we were going. They were professional and calm throughout the notification. The Captain handed control of the airplane to me so he could run the QRC and QRH. I accepted the aircraft and he quickly and effectively ran both checklists to their completion. By the end of his checklists we received a message from dispatch identifying ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 as good diversions. We were closer to ZZZ2 but still in the flight levels. We discussed our options. Considering ZZZ3 was a crew base, maintenance base, and nearly perfect to descend to from our present position we elected to proceed to ZZZ3. After establishing ourselves at 10,000 feet we removed the oxygen masks and donned our normal headsets for easier communication. The Captain gave the flight attendants a full briefing and updated the passengers on what had happened and why we were going to ZZZ3. I flew the airplane with autopilot engaged, managed ATC communications, notified dispatch that we were an [priority] aircraft and going to ZZZ3, and proceeded to obtain ZZZ3 weather, performance numbers, and set up the approach in the FMS. By the time the Captain completed his duties we were at 5,000 feet and on delaying vectors for Runway XXL into ZZZ3. We discussed what both of us had done ensuring we had not missed any items seeking immediate attention. Satisfied, he briefed the approach, we ran the descent checklist, I transferred the aircraft controls back to him, and I notified ATC that we were ready to proceed to the airport. The rest of the flight continued uneventfully. I called Ops to ensure we had a gate, we shot the approach, several emergency vehicles followed us after landing, and we canceled [with ATC] while taxiing in.The Captain detected a light in his peripheral vision. He discovered a short working its way through the window pane.Repeated cycling of the windshield heat in a prior checklist revision likely led to the unit's failure and short. We knew it was likely a matter of time until the window failed. We immediately began planning our descent and diversion choices.I was surprised at how challenging it was to hear ATC and/or the FAs with the oxygen masks on. Our breathing was very loud over the intercom/speaker which made it very hard to hear other voices. It might be worth noting in sim sessions.
ASRS:1808272.s: The First Officer and Captain experienced a left side window heat short and subsequent failure at FL360, causing an emergency descent and diversion to ZZZ3. The crew attributed the failure to repeated heat cycling, donned oxygen masks, and landed safely with emergency vehicles standing by.

ASRS:1808291.n: As Pilot Flying, at approximately 1,050 feet AGL on the ZZZZZ3 departure, we experienced a rapid succession of three bursts. At the same time, I was reducing the thrust levers to CLB mode. The gear was already up and the Captain, Pilot Monitoring, was just checking in with departure. Both of us weren't sure if we had hit a bird or something else. We had another rapid succession of three bursts with associated ECAM that almost instantaneously cleared the screen. The Captain quickly recognized the right engine (#2) indications were 'rolling back' and stated so clearly. He then ensure positive aircraft control by verbally stating, 'Your aircraft'. I responded with 'My aircraft'. The right engine ECAM message went away just as quickly as it displayed. The right engine then showed normal parameters and 'parallel' with the left engine. The Captain reviewed the Quick Reference Card and determined no action from the QRC required. He [advised] ATC while I simultaneously flew the aircraft on crosswind and turned downwind. The thrust levelers remained at CLB setting and flaps 1 on downwind with no other associated engine indications at approximately 2,500 feet MSL. We both agreed the best resolution was to land the aircraft ASAP. Our current weight was below max landing weight. I very quickly briefed a visual approach to Rwy XXR while the Captain loaded an approach in the FMGC. With gear down, I made the right turn on a base leg. I pushed the SPD button for managed speed as I thought we were in APPR Mode however, I quickly pulled the SPD button for selected speed once I noticed the engines were increase thrust for a higher speed. At this point we experienced one more rapid succession from the right engine which quickly resided again with speed now selected and winding back to approach speed. We configured final flap setting to 3 and briefed our potential go-around if required. The Captain successfully ensured our Descent and Before Landing checklist were completed with clearance to land. Upon a successful landing, the Captain ensured the passengers and crew were informed to remain seated while we taxied to the gate. ARFF did a complete review and temperature check of the engines with nothing significant to report. Noteworthy items...the aircraft was hand flown until downwind. Auto pilot was engaged briefly once at 2,500 feet MSL. The autopilot was disengaged when turning base leg and hand flown for the visual approach.Definitely a startle factor, particularly since it happened just above 1,000 feet AGL while thrust levels are normally set to CLB mode. Additionally, the initial confusion as to whether we had hit something (bird?) since the ECAM did not display an action. Furthermore, once the ECAM action did display it was nearly instantaneously gone as the engine continued to attempt to resolve the problem.Since ENG Stall isn't on the Checklist, this scenario could be used in future training events to increase awareness and action based on a low altitude scenario during take-off phase.
ASRS:1808291.s: The Pilot Flying and Captain experienced rapid engine bursts and transient ECAM messages on the right engine during the ZZZZZ3 departure at 1,050 feet AGL. They returned for an immediate landing after the engine parameters normalized, with post-flight inspections revealing no significant damage.

ASRS:1808294.n: The Captain and I were scheduled to depart ZZZZ in a 737 MAX. The flight was full and we knew we had max takeoff weight issues for runway limit. The outside temperature was 16 degrees C and winds were variable for Runway XXR. On our first pushback, we did not have our load closeout and we pushed from gate and began to taxi, even while seeing potential overweight issues. After calling ZZZZ Operations, we received our load closeout and ran the numbers. The temperature increased to 18 degrees C and that significantly degraded engine performance at our weight and required configuration. We noticed that we would be overweight by about 1,100 pounds. We discontinued taxi, messaged Dispatch via ACARS and coordinated a return to gate for overall reevaluation. Dispatch and the flight planning team determined we needed to offload passengers and associated bags and that would fix the problem.Now, enough time elapsed that we needed more fuel and needed a new ATC flight plan clearance. ZZZZ Clearance informed us that we had no clearance in the system and we needed to contact Dispatch. We did that via ACARS as well as through ZZZZ Operations. This disconnect with the clearance occurred more than 10 times over a 4 hour period before they finally got a clearance through ZZZZ ATC. We were told that the issue was that ZZZZ ATC did not like something in the clearance request that ZZZ1 Dispatch submitted. However, ZZZZ ATC would not talk to ZZZ1 Dispatch, nor tell them what was wrong with their submission. ZZZZ ATC would only work through ZZZZ Operations, who does not submit flight plan clearance requests and had no idea what is required. We, the aircrew, decided to not push back until we had our clearance and a valid load closeout. It began to rain during our delay and I requested approximately XX different updates based on new weights, temperatures and runway conditions. Also during this 4 hour delay, Dispatch and the flight planning team repeatedly pulled off many passengers and bags. This required continuous updates for accuracy. The passengers were told to deplane after X hours and were given a time to be back at the gate for departure. We got everyone back on board, received our flight plan clearance, a valid load closeout and departed via ZZZZ Runway XXR. The flight was uneventful and we landed safely in ZZZ2.The main issue on this flight was planning and execution by the company. The company tried to leverage the 737 MAX in an environment where it does not need to be flying with full loads and the flight planning team tried to execute an inherently flawed plan. In ZZZZ, rain is constant, but the temperatures and winds that day were very moderate compared to what routinely occurs in the summer months. Even at 18 degrees C, the 737 MAX is extremely weight limited at this airport's altitude. The 737 MAX should not be flying in ZZZZ during even moderate temperature months with full passenger and cargo loads. The ATC flight plan clearance issue is a procedural or communication issue between the company and ZZZZ ATC. ZZZZ Operations should be able to intercede in these situations and fix any issues that come up, but training and awareness is required. Ultimately, this was a non-issue due to the more time-consuming weight issues associated with this flight. Our flight planning departments must continue to gather data related to the 737 MAX during normal operations at all airports throughout the year. This data will lead to an executable annual route schedule for the 737 MAX and ensure smooth operational tempo while maintaining appropriate safety margins.
ASRS:1808294.s: The flight crew of a 737 MAX at ZZZZ faced a four-hour departure delay due to overweight conditions caused by rising temperatures and a procedural breakdown between Dispatch and ATC regarding flight plan clearances. After offloading passengers and bags to resolve weight limits and securing a valid clearance, the aircraft departed safely.

ASRS:1808303.n: During TO out of ZZZ thrust levers anomaly- TO thrust setting as I remember was 84.6, however, when First Officer selected TOGA the thrust increased to over 90% N1 before reducing. Discussed with First Officer after climb out after verifying First Officer had as I expected acted properly (setting thrust) continued to ZZZ1. Executed the visual approach to Runway XX at less than 50 feet thrust lever(auto throttle) anomaly - executed go around. ATC cleared us to 2,000 - during the Go Around I feel it's safe to say we were in the yellow and mitigating any transition into the red by both actively flying/monitoring aircraft instrumentation and following SOPs and yes very deliberately. There was a surprise effect from the aircraft not acting as directed (thrust levers/ auto throttle) as the approach itself was stable. Then we were vectored in visual conditions back around for a second approach to Runway 31. After parking at the gate in ZZZ1 Maintenance was notified of the irregularities with thrust levers (auto throttle).The aircraft was removed from service by Maintenance.Thrust lever / auto throttle anomaly that added a startle effect and divided attention or required additional attention. We could have after the missed approach disconnected the A/T but felt better about closely monitoring/ guarding the thrust levers. On the take off from ZZZ when I pressed the TOGA button, the throttles rapidly advanced to near full forward, and then slowly retarded to the selected takeoff thrust as we were rolling down the runway. The throttles came forward very rapidly and went further forward then I would expect. We were set for a 22K takeoff with an assumed temperature reduction. After takeoff the Captain and I discussed the anomaly. It was very unusual. The rest of the flight, up to the landing flare, was normal. I was flying the new visual approach. The approach was loaded into the FMS. The autopilot was engaged. I think I remember disengaging the autopilot if the final turn to final. In the flare, below 50 feet the throttles began to advance by themselves. I remember being right on speed prior to this. I felt the throttles move forward, and I remember trying to hold them back. I think the autothrottles were attempting to go around. I felt the aircraft 'ballooning' and I saw that I was now going to fast (I remember seeing 155 knots). At this point I said go around and pressed the go around button. We climbed out and tower gave us a visual downwind to return. The go around was a normal go around. After cleaning up, I went right back to flaps 1 for the downwind. I was trying to process what just happened and the Captain and I discussed it. We were both surprised by the auto throttle. While turning base, the auto throttles were doing a poor job of holding command bug. They were very slow to respond. I turned off my flight director and visually flew a visual pattern (I had no lateral guidance from the FMS, the approach had not been resequenced. I know the airport very well could see where I needed to go. I left the auto throttles engaged but I had a firm hand on the throttles. While on base, the air speed got 5 knots slow and I manually pushed the throttles up to speed up. I completed a visual approach and normal flaps 40 landing with flight director off and auto throttles engaged. The auto throttles functioned normal after I had manually pushed them up, but in retrospect I should have disconnected them and flown manually. They were definitely suspect at this point. The flaps 40 approach and landing was normal and smooth. The auto throttles worked as they should. We had a mechanic at ZZZ1 meet us and we wrote up what had happened. The next morning while eating breakfast, I was 'bothered' by what had happened and I called Name to discuss the anomaly. We discussed the anomaly in detail. He didn't have any answers either, but said he would keep an eye on the aircraft, X. Additional note, the approach was stable prior to the auto throttle anomaly. We were following an [aircraft] that was going very slow. We were minimal space behind them so we were right on speed throughout the approach to flare. I believe the autopilot was engaged until the turn to final.I am not sure if this was a fault with the airplane auto throttle, a 737 Max anomaly or a coding issue with the new visual approach? Thinking about what had happened on the takeoff, I suspect something was wrong with the auto throttles. I am fairly new to the Max. [No suggestions], however in retrospect I should have turned off the auto throttles when it became clear they were not working correctly after the go around.
ASRS:1808303.s: Pilots reported autothrottle anomalies on a Boeing 737 Max during takeoff from ZZZ and below 50 feet on a visual approach to Runway 31, causing unexpected thrust surges and a go-around. Maintenance removed the aircraft from service after the crew manually managed thrust and landed safely, suspecting an autothrottle or coding fault.

ASRS:1808319.n: Captain [on flight XXX] called and said the ZZZ -ZZZ1 leg is delayed because ZZZ ramp unloaded some haz[Hazmat] meant for ZZZ1. When the ramp opened F1, it was full of freight not accounted for on the ZZZ2 -ZZZ [inbound flight] weight and balance. I contacted the Duty Officer, and she recommended the crew fill out a report and contact company. I confirmed that recovery was notified. Crew informed delay is so weight and balance can be fixed in ZZZ to account for the extra freight.
ASRS:1808319.s: The Captain reported a delay on flight XXX due to unaccounted freight loaded onto the aircraft by the ramp team. The delay was required to correct the weight and balance calculations before departure.

ASRS:1808344.n: FO (First Officer) observed a black and white object roughly 2 feet in diameter passed extremely close to aircraft left during climb passing 13,500 feet on the ZZZZZ2 [SID] prior to ZZZZZ [fix]. The object was close enough that he expected an impact. As Pilot Monitoring, I was heads down attending to FMS programming and did not see the object. FO did not see wings or recognize the object as a balloon, nor could he confirm the object to be a drone.
ASRS:1808344.s: During climb through 13,500 feet on the ZZZZZ2 SID, the First Officer observed an unidentified black and white object pass extremely close to the aircraft's left side. The Pilot Monitoring was occupied with FMS programming and did not see the object, which the First Officer could not identify as a balloon or drone.

ASRS:1808410.n: Total engine failure occurred at 12,000 feet MSL. Reported forced landing to ATC. Landed Runway XX at ZZZ.
ASRS:1808410.s: The pilot reported a total engine failure at 12,000 feet MSL and requested a forced landing from ATC. The aircraft subsequently landed on Runway XX at ZZZ.

ASRS:1808423.n: I departed with one passenger to ZZZ on an IFR flight plan. The flight was uneventful until on a 5-mile final when I heard the Tower clear a 'Heavy' cargo plane to take the runway for departure. As we got closer to the runway, we noticed that the heavy cargo plane was just getting off the runway as we were on short final. With traffic behind us in the pattern, I continued the approach opting to land slightly below the glideslope on the first third of the runway so as to avoid any potential wake turbulence put off by the departing aircraft beyond its rotation point. While in the landing phase of flight, approximately 1' off the ground and near stall speed for a normal landing, we encountered sudden turbulence that caused the plane to destabilize resulting in a brief touchdown followed by a balloon and a subsequent stall that caused the aircraft to bounce on the runway. As I saw we were losing directional control, I added full power to initiate the go-around maneuver, regained stability, and completed a left traffic pattern. We came in shortly after another Cirrus on short final and had a normal smooth landing. It was not until after taxiing to [FBO] and performing engine shutdown that I noticed the tips of the props were frayed as the obvious result of a prop strike on our initial attempt.It is my opinion that the cause of the turbulence encountered on the runway was the jet blast from the departing heavy jet rather than wake turbulence as we landed well before its point of rotation. While I do not have a copy of the Tower's audio, I do not recall any warnings from the Tower. Apparently, the 'heavy' jet took an extended amount of time to take the runway after being cleared and departed less than a minute before our touchdown. Since we could not see the plane delay taking the runway from a distance due to haze, the Tower should have warned us to avoid wake turbulence and jet blast during our approach. This would likely have prompted a decision to break off our approach at a safe altitude to allow the jet blast to dissipate, and follow trailing traffic to an uneventful landing.At 120 kts. approach speed, our ETA to land on a 5-mile final was approximately 2.5 minutes. Had the Tower held the 'heavy' cargo jet for the additional few minutes, substantial loss of property and the potential for loss of life could have been avoided. In hindsight, as PIC I could have made the decision to break off on short-final and abort the landing when I noticed the heavy cargo plane had departed so shortly before we were to land. I trusted the Tower to provide safe and adequate separation for our arrival and it could have cost us a lot more than a prop strike. I will not make that mistake again.
ASRS:1808423.s: The pilot of a single-engine aircraft encountered jet blast from a departing heavy cargo plane on short final, causing a destabilized landing, prop strike, and go-around. The pilot attributed the incident to the heavy jet's delayed departure and a lack of Tower warnings regarding the hazard.

ASRS:1808443.n: Called landing intentions on CTAF frequency on approach to airport and prior to entering traffic pattern. No other traffic heard. On downwind leg, observed another aircraft nearby flying approximately same heading but heard nothing on radio. I called my position and intentions on my radio but heard no response. I watched other aircraft continue on course and I landed after flying base and final legs of the pattern and calling my position on the radio. While taxiing on ground after landing, discovered volume of my radio was turned down. Turned volume up and heard the other aircraft calling landing intentions at the airport. They had apparently been flying the pattern too, and extended their downwind while I landed.Factors involved were my inadvertently turning volume down too far, and distraction of passengers (the radio was active with lots of faraway traffic and passenger asked question, so I turned radio volume down to hear better). As a side note, did not see a traffic alert on ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast), suggesting other aircraft was not ADS-B equipped.
ASRS:1808443.s: The pilot reported a near-miss during the traffic pattern at an uncontrolled airport caused by inadvertently lowering the radio volume due to passenger distraction. This prevented hearing another aircraft's calls, though the pilot landed safely after the other aircraft extended its downwind leg.

ASRS:1808462.n: Aircraft X was in a full 300 hour inspection for two weeks in ZZZ at Base XXX. I was leading the project working the hours of XA:00 to XM:00 everyday. We were short on man-power and the ones that arrived to help were only able to help a couple days at a time and then another hand or hands would show up to help. The base mechanic out of ZZZ1 refused to come help. I started the inspection at the tail and was lubing the splines and got pulled to the front due to a crack found in the broom closet which turned out to be structural. We had to remove all the controls and the servo rack up top in order for the repair to get done. A vendor was called in to repair it which took a full two days and I was up there removing anything else he needed. We finished all the inspections and the aircraft went back to the base and after a flight the pilot noticed a nut sitting in the drain hole on the thrust reverser gearbox fairing. Base mechanic was called in and found the nut on the furthest aft hangar bearing bolt (there are one on each side), came off. The other bolt was still in and cotter pinned and the bolt was still in on the left side with no nut. I was having to do a bunch of jumping around due to different hands coming in on several different days and lost focus. I thoroughly believe I put the nut on but didn't cotter pin it.
ASRS:1808462.s: A lead mechanic performing a 300-hour inspection on Aircraft X at Base XXX admitted to likely failing to cotter pin a hangar bearing bolt nut due to staffing disruptions. The unsecured nut later fell into the thrust reverser gearbox drain hole, where it was discovered by a pilot after a flight.

ASRS:1808465.n: I was working the Eagle Lake sector. Our area was getting all of the west arrivals as well as our normal arrivals due to weather. I had been coordinating with Houston Approach as to what was working best for them in terms of arrivals and how they wanted them situated since we could not get in on a normal flow. We had worked out BELLR intersection for both IAH arrivals and HOU arrivals. We were crossing HOU arrivals at 11,000 feet and IAH arrivals at 12,000 feet. After a few had made it in Houston Approach called and indicated that they did not want the aircraft stacked and wanted everyone in trail. He had also indicated that all of the aircraft were deviating upon check in with him. At this point I told him I would take care of it.Because of the weather building and starting to slowly close in I shut our corner post off. We had about 15 inbound and in terms of safety and using my best judgment I thought it would be smoother and safer if we took everyone to the southeast corner post. After I had made the decision and told the supervisor this is when the issue really began. The Supervisor, along with TMU (Traffic Management Unit) did not like this plan. They specifically told us to continue pushing these aircraft through the weather because it 'Wasn't bad enough yet'. That is a complete and utter lack of regard for safety. The mentality at Houston Center is to push aircraft through as much weather as humanly possible until a pilot decides they physically cannot make it happen. This has been the mentality for years and needs to be corrected immediately. I cannot in good conscious work airplanes through an unsafe situation just because someone with a higher position than me thinks it's OK.Ultimately when I am on position the decision should be mine on what is safe and what isn't. I am the Controller talking to the pilots, getting PIREPs and watching the weather develop real time. No one in TMU is talking to airplanes real time. They do not know the flow of the sectors real time. Houston Center's TMU is ungodly bad. They have been for years. There is never a plan and the Controllers are the ones who suffer for it. This needs rectification immediately and needs to be taken to the top of the food chain. Its not a matter of if, but when something happens because of poor judgment on managements part. This needs to be taken very seriously. It has gone on this way for far too long.Management needs to listen to Controllers when they are being told something isn't working or something isn't safe. Yes, any Controller can make a bad plan work. That doesn't mean we necessarily should.This unsafe mentality of pushing aircraft to the limit through weather will result in a safety event and it needs to get fixed before that happens.
ASRS:1808465.s: An air traffic controller in the Eagle Lake sector diverted 15 inbound aircraft to a safer route due to weather, but the Supervisor and Traffic Management Unit ordered them to continue through the weather. The controller reported this management decision ignored safety concerns and reflected an unsafe mentality of pushing aircraft to their limits.

ASRS:1808466.n: Today while working R87/95 our corner post shut down due to SEVERAL reports of moderate turbulence and one report of severe turbulence. Our corner post had weather (both precipitation and turbulence) directly impacting the fixes.Within 2 hours we were asked to try to 'Test ship.' We still had observable precipitation at our arrival fixes, while other corner posts didn't. Before the test ship made any report, TMU (Traffic Management Unit) told us our arrival fix adjacent to the turbulence reports was open. Test ship reported moderate turbulence. TMU opened us back up anyways.Two arrival fixes with moderate and heavy precipitation AND moderate turbulence reports was opened by Management/TMU.
