Why?[Houson Center] has several weather events throughout the year. Because of this, it seems there is a 'Why can't they just make it work?' mindset from TMU/Management. Weather days are nasty, things happen. No one expects flow/management to catch everything 100% of the time. It seems like Controllers are constantly bailing out bad plans anytime there's weather. We have discussions about things getting better but it never does.Our culture is supposed to be about 'safety' but we're pushing things that don't need to be pushed. It's not an 'if' something will happen, it's a 'when' if our culture continues this way.Recommendation: Actually make safety a priority.
ASRS:1808466.s: An air traffic controller at Houston Center reported that TMU opened arrival fixes despite moderate turbulence and heavy precipitation. The controller attributed this unsafe decision to a management mindset prioritizing flow over safety, fearing future incidents.

ASRS:1808491.n: On my flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, I received a HAZMAT NOTOC from the Operations Agent. I signed both copies and returned one to the agent. We were dealing with severe weather at the gate. After a third release and weather reroute, I noticed the NOTOC for HAZMAT was not annotated on the dispatch release. When I landed in ZZZ1, I contacted Dispatch and disclosed the information.
ASRS:1808491.s: The pilot reported that on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, the HAZMAT NOTOC was not annotated on the dispatch release after a weather reroute. Upon landing, the pilot contacted Dispatch to disclose the discrepancy.

ASRS:1808495.n: This was the second leg of an OE for the First Officer who was returning to the line after more than one year on leave. We had planned and briefed a Single Engine Taxi (SET). I asked the Pushback Crew to push the aircraft 'towards ZZZ' to better align us for SET Ops. As we were pushing, I noticed a Company aircraft on the adjacent gate was also getting ready to push and commented to the First Officer that we might have to start both engines to safely taxi away. I then realized we could make a left 270 to make our turn towards the east, to taxi to the planned runway. The Pushback Crew asked for me to set the brakes and I complied, then asked me to set the brakes as they were pulling away. This caused a chuckle from both he and I as he got jumbled with his scripted words. The First Officer had completed the #2 engine start and started his flow. He got to the Air Conditioning panel and asked if it was set correctly.I reached up and turned the #2 engine bleed on and commented that the pack was now being powered. Between the chuckle with the Pushback Crew and the First Officer query, I lost my focus and didn't notice the FO did not complete his flow and callout. I was also concerned with getting the aircraft moving in the left 270 before Company pushed. The FO called for taxi and we proceeded down CS and Mike. After being cleared onto Mike and seeing there was no line for Runway XX, I called for #1 engine to be started. The FO started it and did his After Start Flow, noticing and announcing that we hadn't set the flaps. I verified this, stopped the aircraft and commanded flaps 1, Before Taxi Checklist. These items were accomplished, we continued with normal operations and took off and flew to ZZZ1 without further incident.Don't get distracted during critical phases of flight, specifically when very specific cues are used to command flaps and run checklists. During the Crew brief, and prior to pushing back in ZZZ, the Captain briefed a single-engine taxi (SET). The Captain requested from the Tug Operator that the pushback be angled toward the turnout direction, to facilitate an easier SET break away to begin taxi. When the pushback was complete, we discussed whether or not to start the remaining #1 engine, and abandon the SET plan, because the Pushback Crew had not pushed the aircraft in the position instructed. Ultimately, we decided to request, from the Ramp Controller, a turn in the opposite direction and continue with the SET plan. Being on the second leg of OE, and getting familiar with the switch positions of the pressurization panel, I had stopped my after start flow at that panel, to ask the Captain a question. Inadvertently and after that interruption, I neglected to continue the flow to its completion. Subsequently, we began our taxi without setting the flaps, which helps to trigger the Before Taxi Checklist. When we eventually started the #1 engine during taxi out, I noticed that the flaps had not been set, as I usually re-check the items on an after start flow. We stopped the aircraft, set the flaps, and completed the Before Taxi Checklist. The flight continued as normal.I think that getting further comfortable with the pressurization panel, and that particular flow, will increase situational awareness and become less of a distraction.
ASRS:1808495.s: The Captain and First Officer, on the First Officer's second leg of an OE, began taxiing without setting flaps due to distraction during a Single Engine Taxi. The crew stopped the aircraft, set flaps 1, completed the Before Taxi Checklist, and continued the flight to ZZZ1 without further incident.

ASRS:1808518.n: Proceeding directly to ZZZZZ intersection on the ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival. Was cleared to descend via ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival on [Runway] XXR. Prior to ZZZZZ, at approximately FL220 during descent, noticed that the cabin altitude was at 8,300 feet and increasing. I called attention to the First Officer that we might be losing cabin pressurization. The Pressurization screen on ECAM was displayed and noticed that both the inlet and extract valve were fully closed but the safety valve had opened.Since we had already been cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival and had an altitude of 12,000 set in the MCP I decided to expedite the descent to see if I could control the rate of ascent in the cabin. At approximately FL180 it appeared that we could not control the rate of ascent in the cabin and that at its present rate the cabin would exceed 10,000 feet shortly. I then [advised] with ATC and requested 10,000 feet which was granted. I advised the Lead Flight Attendant that we were experiencing cabin pressurization problems but to expect a normal landing. As we leveled at 10,000 feet I monitored the cabin and noticed that it had climbed to 12,000 feet but stabilized. It took several minutes before the cabin normalized at our cruise altitude of 10,000 feet. I asked the First Officer to see if he could find an applicable checklist to run. During this time I maintained control of the aircraft and communicated with ATC. The First Officer advised that he was able to manually control the outflow valve and that the checklist recommended shallow descents thereafter. I continued to ask for delayed vectors from ATC just north of ZZZ as the First Officer and I reviewed the state of the aircraft and decided it was safe to proceed with the landing. I asked ATC for shallow descents on the arrival to [Runway] XXR into ZZZ. The landing and taxi in were uneventful.
ASRS:1808518.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced a cabin pressurization failure during descent on the ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival due to closed inlet and extract valves with an open safety valve. They expedited descent to 10,000 feet, manually controlled the outflow valve, and completed an uneventful landing after ATC granted shallow descent vectors.

ASRS:1808592.n: Approx 30 knots on takeoff roll, Level 2 Gen Drive 1 Fault alert. Rejected takeoff. Returned to maintenance area for repair. Repeat write up.
ASRS:1808592.s: The pilot rejected takeoff at approximately 30 knots due to a Level 2 Gen Drive 1 Fault alert. The aircraft returned to the maintenance area for repair, and this incident is a repeat write-up.

ASRS:1808599.n: After takeoff autopilot connected at 1,000 AGL. Flaps retracted on schedule in a 180 degree turn off [Runway] XXR. Noticed that the attitude pitch did not match the flight director command followed by a Level Two 'STAB out of trim' alert. We then made the decision for an air turn back, notified ATC, transferred control of the jet to the me (Pilot Monitoring) and advised ATC of the need to dump fuel (gross weight-600K LBS.) with a request for a holding pattern at a block altitude of 6,000-7,000 feet. ATC denied the hold and elected to vector us over the water in their radar holding pattern. The QRH was consulted for stabilizer out of trim which led us to a non abnormal alert 'Stabilizer Inop. We then noticed that the stabilizer trim had not moved from the takeoff setting of 8.0 degrees. Fuel dump continued in the radar hold until 522K gross weight, then the cross feed relays failed and forced the dump command to stop. We flew in the radar pattern for about another 50 minutes within about 35nm from ZZZZ until our bingo fuel of 32K, with now a runway change to XXL. ATC was advised of the need for a 20nm final approach and a request of no traffic in front of us. We discussed the go around possibilities, configured on schedule early of the slats/flaps and gear. Aircraft control was then transferred to the Captain and the autopilot disconnected with noticeable pitch down, landed uneventfully. Failure of trim gear fuse pin." After takeoff autopilot connected at 1,000 [feet] AGL. Flaps retracted on schedule in a 180 degree turn off XXR. I immediately noticed that the attitude pitch did not match the flight director command followed by a Level Two 'STAB out of trim' alert. Elected to keep the autopilot connected thru the turn. After the flaps and slats were retracted, I disconnected the autopilot and had to use a tremendous amount of strength to overcome the aircraft's desire to pitch up. I extended the slats with a speed edit of 210 KTS and that relieved some of the nose up tendency and reconnected the autopilot. I then made the decision for an air turn back, notified ATC, transferred control of the jet to the First Officer and advised ATC of the need to dump fuel (gross weight-600K LBS.) with a request for a holding pattern at a block altitude of 6,000-7,000 feet. ATC denied the hold and elected to vector us over the water in their radar holding pattern. The QRH was consulted for stabilizer out of trim which led us to a non abnormal alert 'Stabilizer Inop. We then noticed that the stabilizer trim had not moved from the takeoff setting of 8.0 degrees. Fuel Dump continued in the radar hold until 522K gross weight, then the crossfeed relays failed and forced the dump command to stop. We flew in the radar pattern for about another 50 minutes within about 35nm from ZZZ until our bingo fuel of 32K, with now a runway change to XXL. With the First Officer still flying (autopilot on) ATC was advised of the need for a 20 nm final approach and a request of no traffic in front of us. We discussed the go around possibilities, configured on schedule early of the slats/flaps and gear. Aircraft control was then transferred to the Captain and the autopilot disconnected with noticeable pitch down, but controllable. Landing, uneventful. Inspect Trim drives on a C check if not already done."
ASRS:1808599.s: Pilots experienced a stabilizer trim failure after takeoff, causing a pitch mismatch and 'STAB out of trim' alert. They returned to land safely after fuel dumping was interrupted by crossfeed relay failure, attributing the incident to a failed trim gear fuse pin.

ASRS:1808607.n: I was Pilot Flying. The right thrust reverser was inoperative and disabled by maintenance, the left thrust reverser was available for use. After touching down and derotating, I deployed the left thrust reverser. When I attempted to move the thrust lever backward from idle reverse to increase reverse thrust I found that the thrust lever would not move and my hand position somehow felt different from usual. In that same moment I realized that instead of lifting the thrust reverser unlock lever I had lifted the shutoff lock and moved the thrust lever into shutoff, shutting down the left engine. I called out the problem to the Captain and told him I would be using only brakes to stop the aircraft. There was plenty of runway remaining and heavy braking was not required. We taxied to the gate using normal single engine taxi procedures.After performing several thousand landings in this aircraft I have a well developed muscle memory for engaging reverse thrust. I also have a well developed muscle memory for shutting down the left engine during taxi. With the right thrust reverser disabled, thrust reverser use required touching and moving only the left thrust lever instead of both thrust levers. I am fairly certain that this interaction with only the left thrust lever subconsciously triggered the muscle memory motions for a left engine shutdown instead of those for activating the thrust reverser(s) which usually involves moving both thrust levers. I had landed the same aircraft the day before with the same inoperative right thrust reverser and properly deployed only the left thrust reverser. I have no other explanation for how I managed to perform the motions for an engine shutdown instead.I will be much more aware of this possibility for inadvertent incorrect hand motions possibly caused by muscle memory triggers when operating an aircraft with a deferred thrust reverser.
ASRS:1808607.s: The Pilot Flying inadvertently shut down the left engine during landing rollout by confusing the thrust reverser unlock lever with the shutoff lock. This error, attributed to muscle memory triggered by operating only the left thrust lever due to a disabled right reverser, resulted in a single-engine stop using brakes only.

ASRS:1808608.n: Arriving in San Diego, we had been cleared for the RNAV Z Runway 27 approach. We checked in with the Tower and were cleared to land. I heard Tower instruct a [heavy jet] to, 'Line up and wait, traffic on an 8 mile final'. Checklists and callouts may have masked additional communications on the frequency because I can't recall whether the [heavy jet] flight was cleared for takeoff, or not. We broke out of IMC at approximately 1400 feet. The Pilot Monitoring called 'Runway in Sight - Landing'. Shortly thereafter, the First Officer said, 'Is that an airplane on the runway? I looked closer and honestly could not tell. The navigation and beacon lights were blending into the approach lights and it was difficult to distinguish the aircraft. We had to get closer before the actual structure of the airplane was apparent. We had already determined that a go-around/missed approach was necessary, but before we could communicate that to the Tower Controller, she issued the go-around instruction, 'Fly the published Missed Approach, and contact Departure'. I had observed that the offending aircraft was stationary on the runway, and not in the midst of a takeoff roll, so I knew that the published missed approach or runway heading was appropriate, and that a sidestep departure for spacing was not necessary. So we complied as instructed. We had already determined our BINGO fuel enroute and knew that we could accept one more approach before diverting to our alternate, so we accepted vectors back for another approach. The subsequent approach and landing was uneventful. The [heavy jet] had been removed from the runway and was still holding short when we landed. No mention of the reason for the go-around was given by the Tower, nor did we ask. Because we knew. There was an airplane on the runway. Cause: [The] decision to work a Maintenance Irregularity while on an active runway. The Tower's decision to put the [heavy jet] on the runway when they were not ready to depart, and then forgetting about them. And our loss of situational awareness based on the radio communications that were, or were not, taking place on the Tower Frequency.In the future, if the First Officer questions the security of the runway, or the landing clearance, I will instruct them to simply, and without delay, to ask the Tower. This would NOT have prevented the necessity to go-around, but perhaps would have initiated the maneuver a little sooner." While on the RNAV Z 27, we were handed off to Tower and were cleared to land. This occurred at approximately SAYAE intersection. The approach continued normally and we broke out about 1,400 feet and then called 'runway in sight', 'runway in sight landing'. Sometime after the 1,000 feet stabilized cleared to land call, I noticed what appeared to be an airplane on the displaced threshold of Runway 27 and said, 'Is that an airplane on the runway? The darkness of the displaced threshold area against the runway lights and the fact that the aircraft was in position pointed away from us made it difficult to tell. However, by the times the words were spoken, we were close enough to see. At the very same moment we began our go-around, the Tower issued instructions to go around and fly the published missed approach, which we did since the aircraft on the runway did not appear to be moving. We proceeded with a normal go-around and returned for a normal landing since we had sufficient fuel. In the simplest terms, we executed a normal go around due to an aircraft on the runway. Why was there an aircraft on the runway? I am not sure. Shortly after we were cleared to land, we heard the tower instruct [another aircraft] to line up and wait, traffic 8 mile final. I honestly don't recall hearing a take-off clearance, perhaps due our being engaged with our tasks and callouts during the approach. We did see the aircraft short of the runway when we returned. It wasn't until later that we read that they had a mechanical issue.Maintaining better awareness of traffic utilizing the runway particularly when we can't see it yet. Better awareness would have allowed us to question if the runway was indeed clear. That may not have prevented the go around this time, it would've depended on how soon we became aware."
ASRS:1808608.s: Pilots on an RNAV Z Runway 27 approach to San Diego executed a go-around after discovering a stationary heavy jet on the active runway. The reporter attributes the incident to the tower placing the aircraft on the runway for a maintenance irregularity without ensuring it was ready to depart, combined with crew distraction from checklists.

ASRS:1808610.n: Immediately after lift off, we experienced a continuous light shudder. Gear and flaps were retracted on scheduled. The unidentifiable shudder continued to increase as airspeed increased. No shudder was felt at the control column. We requested an immediate return to ZZZ. Following an uneventful return to land, taxi in, and shutdown at the designated parking position, it was discovered that the aircraft had a detached elevator balance tab. During the previous flight, when flaps were partially extended, a similar shudder was felt. The shudder ceased when landing gear was extended, and flaps were extended to the 30 position. During a detailed post flight inspection of flaps and gear doors, nothing was detected. The shudder was first felt in the previous approach, when flaps where partially extended. It then disappeared when landing gear was extended, and final flaps were selected. As a result, the post flight inspection was heavily focused on those two main components, flaps and landing gear doors. The balance tab, although included in the post flight inspection, did not appear to be completely loose. A more detailed inspection of all secondary flight control surfaces may have exposed the potentially damaged balance tab.
ASRS:1808610.s: The crew experienced an increasing shudder after lift-off, prompting an immediate return to ZZZ. Post-flight inspection revealed a detached elevator balance tab, which was missed because the initial check focused only on flaps and landing gear doors.

ASRS:1808626.n: Upon initial climb out of ZZZ on the R1 RNAV departure operating Flight XXXX ZZZ - ZZZ1 I noticed that the flight deck seemed much louder than usual. We double checked the security of all windows and proceeded with the departure. Monitoring the cabin altitude we noticed that the cabin altitude kept climbing as we did. Once we reached 11 thousand on the departure the cabin altitude was at 4000 and rising. We leveled off at 13 thousand to see what the pressurization would do. The outflow valves never closed and the cabin altitude kept rising. The collective decision was to notify ZZZ2 Center that we would like to precautionary return to ZZZ. After informing ATC of our issue they gave us radar vectors back to ZZZ and a decent clearance to 10 thousand feet. Center ended up declaring [for our] aircraft in order to get us priority vectors back to the airport. Upon landing the fire trucks and airport ops waited for us to vacate the runway to check on the passengers and flight crew. No injuries were reported and passengers were safely deplaned and escorted inside the location with out incident.Possible failure with some part of the pressurization systemThe crew communication and CRM decision making was exceptional and was all handled with utmost professionalism.
ASRS:1808626.s: Flight XXXX crew experienced a pressurization failure during climb from ZZZ, where outflow valves failed to close and cabin altitude rose to 4,000 feet at 11,000 feet. The crew returned to ZZZ under emergency priority, landing safely with no injuries attributed to a suspected pressurization system part failure.

ASRS:1808637.n: I was performing my preflight checklist and noticed a missing halon AND bracket in the FC OHB RIGHT SIDE. I immediately informed my Captain of this. He notified Maintenance who came 25 minutes later. Plane was boarded ready to go. Maintenance looked at the stowage space and left to retrieve a halon and bracket. 20 minutes later Maintenance came back and said plane is out of service. No brackets in stock room to rectify this situation. We deplaned all passengers and left ZZZ for ZZZ1 an hour and a half later on another 737. Obviously this plane has been flying around the system for A LONG TIME with this violation of missing emergency equipment. Obviously the Flight Attendants before me didn't do their preflight emergency equipment checklist...or this would have been caught much sooner. Obviously when this was configured the proper checklist wasn't followed to make sure ALL equipment is on board. Whoever signed off on this was negligent.
ASRS:1808637.s: The pilot discovered a missing halon and bracket during preflight on a Boeing 737, leading to an out-of-service declaration due to lack of parts. Passengers were deplaned, and the crew departed 90 minutes later on a replacement aircraft after the reporter attributed the oversight to previous crew negligence.

ASRS:1808674.n: Upon touchdown I applied both brakes and beta on the propellers. The airplane veered to the right and I could not straighten the landing path of the plane. The plane went off the right side of the runway into the dirt between the runways. The airplane was not damaged and there were no injuries. The wind was gusty and variable on landing and there was significant turbulence on the final approach. I am not sure why the incident occurred and I am having the plane inspected. There may have been a tailwind on landing.
ASRS:1808674.s: The pilot reported that upon touchdown in gusty, variable winds, the aircraft veered right despite brake and beta application, exiting the runway into dirt. No damage or injuries occurred, but the cause remains unknown, with a possible tailwind suspected and an inspection initiated.

ASRS:1808680.n: [Pilot] was flying her Aircraft X as Pilot in Command at the ZZZ airport, landing Runway XX. I was monitoring from the right seat. [Pilot] was cleared for the option on Runway XX by the ZZZ Tower from the left downwind of Runway XX approximately midfield. She initiated proper airspeed and flap configuration for a stabilized approach from pattern altitude. She applied correct airspeed, pitch, bank, and flap configurations while flying base and final approach. The aircraft maintained proper airspeed, pitch, and crosswind correction while on final maintaining the centerline of the runway as it flew a stabilized glide angle down to the runway. When transitioning into the landing phase, she began a flare and proper attitude to land the airplane. As the airplane was about to land, the attitude of the airplane changed suddenly in a way that was consistent with large rapid change in the characteristics of the wind, [Pilot] attempted to initiate a go-around with my immediate assistance. However, the plane lost directional control, veering to the right and eventually coming to a stop with a nose down attitude.
ASRS:1808680.s: The Pilot in Command and right-seat monitor landed Aircraft X at ZZZ Airport when a sudden wind shift caused loss of directional control during the flare. Despite attempting a go-around, the aircraft veered right and stopped nose-down.

ASRS:1808687.n: I conducted a routine pre-flight of the aircraft and no anomalies were noted. I requested that the aircraft be fueled, and that was done. I also checked weather and NOTAMs for my solo flight. I noted some wind indicated in the forecast - clear, unlimited visibility, wind variable 6 G 13, 30.01 altimeter - but well within aircraft and pilot limitations. Actual weather at take-off was clear VFR and unremarkable.I then had a routine flight for approximately one hour focusing primarily on use of the Garmin avionics system. I did an approach and landing which was uneventful.I returned to [home airport]. My initial approach was stabilized, but I was alert because of wind guests. On touchdown, the aircraft became airborne after a wind gust. I executed a balked landing procedure as the aircraft settled on the runway and went around.On my second approach to land, the aircraft was again on a stabilized approach through flare and touchdown. I was conducting a no-flaps approach because of the wind. After touchdown, there was an exceptional gust of wind which caused the aircraft to veer sharply to the left. I immediately applied full right rudder and heavy braking to maintain control of the aircraft and avoid exiting the runway. Despite my best efforts, the aircraft exited the runway. I immediately released hard braking to avoid flipping the aircraft and focused on maintaining control, which I did.The aircraft came to rest adjacent to the intersecting taxi-way. I could tell that the left tire was flat so I stopped the engine and exited the aircraft to inspect it and assess the situation.
ASRS:1808687.s: A solo pilot flying a Garmin-equipped aircraft exited the runway on the second landing attempt due to an exceptional wind gust that caused a sharp left veer. Despite applying full right rudder and braking, the aircraft left the runway surface and came to rest with a flat left tire.

ASRS:1808701.n: On the downwind I was in a Cessna Skyhawk with a student when Tower told us to look out for traffic joining the downwind on a 45º, it being a Piper Seminole. We had them in sight, however it appeared they were on a continuous course direct to us. Tower clearly told the Seminole they were #2 following us to land however the course they took seemed to be as if they wanted to overtake us in the pattern. When I looked over seeing them directly abeam us, off our 3 o'clock while banking right, I knew they not only were unable to see us while banking. They were extremely close, 400 feet horizontal distance being a hopeful estimate of distance at that point. I requested a short approach to land from Tower to get away from the Seminole and operate the aircraft at a safer distance away from the Seminole.
ASRS:1808701.s: A Cessna Skyhawk pilot and student on downwind reported a near-midair collision with a Piper Seminole that appeared to be on a direct course despite Tower instructions to follow. The Seminole passed within an estimated 400 feet horizontally while banking right, prompting the pilot to request a short approach to increase separation.

ASRS:1808703.n: I arrived to the airport of departure (ZZZ) with the owner for a reposition flight. I was referred to this owner within the Bellanca Crusiair community since I had recent time in make and model, and I am an active tailwheel CFI. The day prior to this flight I met with a very competent and experienced Cruisair owner/pilot, who has 600 hours in make and model to refresh me on systems and flying characteristics of the aircraft. The new owner and I had briefed the route of flight and pertinent details over the phone the days before, as well as in person prior to pushing the aircraft out of the hangar that morning. I conducted a thorough preflight in accordance with the 'Bellanca Crusiair Senior 13-14 Handbook of Instructions.' I also discussed recent maintenance that was conducted on the aircraft with the local mechanic and owner. I found no discrepancies with Aircraft X and proceeded to enter the aircraft along with the owner for our flight. Engine start was normal, as I saw a prompt rise in oil and fuel pressure. Oil temperature closely followed. Soon after I proceeded to taxi to the run up area for the active runway at ZZZ. A run up showed instruments, flight controls, and the engine to be performing as expected and normally. The aircraft was properly configured for takeoff and I made a radio call on CTAF to indicate we would be departing Runway XX straight out. The take off and climb were normal given the high altitude and density altitude conditions that existed. Upon climb out, and at a safe height, I performed the procedure to switch tanks. Switching the tanks resulted in no issues and fuel pressure and engine power was maintained. Shortly after this time I had leaned the mixture to provide adequate power as we ascended in our climb. After 5-8 minutes in a cruise climb configuration and on the left tank we experienced an unprovoked gradual reduction in power. This was indicated by a loss of RPM, thrust, and fuel pressure. I quickly enriched mixture, suspecting that the mixture may have creeped out and the engine was running too lean. This did not completely restore the loss of power, but it did not make the situation worse. I lowered the nose and promptly swapped to the right hand tank, which completely fixed the issue. I turned back towards ZZZ so that I would be closer to an adequate landing area and to decide on the continuation of our flight. Another power loss event occurred, this time with the right tank selected, with a slightly more profound loss in power once I was enroute to the airport. After running the engine in this configuration at a safe altitude and within ample gliding distance of the airport I swapped back to the left tank. I was unable to replicate the issue over time and deemed that it could have been a random anomaly, perhaps air in the fuel lines, and proceeded on course. It was also at this time when I received flight following to ZZZ1, from Center. After 5-8 minutes in a cruise configuration we experienced the issue again, except this reduction in power was longer and more severe. From this point forward several things happened consecutively in order to keep the engine running. I was swapping tanks to hopefully remedy the issue, excising the wobble pump whenever power loss or fuel pressure was nonexistent, and exercised the mixture and throttle controls. We experienced the power loss events regardless of which fuel tank was selected. I was operating each of these systems independently and deliberately, actively attempting to keep the engine running and hopefully avoiding a possible prolonged power failure. Over time the loss of power was random and increasing in severity. It was also during these actions I informed Center of our situation, but not [requesting priority] at that time. After repeated engine failures that seemed to be gradually increasing in frequency and intensity, where at least two of which caused complete power loss for at least 1-2 seconds, I decided to notify ATC in fear of landing in the barren terrain between us and ZZZ. ZZZ3 Approach provided an accurate heading back ZZZ and timely ASOS information, all of which contributed to the safe outcome of this event. Upon reaching the airport, and after deeming a safe altitude, I performed a deliberate power to idle approach since I could not rely on on-demand power. I performed a tight pattern and landed smoothly on the runway. We taxied off the runway under our own power. I contacted ZZZ3 Approach via the local clearance delivery phone number and by radio to inform that we safely landed. We then proceeded to taxi to the hangar of origination and informed the mechanic of what we just experienced.
ASRS:1808703.s: The pilot of a Bellanca Crusiair experienced repeated, unprovoked power losses during cruise climb and cruise phases due to suspected fuel system anomalies. After notifying ATC and returning to the departure airport, the pilot executed a safe power-to-idle landing and taxied to the hangar under own power.

ASRS:1808709.n: On initial climb out at approximately 1,000 ft. my Garmin GTN635 GPS notified me that terrain awareness was unavailable and was in dead reckoning mode. Shortly after this I checked in with Albuquerque Center when they notified me of the GPS jamming in White Sands research area restricted area 5107B. I informed Albuquerque Center that I was unable to maintain my own terrain obstruction clearance and they put me on an IFR flight plan at that time. My portable Garmin 695 had about half the signal it normally does and I was able to use it to marginally navigate. Being unfamiliar with this area and possibly a different avionics configuration I feel my flight could have possibly ended as controlled flight into terrain.
ASRS:1808709.s: During initial climb at 1,000 ft, the pilot's Garmin GTN635 lost terrain awareness due to GPS jamming in White Sands restricted area 5107B. Albuquerque Center placed the pilot on an IFR flight plan after the pilot reported an inability to maintain terrain clearance, noting a potential controlled flight into terrain risk.

ASRS:1808729.n: This was purely human error. I flew previously at this location several times, and obtained the proper LAANC (Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability) authorization via AIRMAP. On this date I was too wrapped up in the ground control logistics, and neglected to file the flight with AIRMAP. Going forward, I will be using a checklist which does include filing the flight and obtaining proper authorization. Note that this flight took place with three visual observers, and we had clear line-of-sight visibility of the UAV at all times. The flight occurred around a [processing plant], and I had full permission from the plant supervisor to fly there.
ASRS:1808729.s: The pilot admitted to human error by neglecting to file the UAV flight with AIRMAP despite having prior experience and ground permission. The flight proceeded with three visual observers and clear line-of-sight, but the pilot plans to implement a checklist to ensure proper authorization in the future.

ASRS:1808732.n: I called the [Radar Controller] for a briefing. During the briefing Aircraft X was given an approach clearance for the ILS XX [at] ZZZ. The [Radar Controller] indicated it would be a missed approach by point at a flight plan on file departing ZZZ. When he asked if I had questions at the end of the briefing, I inquired about the ZZZ1 radar outage and made a comment about its implications. We were now on the same page. The missed approach on the ILS goes to 4000 ft. We had traffic at 5000 ft. looking for a visual approach to ZZZ2. The [Radar Controller] said they would vector the ILS traffic on the missed approach. VFR conditions prevailed at ZZZ. Aircraft X checked in on the missed approach and mode C indicated 1000 ft. Radar was not lost during the approach. The [Radar Controller] immediately vectored the aircraft to a 040 heading. We commonly utilize vectors below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) at ZZZ, but this is not available when the ZZZ1 radar is out of service. In this case, both the [Radar Controller] and [Radar Assist] didn't catch the error in a timely manner. I noticed the error occurred when I called ZZZ3 Approach to [request] the aircraft direct ZZZZZ and climbing to 4000 ft. I immediately told the [Radar Controller] after. We commonly use vectors below the MIA and know the implications of ZZZ1 radar outage. Many use a visual memory aid by marking a cross over the radar station when its inoperative. The outage window on the EDST (Enroute Decision Support Tool) and radar screen are suppressed during normal operations. Outages like VORs and RADAR are easily missed or disregarded. Perhaps better memory aids could be used.
ASRS:1808732.s: A Radar Controller vectored Aircraft X below the Minimum IFR Altitude during a missed approach despite a known ZZZ1 radar outage, an error missed by both the Controller and Radar Assist. The reporter identified the conflict when requesting a climb to 4000 ft, attributing the oversight to suppressed outage alerts and inadequate memory aids.

ASRS:1808816.n: I have written the main cabin door on this airplane up four times. The Flight Attendant can't open it with anywhere close to normal force. I had the First Officer and Flight Attendant film the force required to open the door and they couldn't do it. It only opened after I put IMMENSE force on the handle. My hunch the entire time has been that the door gets stuck once we pressurize to high altitude cabin differential of around 7.5 PSID. This is a safety hazard because the door is the primary exit in the event of an emergency. Of the four times this door was forced open after it was written up, two of the write-ups were done with our own aircraft maintenance personnel on board and two I personally forced the door open with almost all of my strength and leverage.The airplane should be ferry flown to a maintenance base and undergo flight testing to determine what is causing the main cabin door to jam itself shut after flight.
ASRS:1808816.s: A pilot reported that the main cabin door required immense force to open after pressurization to a 7.5 PSID differential, despite four previous write-ups. The pilot identified this as a safety hazard and recommended ferrying the aircraft for flight testing to determine the cause of the jamming.

ASRS:1808874.n: Yesterday we were flying ZZZ1-ZZZ. I was Pilot Flying. The flight was smooth and VFR going into ZZZ. ZZZ was landing Runway XX. The aircraft was downwind and I was at speed 230 and asked for flaps 1, speed 190. Once the flaps started coming out we noticed a light vibration which was consistent. Like driving down a bumpy road. The vibration continued until the gear came out and we slowed to 150. The rest of the landing I did not notice the vibration continue on landing. We landed, exited the runway and parked. Our Maintenance person went outside to do an inspection of the airplane and see if he could find the cause of vibration. The pilot monitoring and me also went out to see if we noticed anything unusual. Extended the flaps and the spoilers checking everything. Maintenance did not see an issue. The second flight going from ZZZ-ZZZ2 I was pilot monitoring. After lift off we noticed the same vibration very quickly. We retracted the gear and flaps on schedule. Then the PF (Pilot Flying) leveled off at 3,000 feet. We still had the same vibration and decided to return to ZZZ. Not exceeding 210 knots. The weather was still VFR and we landed Runway XX. We did not [request priority with ATC]. Once parked, our Maintenance person started a full inspection of the airplane. Into the inspection the elevator trim on the left of the tail was different than on the right. The Captain went into the cockpit and moved the flight controls up and down and the left trim tab was not moving the same as the right side. Maintenance personnel went up and inspected the trim tab on the left and found the control rod was not connected and it moved freely. Making a strange sound. Shortly after this we were told to head to the hotel so Maintenance could work on the issue. The aircraft recently sustained substantial damage in ZZZ3. The aircraft tail was damaged. I believe the two are connected. We came back and landed in ZZZ, very quick flight.
ASRS:1808874.s: Pilots reported a consistent vibration during flap extension on two flights, which led to a return to ZZZ. Maintenance found the left elevator trim control rod disconnected, likely due to prior tail damage sustained in ZZZ3.
